en: From the *Shimoyanlun Tongxuan Chao*, citing the Imperial Preface composed by Emperor Wen Tianyou:

"I have heard that when the Tathāgata inaugurated his destiny, he manifested the four wisdoms to spread his sublime luster; when the holy teachings discourse on the profound, they respond to the three vehicles."
Since the compilation of the teachings began and their dissemination continued, who but sages and worthies could have provided such enlightenment?

Thus, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa was precisely that person. Having long since realized the fruit of the ten bodies while manifesting as dwelling in the causal stage of the eighth bhūmi, he sought to refute heterodox schools and perpetuate the True Dharma.
He composed one hundred treatises to explain ten billion sūtras, or—
Its titles are established through elegant phrasing, and its headings encompass profound meanings; thus, it may truly be called the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*.

Its language is concise yet profound, and its principles are comprehensive and penetrating. It gathers the essence of the five divisions [of the Mahāyāna] and opens up the hidden depths of the two gates;
it is indeed a sacred scripture of this age. Next, there was a Bodhisattva named Nāgārjuna, who, wishing to repay his teacher’s kindness, extensively...
He proclaimed the intent of the treatise and composed a commentary in ten fascicles that circulated in the world;

its meaning was brilliant and radiant, like the three luminaries adorning the heavens, visible to all as they behold their splendor. Its words were vast and profound, like the four oceans encompassing the earth, whose shores and limits cannot be measured.
Subsequently, those such as Ratnavarman and others translated it previously, while Fazang and Wŏnhyo [further elucidated it].
The Master annotated this at the end; its fortunes have risen and fallen across several dynasties.
In the intervals of my governance, I have applied myself to the study of Buddhist scriptures, and my interest in this treatise has been particularly keen as I have sought out its profound mysteries.

Now, the śramaṇa Zhifu of Chongxian Temple on Mount Dongshan—who has inherited the virtue of the Vulture Peak and whose reputation is as vast as a soaring phoenix—declares that this text is uniquely excellent, encompassing the subtle essence of all teachings.
The essential core of the true vehicle lies in its proclamation and requires supportive exposition;

therefore, having investigated the origins and examined the fundamentals while extensively gathering the refined meanings, I have compiled this *Shi-moheyan-lun-chao* (Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śāstra) in four fascicles.

Now, having edited the chapters for presentation and desiring to carve them into printing blocks for wide dissemination, I have reverently poured forth my earnest intentions, wishing to provide a preface. Having graciously granted my request, I shall briefly record the reasons herein.
I have thus used the two characters "Tongxuan" (Penetrating the Profundity) as the title.
This concludes the first fascicle of the *Shi mahuoyan lun tongxuan chao* (Explanatory Notes on the Penetrating Profundity of the Mahayana-samparigraha-śāstra).
The Imperial Preface concludes the explanation of the title;
here begins Volume Two,
the Explanation of the Section on True Suchness (Tathatā).
Volume Three.
Having explained that there is no difference in their essential nature,
[the discussion continues] in Volume Four.
The Explanation of the Essential Nature, Characteristics, and Functions, down to the end:
The Table of Contents for the *Tongxuan Chao* (Commentary on the Profound Mystery) of the *Sheluo Mahāyāna-śāstra*. End.
*Sheluo Mahāyāna-śāstra Tongxuan Chao*, Fascicle One.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìfú, a recipient of the purple robe and Grand Master of Compassionate Conduct Tongyuán, who holds the rank of Chónglù Dàfū and serves as Minister of Works (Sītu) at Mount Yímǔlí in the Great Liao.
A Separate Clarification of the Title, Opening with Two General Gates: 1. The Governing Framework of the Textual Composition; 2. The Detailed Outline for the Elaboration of Meaning.
In the opening passage, there are three sections. The first character belongs precisely to the *Nāga-śāstra*, which is the teaching that expresses [the meaning];

this is because the subsequent text states, "I proclaim the original text as an explanation. Thus, it also encompasses the *Aśva-śāstra*. Next, the subsequent text states, "Now I compose this treatise to re-explain the Mahāyāna";
therefore, the following three characters belong precisely to the *Aśva-śāstra*, which is the dharma expressed [by the teaching]. Below...
However, since the main text itself is called *Mahāyāna*, and because this is the title of the treatise (*śāstra*) being expounded here, one might ask:
why does it not correspond to what is explained in the Buddha’s sūtras? To answer: while such a claim may hold true in general terms, it is not so when applied to the specific text.

This is because, in comparison with the commentary (*vyākhyā*), the Buddha’s sūtras are remote from the main text; therefore, they do not correspond. This is based on the fact that the word "commentary" (*vyākhyā*) properly refers to the concluding portion of the text. If...
Furthermore, this also applies to the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*). The word "latter" (*paścāt*) applies to both treatises;

below, it designates the title of the root text as the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* and also designates the commentary text as a "treatise. Therefore, the question is asked: if these five characters belong entirely to the root treatise, how can they serve as the name for the commentary (*vyākhyā-śāstra*)?
The answer is: the latter part follows the former entirely through a possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*). This is as follows:
Because the title *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna) belongs to the preceding section on the text, the following section concerns the exposition of its meaning.

Regarding the initial explanation, "commentary" (*śāstra*) carries the sense of dissolving and elucidating; that is, it refers to opening up, explaining, and expounding the distinct names and meanings of the Mahāyāna Dharma so as to give rise to faith, and because it can dissolve and disperse the minds of sentient beings' doubts, it is called a "commentary. Therefore...

The following verse states: "In order to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments (the three characters 'this below' correspond in meaning to the 'delusions' above), so that they may give rise to correct faith in the Mahāyāna and ensure that the Buddha-seed is not severed."
Next, regarding "Mahāyāna" (摩訶衍): this is the translated name for "Mahāyāna" (大乘) found in the original title.

While there are differences in the phonetic transcriptions between the languages of the East and the West, the names and their meanings are fundamentally identical without discrepancy. "Mahā" (大) takes the essence as its designation and inclusion as its meaning;

"Yāna" (乘) is a term based on metaphor, referring to the function of transport and carrying as its practice. Because the metaphor and the practice are raised together, it is called "Mahāyāna. This, then, is...
This precisely corresponds to the two kinds of "dharmas entered" (*praveśya-dharma*) explained in the present treatise;

when combined with the remaining fifteen, these constitute the sixteen "dharmas entered," which, together with non-dual Mahāyāna, total seventeen when properly integrated. Therefore, the subsequent explanation states that there are "dharmas capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in Mahāyāna.
Here, "dharmas" refers to the sixteen kinds of dharmas that serve as the gates of entry, which are capable of giving rise [to such faith].

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is the characteristic of the gate-dharma and its activity; the Mahāyāna consists of the sixteen dharmas of entry as well as the non-dual essence of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, among the names of the gate-dharmas listed below in various treatises, only those that are "dharmas of entry" bear the name "Mahāyāna";

it is not the case that the "means of entry" (the practitioner) is so named. For example, as in the phrase "the single essence, the single mind, the Mahāyāna"—this is precisely the name of the dharma—and likewise "single essence, single... [mind].
Regarding the "Gate of Mind" (which is the name of this gate), among the ten distinct names for each of the gates and their respective dharmas, only the eighth dharma is named the *Mahāyāna-gate*.
This specific name does not exist [in other contexts]; rather, as stated previously, when one says "the eighth," it refers to the meaning of *mahāyāna*.

Throughout the preceding and succeeding sections of this treatise, where the gates and their dharmas are contrasted and analyzed, there is not a single word of explicit textual evidence stating that the name of the gate through which one enters is "Maha."

Question: If it is as you say, would the *Hāyāna* (Mahāyāna) not then fail to be the Great Vehicle? Answer: If one considers it according to the permanent teaching (*nitya-śāsana*) and its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it may be called the Great Vehicle.
However, in the present treatise, since the gates of the Dharma are distinguished, it is not termed the Great Vehicle.

This is because the Dharma is of a single flavor (*eka-rasa*) without many distinctions; therefore, only the general name "Mahāyāna" is established, just as the title "King" is used for the sovereign within the main hall.
The marks (lakṣaṇa) should not lack four distinct names simply because they are called "kings," for since the gates [of their qualities] possess many distinctions,
different names are established to provisionally manifest that single flavor (ekarasa) into which they enter; furthermore, according to the differences in the gates through which they enter,

they are distinguished— just as the four wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron differ in direction to signify the differences in the kings' names, such that one is called a "Golden Wheel" (Cakravartin) or a "Silver Wheel."

"Equality" (samam) means that from antiquity until now, no country has had two sovereigns; observing which wheel [of authority] is appropriate, one accordingly bestows a name upon them—this is the meaning of the metaphor.
One should reflect on the principle according to the Dharma; thus, the text below states: "The names of the dharmas entered therein are established either based on the dharma that enters.
This is precisely that meaning. To summarize this intent: the Buddhas desire to cause all sentient beings to enter [the path].
The Mahāyāna takes this very state as its ultimate point of return;
however, because sentient beings are unable to enter directly by transcending language, it provisionally relies upon that nameless dharma to provisionally designate many distinct gates of entry.
Only then do sentient beings awaken and enter through these gates, just as different paths lead to the same destination. Thus, the second treatise explains the passage concerning the eleventh mind.
The *Cittadharmasūtra* cited therein states: "The mental factors (*cittadharma*) are not produced by a single cause, yet because they are unitary, they are conventionally designated as 'one.
The mental factors are not produced by all causes, yet because they are manifold, they are conventionally designated as 'all. Furthermore, the "Section on Comprehensiveness and Establishment" states:
"Within each of the many and the one consciousnesses, there are various capacities that can produce all manner of names; yet it is only..."
"A single consciousness never has any other dharmas [beside itself]. Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* states: "Because it can function as the name and meaning for its own dharma.
Based on this explicit text, we know that the name and meaning, which serve as the gateways, are the supported (the dependent), while the substantial entity is the support (the basis).

Therefore, only that which is entered [the support] receives the general name, whereas those which serve as the gates of entry each receive their own distinct names, such as the eleven categories of form (*rūpa*).

If one does not differentiate between the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), the general name "form" (*rūpa*) is established for all of them, just as the general term "Mahāyāna" is applied without differentiating its specific categories.

However, if one does differentiate between the faculties and their objects, only that which is seen by the eye is independently designated by the name "form," while the others do not receive this title; thus, each is established with its own distinct name.

This is like the case of the "gateways" (*mukha*): only the phenomena that enter through them are independently given the general name "gateways," whereas the others do not bear this designation and instead have their own individual names.
If this is so, why does the subsequent text speak of thirty-two kinds of profound, peaceful chariots? The answer is:

that passage merely explains the single character "vehicle" (*yāna*) within the root treatise; it is not a comprehensive exposition of the meaning of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

According to the original title, it should have been titled *An Explanation of the Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna*; however, since the meaning is sufficient in this abbreviated version, there is no need to state it explicitly.
"Arising faith" means that, upon the single-flavored essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are provisional designations and meanings established as gateways for entry;
because within these gateways there exists the functional activity capable of initiating faith, although this is not explicitly stated in the text, it exists in meaning.
Otherwise, how could it be called an "explanation"? Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "That which can give rise to the root of faith is the gateway-dharma."

The characteristics of the activity of practice (*karmakriyā*) are precisely the arising of faith; this belongs solely to the agentive function of initiating action and does not belong to the faith that is initiated.

However, if one follows the subsequent explanation in the text regarding the determination of faith, the progress of the mind, the roots of goodness, and the methods for cultivating practices, these may also be understood as belonging to the category of that which is initiated.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna is taken as the central tenet (*siddhānta*), as it is what this treatise most highly esteems.
Therefore, the opening statement says: "Now, in composing this treatise, I shall re-explain the Mahāyāna. One might ask: "Is this not the common tenet (*sāmānya-siddhānta*) of the Ten Treatises?
The answer is: while the name is common, the meaning is specific; for each school establishes its own particular object of exposition (*abhidheya*).

Furthermore, the nine other treatises each designate their own titles as their "tenets" (*siddhānta*), as most teachings take their titles as their defining tenets. Thus, these are distinct tenets, and there should be no doubt regarding this.

"Lan" (entry) refers to causing [beings] to enter by means of generating faith; that is, it is the intent of this treatise to explain the distinctions in names and meanings within the primary school [of Yogācāra] in order to lead them toward the single flavor of Mahāyāna.
Therefore, in the subsequent explanation of "generating correct faith in Mahāyāna," there are four gates, all of which state:
"to cause [them] to enter the profound, correct path of Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the title of the section states: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the missing portion of the original text.*

This is because one is able to rely upon and enter the gate of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the ancient masters said: "That which is esteemed in speech is called the thesis (*siddhānta*);
that to which the thesis returns is called the goal (*yukti*).

This is what is meant. Later, those who engage in debate discuss and evaluate; "discussion" refers to the provisional establishment of proponent and opponent, their mutual exchange, and their critical examination and measurement of the correct [view].
Because it is based on principle, it is called a "treatise" (śāstra); therefore, it is titled the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "I pay homage," these two verses proceed through successive causes and consist of three sections: first, the characteristics of the subject and object of veneration;
second, the sentiment of that veneration; and third, the cause of that sentiment.

Regarding the "gate of the *tán* (storehouse) separated by a wall," the *Shengfajì* (Record of the Holy Dharma) states that it is a designation for entering the gate of the *yìrúizàng* (wishing-jewel treasury), and that those in the stage of "heading toward" (*xiàngwǒ*) are also designated as entering the gate of the *yìrúizàng*.
These two gates correspond respectively to the metaphors for the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

This is explained in the *Longming Púsà Xīndì Pǐn Lùn* (Treatise on the Bodhisattva Longming’s Chapter on the Ground of the Mind). Its intended meaning is as follows: according to the present sutra, the treasury [is the ground].

Passing through the two gates, inner and outer: when one sees through the outer gate, it is like entering the stage of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) where the realization has not yet reached its ultimate;
if one opens the inner gate and personally attains clear understanding, it is like entering True Suchness (*tathatā*), where one finally exhausts the subtle and wondrous.

This is because, according to the five teachings, those preceding are shallow and provisional, while those succeeding are deep and real. Regarding the phrase "partially repaying the Master’s kindness," it is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

A verse from a cited sutra says: "Even if one were to carry [the scriptures] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and use one's body as a seat throughout the three thousandfold world-system, yet if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there is ultimately no way to repay their kindness.

Only by upholding and maintaining the treasury of the True Dharma, proclaiming its teachings and principles to all beings, and practicing for even a single thought-moment to accord with Suchness, is one truly repaying the Tathāgata."

Regarding the question of what distinguishes the two meanings—the verse and the prose commentary—following this inquiry: the answer is that the verse clarifies the sense of paying homage, while the prose commentary clarifies the purpose for composing the treatise;
thus, the two are not the same. In some instances, where the prose is also said to express the purpose of composition, this is done with respect to opening a sub-section (*khaṇḍa*).
If viewed in connection with the main text, it belongs entirely to the sense of paying homage. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these various passages.

Regarding the phrase "The treatise says, etc.," this refers to the reasons for composing the treatise, which apply to both masters. First, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is explained by masters such as Sthiramati that the reasons for the Master of the Root Verses (*mūlakāra*) composing the treatise are presented here in the same manner as in that work;
thus, this commentary recounts the original [reasons]. If one asks: "Since those verses in that [work] are incomplete, they must be supplemented;

but since these original reasons are already complete here, why trouble yourself to recount them again? The answer is as stated in the *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith): "It is like... [as follows].

The ten reasons for its composition are manifold and cannot be standardized by a single rule. In the commentaries on various chapters of the Buddha’s sutras, the causes and conditions are frequently recounted;
now, this Master’s own account is likewise so. If one considers it in relation to the Buddha’s sutras and the root treatises (*mūla-śāstra*), it is called a "re-commentary" (*vṛtti*);

if one considers it in relation to the original text, it is called a "commentary" (*bhāṣya*). Thus it is said to be a "re-commentary. Regarding the phrase "to manifest equality," etc., of these eight lines in this section, the first line establishes the definitive determination.

What is clarified here is as follows: the next two [sections] concern the inconceivable merit of the fruits; the following two concern the inferior practice of the causes; the next one correctly clarifies ignorance and darkness;

and the final two clarify the process of dispelling and sweeping away through contrast. This text encompasses two meanings: first, that the essence of the *shengmie men* (the gate of arising and ceasing) is itself *nirvāṇa*, and its ultimate limit is *bodhi*;

this also extends to both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). "Ultimate limit" (*qiong*) carries the sense of thorough investigation and penetration, which pertains to function (*yong*). Thus, it is as follows:
Next, these are the six virtues of the essence and function of the principle and wisdom of the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

The second phrase [indicates that] because the three stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) have not yet given rise to noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), they cannot personally attain it; the third phrase [indicates that] because those of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) have not yet given rise to firm faith, they cannot possess deep conviction;

the fourth phrase, "obscure" (*mo*) and so forth, refers to the characteristic of non-comprehension. As the treatise explains regarding the obstruction of wisdom: "Because its nature is obscure and dark."
Furthermore, Sengzhao’s commentary states that it is not clear.
"Kui" (窺) refers to looking with the eyes.
"Contemplation" refers to the mind's observation; because neither [of these two] can be attained, it is described thus. These two apply to both gates:

their essence is solely *tathatā* (suchness), while their ultimate nature is solely birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha*). Therefore, the subsequent section on the gates of identity and difference states: "Suchness is the essence and nature, while birth-and-death constitutes the characteristics and functions."

Because that which has not yet attained correct realization belongs exclusively to the gate of reality (*tattva-mukha*), the main text states: "Because the realm free from conceptual thought corresponds only to direct realization.

Because that which has not yet emerged from erroneous practice belongs exclusively to the gate of birth (*utpāda-mukha*), the commentary states: "Erroneous practices that are not the Path are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
All delusive defilements are termed "erroneous conduct," which even Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment cannot fathom; this is like viewing the moon through a fine silk gauze.

Furthermore, all eight phrases apply to both gates: those whose essence belongs to the "essence-as-true" (tǐzhēn) can also accord with and enter [the gate], and those who exhaustively investigate the "phenomena-as-true" (xiàngzhēn) can likewise accord with and enter it.

Regarding the "principle that is expressed" (*so-ch'üan li*), "expressed" (*ch'üan*) means "concluded" or "revealed. Here, we take the sense of "revealing," meaning that one reveals the dharma to be entered by relying solely upon the gateway;
thus, the subsequent passage states, "skillfully entering into the principle that is expressed"—this is precisely what is meant.
Regarding the term "nurturing" (*tingdu*), the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states it means "to nourish and raise.
As for the statement that "one divides [the merit] into small portions to repay the great kindness of the Teacher," the *Clear and Cool Commentary* (*Qingliang shu*) says:

"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, from the moment they first resolve their minds, universally take all sentient beings as their object" (the sub-commentary explains: "The Buddha possesses ten kinds of kindness; the first is the kindness of the universal benefit of the initial resolve"). This refers to the "kindness of difficult practices and asceticism" (the second is the kindness of difficult practices and asceticism).

Just as a compassionate mother swallows the bitter and spits out the sweet—giving away her head, eyes, marrow, and brain; her kingdom, city, wife, and children; cutting her own body to provide lamps for a starving tigress; scattering her bones at the City of Fragrance (Gandhavatī); and casting away her body on the Snowy Peaks (Himālaya)—all such deeds are performed solely for the sake of sentient beings.

She disregards her own person, acting with single-minded devotion for others, never for even a single thought of herself. Just as a compassionate mother does not hesitate to sacrifice herself so long as her child is happy, the Sūtra says:

"The meritorious practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva are neither for themselves nor for others, but because they benefit sentient beings with a mind of supreme wisdom, they dedicate [the merit] toward this end. Fourth is the grace of manifesting forms within the six realms of existence (*ṣad-gati*). This refers to the grace of having already...

Having realized the Path to Cessation (*nirodha-mārga*), he ought to enjoy the bliss of unconditioned tranquility (*asaṃskṛta-śānti-sukha*), yet he manifests forms within the six realms and enters the three miserable destinies (*tri-durgati*) to redeem all sentient beings with his own body.

[5. Following Sentient Beings] (The fifth [aspect] is following sentient beings. As explained above regarding the "horizontal" pervasion of the six realms, here we focus on not abandoning them for long kalpas. Just as a child sees its father, he regards them as a father alone, lacking any thought of seeking personal liberation. The Tathāgata follows them, fully employing the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*) to follow, pursue, and rescue them.

Seeing them commit evil is like having one's limbs severed. (The sixth [aspect] is the profound and heavy grace of Great Compassion. Thus, the youth Sudhana said to the deity Viśvāmitrā: "Noble One, it is as if there were a person who has only one... )

Out of the utmost depth of his paternal affection, when he suddenly saw [his son] having his limbs severed by others, his heart was so acutely pained that he could not find peace; yet, until he attained Perfect Enlightenment, he concealed his supreme virtues (7. Concealing the Superior and Manifesting the Inferior).

His grace—manifested as marks as numerous as the atoms within a Lotus Treasury World, whose inexhaustible merit would be difficult even for a drop of the ocean to describe—was entirely hidden and not displayed. He spoke only of having cultivated the thirty-two marks over a hundred kalpas, and of severing the afflictions of the views and the path of cultivation through thirty-four moments of mind.

When the fivefold Dharma-body was first perfected beneath the Bodhi tree, he appeared like an old bhikṣu, equal to the five arhats. Thus, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, he cast off his precious robes and put on tattered, filthy garments, taking up a dustpan to go to where his son was, appearing in the guise of a poor man.

8. Inducing, gathering, and rescuing through the Dharma they delight in: By concealing the ultimate and manifesting expedient means, his grace fulfills the One Vehicle. He conceals [the ultimate] and does not preach it, instead teaching and transforming sentient beings with the minor Dharmas of the Three Vehicles and the human-and-deva realms.

These two aforementioned graces are as described in the "Incense Accumulation" chapter of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where the bodhisattvas who come from other lands praise him, saying: "Just as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings by means of the Dharmas they delight in, which are like those of the poor.

9. Seeing their arrogance and self-indulgence, he manifests the trace of nirvāṇa: Because of the grace of concealing the Real and manifesting the Responsive, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "If one were to see that the Tathāgata always abides and never perishes, one would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence."

Yet, harboring weariness and indolence, [the World-Honored One] retained his remaining merit and teachings to rescue those in peril and suffering. (10. Compassionate Remembrance of Infinite Kindness: This refers to how the World-Honored One, sharing the human lifespan, should have lived for one hundred years, yet retained twenty years of that life’s merit to protect his disciples in the final Dharma age.

Regarding the "retention of the teachings," this refers to the Three Pitakas and the Eight Collections which extensively benefit sentient beings; by practicing according to them, all may attain Buddhahood. Even images, stupas, and temples—should they be established and worshipped a thousand times—even a single relic will cause one to be reborn in heaven.

The above constitutes the initial listing of the ten kinds of kindness, followed by the conclusion that these kindnesses are profound. It says: From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, from birth until death, all...

Regarding the Buddha’s protection, how can such benevolent virtue ever be repaid? (As later cited from the sutras as proof: "When one receives even a small kindness from another, one should always harbor the intent to repay it greatly" (*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*);
"Those who do not recognize kindness often meet with untimely death" (*Avataṃsaka Sūtra*). Because these ten aspects are fully present, it is called "great kindness."
"Because it refutes [other] tenets" means that this treatise venerates and upholds the profound sūtras of a hundred billion volumes. "Aśaya" (āśaya) here is translated as "intention" (yìlè);
it refers to those sentient beings with whom one has a karmic connection in the future who, upon merely seeing the text of the treatise, [attain realization].

It is as if one were personally facing [the Master] to deeply receive the essential tenets, gaining faith, understanding, and realization; this is the intention behind Qingliang’s composition of the sub-commentary (*chao*), which says:
"I hope that in distant lands and for all eternity, everyone shall be as if meeting him face-to-face. This is also what may be called composing a treatise in accordance with the command.
Regarding the *Mahāra-śāstra* and others, the Venerable Master [Amoghavajra] recorded their translations in sequence as follows:

the *Cintāmaṇi-śāstra*, the *Vistara-saṃgraha-śāstra*, the *Mūla-vistara-vyākhyā-śāstra*, the *Kuṭila-mūla-vyākhyā-śāstra*, the *Vistara-kuṭila-vyākhyā-śāstra*, the *Ekāntārtha-śāstra*, the *Siddhānta-vistara-saṃgraha-śāstra*, the *Miśraka-śāstra*, the *Akṣaracakra-śāstra*, the *Mantra-śāstra*, and the *Gāthā-nirmita-śāstra*.
(In the upper and lower volumes of this translation, the terminology largely follows that of the Venerable Master.)
The ninety-nine types of literary works refer to the ninety sections, which are subsumed within the nine kinds of *puṣpikā* (ornamental) treatises.
Their names are listed in full in the *Āryadharmasaṃgraha*: first, the *Svarapuṣpikā*; second, the *Arthavanapuṣpikā*;
third, the *Bimbapuṣpikā*; fourth, the *Ekākṣarapuṣpikā*; fifth, the *Vicitrakathāpuṣpikā*; sixth, the *Ākhyānapuṣpikā*.

Regarding the phrase "distinct causes and effects" and so forth, these three phrases explain one another in succession from beginning to end; furthermore, they may also be understood individually.

When the Buddha speaks of those who propound heterodox doctrines, he refers to such persons.
That which is inexpressible, pure retribution, and empty is precisely not what others say; "empty" here signifies non-existence (*abhāva*). It should be [understood] thus.
Knowing that those with false views deny the pure karmic fruits and retributions of the five vehicles, the Buddha directly refutes them;
subsequently, he raises the existence [of such fruits] to dismantle their claim of non-existence. Since pure retribution exists, how can one say it does not exist?
Regarding the eight kinds of *miśraka-piṭaka* (mixed collections), the *Yilin* (Forest of Meanings) states that the Vātsīputrīya school also speaks of four collections:

If two expositions (*vyākaraṇa*) or three expositions are combined, it is called the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*. Furthermore, according to the tradition of the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, there are four:

Because it is capable of discerning the unerring meaning, these two—when categorized according to both the primary and the secondary—are as follows:

among the three baskets (*piṭaka*), the Sūtra primarily elucidates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Vinaya elucidates ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the Śāstra elucidates wisdom (*prajñā*), while each also secondarily encompasses all three. "To uphold" (*dhāraṇī*) means to "hold," which is synonymous with "to gather" (*saṃgraha*), and thus carries the meaning of "repository" (*piṭaka*). therefore, these [sūtras] are here attributed solely to the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) as their explained content, and thus are said to concern only practice. This is not fixed, as it depends on the specific context.
The meaning of this is that each of the aforementioned collections (*piṭaka*) is capable of encompassing the respective practices (*caryā*) it explains, as appropriate.

*Sūtra* is translated here as "Scripture" (*qi jing*). First, regarding its general characteristics, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "From 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning, up to 'rejoicing and putting it into practice' at the end, all are *sūtra*.

*Vyākaraṇa* (prediction) is translated as "bestowal of prophecy," which has two aspects: first, predicting the causes and effects of a disciple’s death and rebirth; second, [predicting their future attainment].
When a Bodhisattva is about to accomplish the work of a Buddha, there are *gāthās*—here translated as "recitation"—which refers to verses that arise independently (*udāna*).

First, they are for the sake of making them easy to recite and retain; second, they are for the sake of those who delight in verse. There are also *udānas*—here translated as "spontaneous utterances"—first, so that [the audience] may know how to request the Dharma;
second, so that those to be converted may develop a sense of profound reverence. One should mindfully contemplate the Buddha’s compassion, for he is a friend who does not need to be asked.
*Nidāna* is translated here as "Origination. It is taught for two reasons: first, because the Dharma is weighty and must be explained only upon request;

second, so that one may understand the beginning and end of a matter. *Avadāna* is translated here as "Parable. It is taught for two reasons: first, to enable those of deep wisdom to comprehend the truth;
second, to lead those of shallow understanding toward faith by means of analogies suited to their dispositions. *Itivṛttaka* is translated here as...
*Itivṛttaka* (Past Events) refers to two types: first, those recounting the past deeds of the Buddha; second, those recounting the past deeds of his disciples.
*Jātaka* (Birth Stories) means "former births," referring to accounts of bodies previously received; these are of two types: first, those concerning the Tathāgata;

second, those concerning others. *Vaipulya* means "Extensive" (or "Broad and Great"): first, because it brings great benefit and happiness; second, because it extensively expounds the True Dharma. *Adbhutadharma* means "Marvelous Teachings."
First, because their virtuous deeds are extraordinary; second, because the essence of the Dharma is rare and marvelous. *Upadeśa* is translated here as "discourse" (*lunyi*).

First, it is called a discourse because its principles are profound and vast; second, it is called a discourse because its meaning is not fully understood. The above is from the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*, where each [term] possesses two meanings.
"Vasayigano" means "extremely subtle and minute," like a speck of dust on a rabbit's fur;
yet it can contain the colors of light and darkness filling the ten directions. This treatise is also like this.
The term *pattra* followed by *ceti* is translated here as "wind-thread" (*vāyu-sūtra*), which refers to the thread of a dragon;
that is to say, within the tongue of a dragon king there is a single wind-thread that is extremely subtle, like a hair, yet it can emit and absorb various dense clouds filling the ten directions.
This treatise is likewise so.
Regarding the phrase "listing the headings of the sutras" and so forth: this means that the essential quintessence of various sutras has been gathered to form the grand framework of this treatise.

Although it originally had no title, the title was directly adopted to correspond with its subject matter, as in the case of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, where it is generally referred to as the *Mahāyāna-sūtra*.
Within that sutra, it is stated thus, and even Ārya Aśvaghoṣa Bodhisattva correctly subsumed those passages [into this work].
Therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna comprises many texts in total.
There is no contradiction or error, for although [the teachings] appear differently across the six periods, their fundamental essence is one; how could there be any contradiction?
It is not that this single treatise was composed by penetrating all six periods; rather, the intent of the preceding question was to address the matter from the perspective of six individuals.
Because each individual [teacher] has a distinct identity, doubt arises as to which of the six [masters] the present Aśvaghoṣa might be.

The intent of the current response is that the six persons are one in essence, so there is no contradiction whatsoever; this is merely a question regarding the person, not the time. Therefore, the preceding heading states:
"Next, the author of the treatise," and it further asks only: "The present Master Aśvaghoṣa," concluding later with: "The person has already been explained."

Because they are distinct characteristics, this refers only to the person. If we discuss it in terms of time, it should be as stated in the *Āryadharma*: "When did this Bodhisattva compose these treatises?
During which of the six periods? (This question concerns the heterodox theories. It is said that he composed them during his one hundred-odd years of life:
first, the *Catuḥratnakoṭi-śāstra*; second, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; third, the *Gūḍhārtha-śāstra*; fourth, the *Mūlapravṛtti-śāstra*; and fifth, the *Viśuddhi-śāstra*."
Furthermore, in the *Śāstra* and other texts, Xianshou cites a sūtra stating that the treatise was composed six hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing];

additionally, the lower vow says, "After the Master’s parinirvāṇa, I shall compose this śāstra. This, therefore, establishes a specific time rather than being general for all six periods. Regarding the phrase "the great compassion is fulfilled" and so forth, this verse consists of ten lines divided into three sections. The first three lines praise his name and virtues:

the first line states his name, while the latter two lines manifest the perfection of his virtues—"fulfilled" meaning accomplished or complete. The next three lines express grief upon hearing of his passing.
The final four lines employ the superior to illustrate the inferior.
"‘Do not slight [others],’ etc., refers to what the ancients said: ‘A great elephant does not travel on the path of a rabbit; one of great ambition is not constrained by minor details.

Regarding the phrase "I take refuge," the Venerable Xianshou (*Bhadramukha*) states that this treatise consists of three parts: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.

the three verses at the beginning of the treatise consisting of the homage, the request for grace, and the invocation of assistance constitute the basis upon which the author relies to initiate his practice. Second, from the treatise...
It is said: First, for the sake of sentient beings, he expounds the practice of the Dharma-gift of the Master of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra*;

Second, regarding the Dharma itself, there are three [parts]: first, the section on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

To establish the two [sections] for the sake of the faculties: first, the Section on Establishing the Meaning; second, the Section on the Correct Bestowal of Understanding and Practice;

third, the Section on Exhortation to Practice, which cites the benefits and exhorts practice so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed. Thus, these three sections together constitute the practice by which sentient beings enter the Dharma.

Among the three preceding gates, the first is distinguished individually, while the latter two are explained in combination. Therefore, all five sections constitute the main body of the treatise, as they are all part of the discourse.

What has been explained constitutes the *abhidharma* (the orthodox teaching), while the various verses at the very end that exhort one to uphold [the teaching] and generate aspirations constitute the *pravartana* (the dissemination).

The structure of this treatise is entirely identical to the three previous sections above; its thematic force regarding "hearing" follows exactly that of Xianshou, so I shall not elaborate further.

Now, by taking the majority of these elements, they also constitute the introduction (*nidāna*).
"Returning in accord" (kuei-ch'i) means, in intent, to be in harmony with and to turn toward the Buddha; this is the explanation of the meaning of "returning" mentioned above.

Regarding "welcoming and praising," the manuscript from Qianshan has the character "looking up" (yang), meaning to reverently offer oneself in devoted reliance; it was erroneously written as "welcoming" (ying).

Regarding the "four abodes of sudden and gradual," these refer to the first four among the five. The *Yìfēnzhì* (Limitation of Meaning) states: "In the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), the severance of delusions does not distinguish between the discriminative and the innate;

rather, they are suppressed during the stage of Worthiness (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), while their seeds are severed at the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are discarded at the Tenth Ground.

Thus, because the seeds are severed all at once upon the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), it is said that "the four abodes are suddenly severed," as is explained below in the section on Initial Enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).

Regarding the classification of the nine fetters (*navasaṃyojana*), the original manuscript of the *Jianyuan* (見元) contains the character "cáo" (草), which resembles the clerical-style character for "bàn" (絆). Upon examination, it was found to be a transcription error. Question:

What is the difference between "most" (*zuì*) and "superior" (*shèng*)? Answer: [The former] refers to being far removed from the faults of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*), while [the latter] refers to the accomplishment of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*).
Because of these virtues, the two are not the same. What are the four wisdoms? There are two meanings:

first, the four wisdoms according to the common teaching (*samāna-śāsana*), which means that the present practice and teaching are the same as those of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*). They are:

(1) the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), (2) the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), (3) the Wisdom of Accomplishing Activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and (4) the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). Second, the four awakenings according to the distinct teaching (*viśeṣa-śāsana*). These are: [the four bodies of awakening].

Because it differs from the Initial Teaching (śikṣā), there are four categories: first, the intrinsically pure and impure original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*); second, the purely clean original enlightenment; third, the initially awakened state that is both defiled and pure;

and fourth, the initially awakened state that is purely clean. Here, "purely clean" signifies the meaning of immutability (*avikāra*), while "defiled and pure" signifies the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya-anuvidhāna*).
This assignment is made by way of manifest characteristics; let us examine this in detail.
Regarding the "four unhindered [knowledges]" and so forth, there are two gates. First, the general meaning is clarified: "Dharma" refers to the essence of the Dharma as a single flavor;
"Artha" refers to the principles and meanings upon that essence, as stated in the subsequent text: "one Dharma and two meanings," and so on.

Regarding the distinction between the two types, *vākya* (words) and *gīti* (music): the general exposition of the meaning of the Dharma is called *vākya*, while the detailed and specific exposition is called *gīti*.
Furthermore, *vākya* predominantly expounds the Dharma, whereas *gīti* predominantly expounds the meaning; thus, there is a distinction between the two. (From the *Qingliang shu*).
Hereafter, the text will be explained in detail.

What is called "true reality" (*dharmatā*) is precisely the dharma entered through the single mind and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Aspect" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to its essential nature (*svabhāva*);

it is not restricted solely to its attributes (*dharma*), but rather it is that which is neither attribute nor nature, yet is capable of being both the nature and the aspect of the substantial reality of all phenomena.
Therefore, the *Zizti jing* (Self-Body Sūtra) states: "The Great Divine King encompasses all things," and this is not of the mundane world.

Worldly dharmas (which are not characteristics) and supramundane dharmas (which are not natures)—what is called their "shared yet distinct characteristics" refers precisely to the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*) as the gateway for entering the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.

"Characteristics" refers to their conceptual meanings and is not restricted solely to phenomena; it thus encompasses both the two truths and the three greatnesses. This concludes the general explanation of the distinctions.
Regarding the opening [of the gates]: one interpretation states that "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) refers to the fundamental [principle], while "commonality" and so forth refer to the second meaning.
Because these three great aspects are mutually distinct, they are called "differentiation"; because the myriad phenomena are identical therein, they are called "common.

Another interpretation holds that true reality is the dharma that is entered, while commonality and so forth are the gates by which one enters; since these gates pervade all phenomena, they are termed "meanings."

Because their characteristics are each distinct, they are called "shared differentiated characteristics," as explained below in the treatise. The three kinds of great meanings all penetrate both gates.

Next, regarding "true nature" (*dharmatā*), this refers to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*); because the principle is solely its own self-nature, it is called "nature. This is the essence of phenomena (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding "the characteristic of arising and ceasing," this refers to the gate of arising and ceasing; thus, these meanings and characteristics are not merely matters of phenomena.

Therefore, regarding the "distinctive characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇa*), it is said that they are intended to demonstrate that while there is only one True Suchness (*tathatā*), the names, marks, meanings, and functions of all phenomena are each distinct and their operations differ.
Thus far, these have been opened up to form two pairs of dharma-meanings: (1) the mutual distinction between the single reality and its various appearances;
and (2) the distinction between the true nature and the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Hereafter, these shall be combined into a single pair of dharma-meanings, namely: Reality.
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "reality-nature" (*dharmatā*) are both alternative names for ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and both belong to phenomena (*dharma*).

That is to say, "characteristics" refers to the *tathatā* of those characteristics, while "nature" refers to the *tathatā* of their essence. "Commonly differentiated characteristics" and "characteristics of arising and ceasing" are both alternative names for conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and both belong to meanings (*artha*).

Among these, "commonly differentiated characteristics" refers to such terms as suffering (*duḥkha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while [the latter] refers to form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.

Because it concerns names and the characteristics of arising and ceasing, Guifeng said: "In the Nature School (Xingzong), the single true nature is taken as the 'Dharma,' while the various distinctions such as emptiness and existence are taken as the 'meaning.
Thus, a sutra says: 'The immeasurable meanings arise from a single dharma. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* says: 'The Dharma is the knowledge of self-nature;
the meaning is the knowledge of arising and ceasing; the Dharma is the knowledge of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); the meaning is..."
Knowing the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in this way, the tenfold explanation of the meaning of the two types of unimpededness— of phenomena (dharma) and meaning (artha)—
is stated thus because phenomena constitute the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and meaning constitutes the conventional truth.

Regarding the phrase "the essence encompasses," the intended meaning is as follows: in the original text, the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the preceding verse’s phrase "throughout the ten directions.
Alternatively, it may refer to the Master of the Treatise himself. Thus, the bodily forms of the sentient beings of those ten directions are of the same essence as my own;
this reveals that our essence is identical. This is as Master Sengzhao said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; all things share the same body as I. This is precisely what is meant.
The meaning of "comprehensively reaching" (*zǒngdá*) is that one penetrates and attains the Dharma and the Sangha; this is precisely the explanation of the term "and" (*jí*) and its significance.
This, then, is the intended sense [of the preceding passage]. Therefore, the subsequent verse says: "Comprehensively returning to the ten directions," and so forth.
Regarding all phenomena, the equality of their essential nature and the ultimate transcendence of attachment—
these three phrases explain, respectively, the meaning of the three characters "intrinsic nature," "true suchness," and "reality."

Regarding the question, "Why is it necessary to encompass all [beings] as equal? the intended meaning of the inquiry is: why must one share the same essence (*samatā*) with sentient beings for the mark of reverence to be established?
Would it not be established even if one were alone? The answer intends to say: if there is no shared essence, the Buddhas do not rejoice in prostrations and so forth.
It is necessary to have a shared essence because when self and other are non-dual, one accords with the Buddha-mind; therefore, the Buddha rejoices. This is the reality.
This teaching of the Mahāyāna is the discourse on the ultimate meaning that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

and third, the object that opens the gate. First, the Mahāyāna; second, the thousand meanings produced [therefrom] as the gate;
and third, the section on explanation, which is like the object that opens the gate. This may also be divided into an analogy.
Regarding the two categories of "seeing and hearing" the jewels: if explained according to the general teaching, there are two types—great dragons and ordinary dragons.
Those with sharp faculties see them directly without the gates being opened, just as one who does not need an explanation understands immediately.

Those with dull faculties must have the gates opened before they can see, just as one requires an explanation to know. These two cases are different; however, even when considering the moment of entry, both likewise depend upon the gates.
Entering [the state] by means of the Great Dragon involves entering directly without opening the door; those of sharp faculties do not require conceptual understanding to realize it.

Entering by means of the various dragons involves entering only after the door is opened; those of dull faculties must first have understanding before they can realize it. Thus, there are two differences.
As for the aforementioned "entering without opening," this refers merely to passing through the doorway; this is based on the first of the three meanings mentioned above.
Regarding the meaning, one should reflect upon the latter two meanings by analogy. The above constitutes the general presentation of the main intent.

As for the phrase "the manifestation of the tongue’s majesty" and so forth, the meaning is that the tongue is extended to manifest majesty, not competing [with others], but rather entering toward and proceeding to the gateway.

"Opening and penetrating" (*kaītō*) means the sense of entering. The intent is that although one opens wide and penetrates to enter and proceed toward the gate, one does not approach or go directly through the *gedan* (intermediate) gate.
"Proceeding toward" is like the outer treasury gate today; the *gedan* is like the inner treasury gate today;
and the *maṇi* is like the objects within the treasury. Perhaps it is not that one enters the gate competitively, but rather that one opens and penetrates to proceed toward the long [distance].

Reading these words as a continuous phrase constitutes the first interpretation, which relies on Xianshou’s Five Teachings: it holds that the former are provisional while the latter are real, and that one enters from the teaching of arising and ceasing into the teaching of True Suchness.
The subsequent interpretation relies on the Five Teachings and Two Gates established side-by-side;

its doctrinal meaning is explained in the *Fahua* (Lotus Sūtra) Commentary, which states: "One diligently applies effort to augment superior progress. This combines with the preceding passage on the manifestation of the tongue-organ’s majestic power, not competing with other gates; the intended meaning is as follows.
Yet, while one exerts diligent effort in hearing and contemplation, increasing familiarity with them, one applies little effort to the actual cultivation of practice.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like a person drifting on water who, fearing drowning, dies of thirst; likewise, those who do not practice the Dharma through its various gateways. (The commentary on this passage explains:

The first metaphor illustrates the fault of following the literal meaning of the text. It means that the waves of the textual meanings drift away one's mind and deliberations; though fearing drowning, one lacks the eyes of practice and thus cuts off one's own progress.)
Because their wisdom-life is thus [lacking], they die of thirst. Just as a dragon, though greedily displaying its majestic spiritual power, does not enter its own gate;
this combines the meaning of the latter two lines with the preceding "opening up" to explain the intent of the final two lines. Here, "fang" (方) means "to compare.

It signifies that although one may cultivate a faith toward the arising and ceasing [of phenomena] that is as firm and sharp as a vajra, one has not yet cultivated firm faith in *tathatā* (suchness); it is like a dragon that, despite moving forward, [does not reach its destination].
The preceding section, up to "not entering the partitioned dāna," corresponds to the above [section] on "entering the real from the provisional" (*t'ong-kwon ir-sok*).

Alternatively, if one reads it continuously with the preceding "vajra-like" (*konggang*) passage, it means that what has been long practiced through hearing and reflection has become ingrained in one's nature and is difficult to destroy.

Thus, the first three lines may all refer to cultivation within the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing (*myeongwol mun*), while the fourth line refers exclusively to cultivation within the gate of True Suchness (*jinnyo mun*); however, this latter line may also be understood as applying to both.
Regarding these two gates, this corresponds to the meaning of standing upright together above. Alternatively, "fang" (方) may mean "dharma" (法); dharma here means "principle" (則).

This merely serves to generally harmonize with the preceding metaphors; it is not necessary for every phrase to correspond exactly. The previous metaphor was complete, whereas this one is partial. The general intent is to say:
if one applies oneself exclusively to drilling and gazing at the tips of the fingers during hearing and reflection, one will not [attain] the actual reality of the original moon.
Regarding the cultivation of firm faith,
the statement that one "attains the treasure-trove of the Dharma-realm" and so forth means that if one does not rely upon the gates to cultivate sublime practices,
one will ultimately not achieve the treasure-trove of the Mahāyāna into which one enters; how then could one attain the fruit and realize the profound principle?

Regarding the phrase "retreating further and further," this meaning applies doubly to both the heterodox and the non-dual groups. Below, the eighth cause refers exclusively to those fixed in heterodoxy (*mithyā-niyata*).

As for the term *dhāraṇī*, the *Yuánjué shū* (Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) translates it as "Gathering Bestowal" (*jíshī*), meaning that many meanings are gathered and condensed within a few words.
"Because of bestowing [the teaching] upon others and reciting and upholding it.
Regarding the "one hundred and sixty," this refers only to the sixteen [categories] entered therein;
since each of these is further divided into ten according to that treatise, they constitute one hundred and sixty dharmas.
Within these eight causal conditions, there are two main points for each: first, the capacity of the recipient to be transformed as the occasion for arousal;

second, the teaching to be aroused by the transformer. Therefore, the preceding text states: "In order to manifest the sublime medicine of superior flavor, it must arise through the appearance of the obstacles of illness to be countered;
the teaching to be transformed is necessarily initiated by the faculties of the recipient who is to be cured. Prior to the illness, [the teaching] does not exist.
Since the medicinal [teachings] do not exist prior to the capacity [of the recipient], the capacity and the faculties alone constitute the substance of the causal conditions (*pratyaya*).
However, according to the exegetical tradition, these are generally divided into three categories: the second is the faculty of the one to be converted (*vineya*) which gives rise [to understanding];

the first and the third are both the teachings given rise to by the converter (*viniyaka*). Thus, since these are distinguished in relation to the teaching, one should not claim that the teaching itself is also a condition.
In its substance, the original text is mutually deficient in certain respects: for instance, in the third, fourth, and eighth [sections], the first [point] of that [text] is missing;

yet it is implicitly contained within the character "wei" (to act/serve) according to its meaning. Similarly, in the fifth, seventh, and eighth [sections], the second [point] of that [text] is also implicitly contained therein.

Regarding the general characteristic of causes and conditions (*nidāna*): the first two characters belong to the sense organs (*indriya*), while the latter two characters refer to phenomena (*dharma*).
This is the general characteristic of causes and conditions, which is precisely the teaching that performs transformation.

Regarding the "eight kinds of fundamental totality" and so forth, this refers to what is stated in the following passage: "Within the fundamental Mahāyāna, eight kinds are opened [this is the totality];
within each of the three great meanings of the single-mind dharma-realm, two kinds are opened [this is the specific characteristics]," and so on.

As for the character *lanxiu* (藍修), in some manuscript versions it is the character *jian* (監); it is like the phrase "a minister supervised the compilation of the national history," where the master here [supervises].
Because he edited the Buddhist scriptures, the *Shengcao ji* (Collection of Sacred Ancestors) and the *Zhi* (Record) state that the Venerable Master supervised the editing at Gaozuo Temple;
this serves as excellent evidence.
As for the phrase "gathering ten billion [monks]" and so forth, it refers to the difference between the broad-minded respect shown toward superiors and narrow-minded pretension.
The three grades of the ten faiths and the three grades of the ten understandings constitute the "arousing of the mind through the perfection of faith.
The three grades of the ten practices and the three grades of the ten dedications constitute the "arousing of the mind through understanding and practice."

Regarding the three grades of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this refers to the "realized awakening mind" (*sākṣātkāra-citta*). That is to say, because these ten stages collectively comprise three grades, they correspond to the three grades of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Alternatively, within each stage, the minds of entering, abiding, and emerging may be divided into three grades, as explained above in the one hundred and twenty types.
The three grades for each of the three levels of the "worthy ones" (*tri-kṣānti*) are to be understood according to these two explanations.
Why are the three parts opened and explained separately? If one follows this text, it is not only the *Vyavasthāna-vibhāga* (Section on Establishing the Meaning) that is explained;
the latter two parts are also explained therein. If that were not the case, why would it be said that "all the teachings of the Dharma are exhausted within the *Vyavasthāna-vibhāga*"?

For the latter two parts would then not be the dharmas established by the *Vyavasthāna-vibhāga*. Rather, it is simply that the former part explains them individually, while the latter [parts] explain them collectively.
This is because it provides a general explanation.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) regarding the practice of the Dharma," the word "Dharma" in the preceding verse applies to both of these meanings:

namely, that each individual cause clarifies the method of practice that gradually increases, and since there is no superiority or inferiority among them, the sequential nature of the eight dharmas must be so.
Regarding the phrase "excluding [those such as] the *chanda*," the following section provides a detailed explanation of each difficulty in turn, showing their progressive superiority.

These four types—lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), attachment to self (*ātmasakti*), fear of suffering (*duḥkhabhīrutva*), and renunciation (*parityāga*)—are precisely the four obstacles described in the subsequent text. The first is named identically; the second is the obstacle of the ordinary person’s attachment to self;
the third is the obstacle of the *śrāvaka*’s fear of suffering; and the fourth is the obstacle of the *pratyekabuddha*’s renunciation of compassion. This means that one abides by means of deep faith.
Because the arising of principle, practice, and dedication can sever the four kinds of obstacles respectively.

Regarding the phrase "the fundamental diagram and sound are one" (*ben tu yin yi yan*), the interpretation follows the sequence of the meaning: it means that the perfect [nature] and the sounds are without before or after, being manifested simultaneously.
If there were before and after, the fault would be as clearly revealed in the commentary; furthermore, all sounds are of one time.
The "vast and profound Dharma of the Tathāgata" is identical to the final verse, which states:

"The Buddhas" (referring here to the Tathāgata, who belongs to the non-dual Mahāyāna), "profound" (referring here to the profound Dharma, which belongs to the dharma entered), and "vast" (the two texts are identical; these belong to the gate of entry).

Regarding the phrase "such as light" (*ābhāsa*), according to the *Chao* (specifically the *Qixinlun Chao*, Part II, where the citations are identical), there are three objections to this interpretation: first, the objection that "light" and "great awakening" (*mahābodhi*) and so forth are redundant and disordered;
second, the objection that the phrase "now creating" and so forth conversely results in the fault of seeking profit;

and third, the objection that the phrase "ultimate" and so forth implies the fault of the Buddha’s teachings being incomplete. However, of these three objections, the former two are contrary to the latter one.
If one attempts to avoid the former two [criticisms], one inevitably incurs the latter one; if one seeks to escape the latter one, one returns to fall within the scope of the former two.
Furthermore, these former two mutually reinforce one another in turn.
That which is ultimately worthy of honor and trust refers to a sutra that is venerable and credible, and which ultimately exhausts and reaches the end of all principles.
Furthermore, "one flavor" (*ekarasa*) refers to being like the saltiness of seawater; "equality" (*samatā*) refers to being like space.

Regarding "transference," this is based on the arising and ceasing of a single period (*ekakalpa*); when designated according to moments (*kṣaṇa*), it is called a "sūtra" or a "treatise" (*śāstra*). As for "pen" (*han*), it refers to the brushstrokes [of writing].
When inscribed upon inked bamboo or wooden tablets, the sūtra scrolls and treatise scrolls are of a single flavor and are not differentiated;

they are explained as equal and not distinct. This analysis of their distinctions means that because these are precisely the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they possess only a single flavor and are equal.
*Gāthā-sūtra-piṭaka* is translated as "The Collection of Extensive and Abridged Sūtras.
*Vyākhyā-sūtra-piṭaka* is translated as "The Collection of Extensive and Abridged Commentaries.

Regarding the term "perfect" (*yuan*), as explained in the commentary on the "Perfect Sound": "Each and every vocal sound pervades and reaches the limits of the realm of sentient beings"—this explains "perfection."

Furthermore, their phonetic qualities are never confused or disordered (this explains the sounds). Since the subsequent text states that one must possess both of these [qualities] together to attain understanding, it is clear that these two are inseparable.
Next, from "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) onwards, it clarifies only the different types; next, from "Or perhaps" (*atha vā*) onwards, it clarifies only equal understanding (*samatā-vijñapti*).
*Saṃnāha* is translated here as "vow" (*praṇidhāna*). *Āśaya* is translated here as "intention" (*abhiprāya*).

Regarding the phrase "the seeds of the four assemblies of noble ones" (*catur-ārya-varga-bīja*), "seed" refers to the cause; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because they can produce the various noble ones, they are called 'noble seeds' (*ārya-vaṃśa*).
The essence of these four noble seeds consists of: first, the noble seed of contentment with clothing; second, the noble seed of contentment with food and drink; [and so forth].

The noble lineage of contentment with robes, the noble lineage of contentment with alms-food, the noble lineage of contentment with bedding and seats, and the fourth, the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation—this refers to delighting in the abandonment of afflictions and delighting in the cultivation of the noble path.
Question: Since the fourth noble lineage is not itself contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*), how can it also have non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essential nature?
Answer: Because it is able to relinquish sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), this fourth [lineage] is likewise characterized by non-attachment.

Question: Why are these four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) necessary? Answer: The first three noble lineages serve as the requisites for the development of the path, while the final noble lineage serves as the activity of the path.

Since the disciples have abandoned their worldly requisites and worldly activities, the World-Honored One, out of compassion, established these requisites and activities for the path so that practitioners may attain liberation before long.
Question: For what reason are these two matters established in this way? Answer: The verse states that it is for the purpose of counteracting the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
First, craving for clothing; second, craving for food and drink; third, craving for bedding and seats; and fourth, craving for existence and non-existence (*bhava-vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).
Because they counteract these four cravings, the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are established; thus they are called the "four noble lineages."
Regarding the statement that "the eight kinds are opened within the fundamental Mahāyāna": this refers to what the original text calls "Mahāyāna," which is the general term.
This [first category] refers specifically to the dharmas entered upon in the first stage.

Next, regarding the statement that "the single-mind dharma-realm and the three great meanings each have two kinds," this likewise refers to what the original text calls "there are two kinds of teachings. What are these two? First, the Dharma; second, [the teaching].
This is the meaning. This refers only to the first stage, the gate of being able to enter.
As for the question "Why is it called 'able to enter' and so forth?"—it means that immediately below "one mind" is precisely the gate of the first stage, the ability to enter.
Because the four names were not previously indicated above the "dharmas," they are now specifically indicated above this "gate. This is because previously, at the level of *mahā*...
Within the *Mahāyāna* [treatise], eight types are opened up because they are not included within the four; therefore, there are no names for those four.

Alternatively, "each" refers to the subsequent repetitions which serve as the gates for entry—meaning that since the four names were already indicated within the preceding dharmas, they are not indicated again within these current gates.
The use of the word "alternatively" (*vā*) indicates an indefinite sense, meaning that what was previously...

The one mind, the three greats, and the four superior [stages] open up to form eight "objects of entry" (*praveśa-dharma*). Now, because these four superior stages further open up to form eight "gateways of entry" (*praveśa-mukha*), the term "or" (*vā*) is established.
This means that they either act as gateways or function as dharmas; thus, it is said "gateways" to distinguish them from the preceding dharmas.
Consequently, this applies only to the opening of the first layer of gates, while the second layer of gates and the dharmas [are treated differently].

It is only because [the teaching] is opened within the first "heavy gate" (*zhòngmén*) that it is as stated in the formal proposition: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings," and so forth.
This cites the opening of the first heavy gate as the "Dharma" for the subsequent heavy gates. Furthermore, the text below states:

"The gate of the single essence and single mind," and "The third, the gate of the self-same single mind," and so on. This is truly because, when viewed from the perspective of the single mind (*yīxīn*), it possesses [all attributes] such as the single essence (*yītǐ*). It is not [that the single mind is merely one among them].

The two meanings of "neither identical nor different" arise from this single mind. Because the mind is not different from that [dharma], it belongs to the first gate; because it is not identical, it belongs to the latter gate.
Furthermore, these dharmas are unified as one and subsequently differentiated into two. In relation to the initial dharma, they likewise possess these two meanings:
by virtue of the meaning of non-difference, they are of a single flavor without distinction; by virtue of the meaning of non-identity, they are divided.
Because there are two layers, the following verse says: "Equal and equal, they are one and all without distinction, for each encompasses all phenomena;

yet, in the end, they are never confused. The commentary states: The first three phrases prove that [the gate and the phenomena] are not different, while the final phrase proves that they are not one.
Question: This only clarifies that the gate and the phenomena are not one when viewed from the perspective of the first layer alone. How is this so?
Question: How is it proven that the preceding [levels] look toward the subsequent dharmas? Answer: By opening the first set of gates as the subsequent set of dharmas;
because the first gates of the subsequent dharmas do not possess two distinct entities, they are thus proven. Question:

Since the sixteen entries are already opened upon the foundation of the one mind, the three greatnesses, and the five dharmas, why does the text above state that the Mahāyāna is "one"? Answer: The text above discusses the reality (tattva).
In substance, it is taught that there is only one; however, based on the subsequent text within the "Establishment of the Meaning" (*siddhānta-vibhāga*), it is gradually explained as being fivefold.
Furthermore, if it were stated below that the Mahāyāna consists of eight types in total, one might then speak of nine dharmas by opening up [the previous categories].

Now, since it is simply stated that there are two kinds—namely, the Dharma (*dharma*) and its meaning (*artha*), and this meaning is further divided into three—[the fivefold classification is established].

There are five [aspects], yet their substance is one; when discussed in terms of their meanings, they are many, as in the analogy of reflecting pearls—the principle of the Dharma is easily understood by comparison.
That which is "fundamental Mahāyāna" is, in its totality, exclusively subsumed under the first category.

What is entered therein is precisely what was mentioned above as the eight kinds opened within the fundamental Mahāyāna. However, this term "totality" (zǒng) ranges from the narrow to the broad, comprehensively encompassing all three.

Regarding the meaning: first, if restricted to the text, it refers exclusively to what is entered in the first section; this very passage is that [text]. Second, if considered according to the meaning, it also applies to what is entered in the subsequent sections;
as indicated in sequence, it says: "That which is called 'looking up' and 'looking down'"; thus, one should descend and say:
"Based on this mind, the general meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed," and so forth. Third, if considered according to the meaning alone, it is restricted exclusively to the thirty-third [section].
Because it is that which can express [the meaning], in the tenth treatise’s commentary on the root verse, I shall now explain it in summary according to my capacity, saying:
"The gate of the phonetic characteristics of words can only be expressed by means of the 'total' (samasta) syllable. That text points to this very "total" syllable herein;

furthermore, by looking back at what precedes and forward at what follows, it stands to reason that while the established definition applies universally as a whole, a single portion should be stated as *ma*.
Regarding the term *mahāyāna*, it is generally explained as being of two kinds; otherwise, how could it serve as a comprehensive designation?

It is not that the five characters of *mahāyāna* are taken collectively as the expressive words (*vācaka*). In the section below on the "gate of the characteristics of the expressive words," the text explicitly states that the single character "total" (*tong*) is what is meant.

Therefore, among the three meanings mentioned above, the first two constitute the total essence (*tongti*), which is the name for the "total"; this is precisely the expressed meaning (*vācya*), as clarified in the treatise.
The text states: "Regarding the fundamental universal gate of entry, because it is the universal totality within the two locations, the latter one is collectively termed 'universal.
Since this is the expressive [medium], the treatise says: 'I shall now, according to my capacity, explain the gate of the phonetic characteristics of the expressive syllables.
As for the statement that there are two kinds, up to the second point regarding their meaning, this pertains exclusively to the first level of the primary [classification]."
"Entering" refers to what was stated above regarding the single-mind dharma-realm (*ekacitta-dharmadhātu*) and the three great meanings (*trīṇi mahārthāni*), each having two aspects.
Because the faculties of those initially targeted [by this teaching] are sharp, there is no need for extensive explanation, as they have already developed understanding.

As for why Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna did not provide a separate commentary, it is because this has already been clarified prior to the text and within the "entry"; thus, he considered that people would easily comprehend it and did not elaborate further.
Having completed the introduction, the first layer has been explained; next, the subsequent layer is indicated. That which is called "Dharma" refers to the mind of sentient beings.
Below this, the gates of the first layer are extensively expounded to serve as the Dharma-gates for the subsequent layer.

Because there are two [layers], dull-witted sentient beings cannot comprehend the initial brief explanation; therefore, the first gate is restated and extensively analyzed, resulting in what is known as the two layers. This indeed has its reason.
Because this is not like ordinary cases where two layers are distinguished, the first part provides a brief indication followed by an extensive explanation;
thus, the first layer is the general and brief exposition, while the second layer is the specific and extensive exposition—this constitutes their difference.

This mind (is the single dharma into which all mental factors enter) is the manifestation of the characteristic of True Suchness (the gate), and it is the essence of Mahāyāna (the dharma)—thus it is the gate. The following commentary explains this as follows:
