The character for "turning back" (*huí*) is positioned above the character for "ma" (*mó*). The text states: "This immediately reveals the single essence of Mahāyāna. The next [character] follows this same principle;

"turning back" makes it easy to understand that this is the mind (which is the dharma entered by the universal one-mind). "Arising and ceasing through causes and conditions" is the gate; "being able to reveal Mahāyāna" is the dharma;
"because of its own essence, characteristics, and function" is the gate. First is the greatness of essence (*tǐ-dà*), which refers to the section ending with "therefore" (the gate).
"Regarding 'all dharmas' (this refers to following conditions, and is also the mundane world); 'the equality of true thusness' (this refers to non-alteration, and is also the supramundane world);
'because there is no increase or decrease' (this applies to both of the above). Second is the greatness of characteristics (the dharma), which refers to the three phrases beginning with 'equality.

Regarding 'Tathāgatagarbha' (this refers to following conditions, and is also the mundane world); regarding 'endowed with immeasurable natures' (this refers to non-alteration, and is also the supramundane world), it is because of its merits."

[The term] "this" (refers to the two preceding categories). Third is the Greatness of Function (*yòngdà*; the Dharma), which refers to the section from "down to" [the phrase] "therefore" [in the text]. This means that in the *zhēnrú* (True Suchness) gate, the rational nature is immutable, being exclusively good and exclusively pure;

therefore, it is designated by the name "good. In the *shēngmiè* (Arising and Ceasing) gate, however, truth and falsehood are blended, and it encompasses both the defiled and the pure; thus, "good" is not established there.
Therefore, Qingliang’s commentary on the passage "without limit in its coming and going" states that this is the Greatness of Function, as it penetrates through the defiled.

Jing asked: "How can one contradict the usage of Xianshou [Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra] while asserting that it is solely 'good'? He replied: "That [text] distinguishes between what is concordant and discordant; its nature is good.

Now, based on the arising of the nature through both essence and function as function, the perspectives differ according to their respective meanings. Thus, there is no contradiction between the two masters (since the former was intended for the two gates explained in the present treatise)."

First, regarding "that which is entered" and so forth: the two preceding sections, when compared with one another, can form five pairs—namely, subject and object, root and branch, general and specific, essence and characteristic.

Within these pairs of subject and object, because they rely on the distinctions of "entering," if one truly understands the meaning of these five pairs, more than half the purpose of this entire treatise will have been grasped through reflection.
First, "equality" refers to the single essence (which serves as the second gate below); "one mind" refers to the principle (which serves as the second dharma below);

"three self-" refers to the gate below; "one mind" refers to the dharma below; "immeasurable" up to "not diminishing" refers to the gate below; "greatness of essence" refers to the dharma below; "quiescence" up to "not ceasing" refers to the gate below;

"greatness of essence" refers to the dharma below; "as" up to "virtue" refers to the gate below; "greatness of characteristics" refers to the dharma below; "endowed with" up to "virtue" refers to the gate below; [and] "characteristics."
The Great [Lower Dharma] can produce the fruit of reaching [the goal] (lower gate); the Great [Lower Dharma] can produce the cause and fruit of reaching the wholesome (lower gate).

Regarding the Great [Lower Dharma], the preceding commentary takes one type from the first section of the initial gate and treats it as the dharma of the subsequent gate. Therefore, [it is so stated].

Regarding the "eight kinds of body-dharmas" (*kāya-dharma*) and so forth: according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, "body" (*kāya*) is explained through three meanings—substance (*tattva*), basis (*āśraya*), and collection (*rāśi*).
Since the present context concerns the first two [meanings], it is called "body. The text cited in the root treatise must be from this very sutra;

therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa correctly subsumes that passage. Consequently, the term "Mahāyāna" is used here as a general citation based on its meaning. (This then...)
The headings of the sutra correspond to the framework of the treatise).

Looking upward and downward, what is "overlooking" (lin) should flow down to the subsequent section on the "dharmas entered. Furthermore, beneath the second instance of "Mahāyāna," the character for "general" (zong) should be placed in all cases below it. It should state:
"Based upon this mind, the general meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed. Subsequently, the character "general" (zong) should be added beneath each instance of "Mahāyāna."

Furthermore, because it summarizes the greatness of essence (svabhāva-mahattva), the greatness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-mahattva), and the greatness of function (karitra-mahattva), it says "and" and "reaching down below.
Regarding the term "equal":
this is stated according to the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as meaning "not different," and does not mean that they are definitively one according to the method of affirmation (*vidhi*).
If this meaning were not so, how could each [category] encompass all phenomena without distinction of superiority or inferiority, or breadth and narrowness?
It is clear that this text is based on the principle of non-differentiation; it is based on the principle of non-identity that they do not become confused. As the *Treatise* states:
"These two gateways both comprehensively encompass all phenomena, because these two gateways are not mutually exclusive; that is to say, the phenomena of each gateway are each universal."

Therefore, it is stated twice as "pervasive, pervasive. Its equality and equality are likewise so. Regarding the phrase "concluding its beginning and end," this refers to the character *rán* (然) cited in the *Zhǔnchāo*.

"The assembly" refers to the assembly of the four vehicles; the level tone (*píngshēng*) marks the name, while the departing tone (*qùshēng*) explains the meaning—it does not mean that the preceding title is also the same.

This [term] "sentient being" (*sattva*) is explained according to the standard teaching as follows: because there are numerous births and deaths, and because they are produced by numerous causes and conditions, they are called "sentient beings.
As the treatise below states: "Why are the mental faculty (*manas*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) called 'sentient being'?

Because the mental faculty and the mental consciousness arise from the gathering together of all defilements, they are called 'sentient beings. It cannot be explained using the departing tone (*qùshēng*)."

Regarding the formation of the name based on its meaning, at the time of its establishment, one also calls it *yà* (耶). This dharma derives its name from the gate [of its constituents]; it is merely the mind of sentient beings. Furthermore, the *Yàncào* (演奧鈔) states:

"If one relies on the various teachings, there are five general interpretations: first, 'a collection' (*zòng*, 藏); second, 'the gathering of characteristics' (*xiàngjí*, 相集), referring to the aggregates (*skandha*);

third, 'arising by relying on conditions' (*zhàngyuánérqǐ*, 仗緣而起), referring to birth; fourth, 'the coalescence of the true and the false' (*zhēnwànggòngyù*, 真妄共聚); and fifth, 'not being existent' (*fēiyǒu*, 非有), referring to the collection."

Regarding "semblance-existence" (*yǒu-sì*): it is said that birth depends upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, and there is a mind subject to arising and ceasing. "The three assemblies" refers to the four types of Mahāyāna sentient beings;

"the four types of birth" refers to the four kinds of birth. The first two depend on the Final Teaching (*jiōngjiào*). Fourth, the provisional gathering of all phenomena is called "sentient beings," while the mark of non-arising is called "birth"—this refers to the Sudden Teaching (*dùnjiào*), because sentient beings are identical to the unchanging nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Fifth, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*), "one is many," which is called "assembly" (*zhòng*).
The principle is unimpeded by phenomena, which is called "arising," because a single phenomenon encompasses many phenomena and is vividly manifest.
As for "single substance," it is like a pearl, whose substance consists of lightness and heaviness; therefore, it cannot be analyzed.
Regarding "one characteristic": because it has the characteristic of being like a bright, round pearl, it cannot be separated or dispersed;
yet, although it is a single characteristic, it can be analyzed, for this side does not possess the characteristic of that side.
Regarding the phrase "subsuming the supramundane," the character for "supramundane" (出) appears above the characters for "thousand mountains" (千山) in the original text;
all are treated as the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), etc. The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The two dharmas may constitute the Dharma-realm, or the Dharma-realm may constitute the two dharmas.
This must be due to an incomplete transposition of the text, as it is explained below: "This is the True Suchness-characteristic of the Mind," where it says they are "treated as one."
The phrase "the mind of the dharma-realm, suchness, and so forth" refers to this single dharma-realm mind (the original text has "this mind," which is explained here).
The phrasing [of the Chinese] as "acting as the gate of suchness" and so on is also a result of incomplete rephrasing that does not fully accord with Western (Indian) terminology.

The former [section] involves subsuming the derivative into the fundamental (this accords with the topical outline), while the latter involves the fundamental flowing forth into the derivative (this accords with the subsequent treatise).
Regarding the *Svabhāva-sūtra* and others: it refers to the Great Divine King of the Mind of the Single Dharma-realm, which encompasses all phenomena in two ways:
first, the phenomena of the gate of birth-and-death; second, the phenomena of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Within the first, the gate of birth-and-death, there are two parts.
"All various kinds of ignorance" and so forth refers to the meaning of non-awakening (*a-vibodha*); that is, the first phrase constitutes both the root and the branches.

If one does not realize the subsequent phrase, then the various kinds of pure dharmas belonging to all six types of defiled minds—whether associated or dissociated—are precisely the meaning of "realization. The term "various" (zhongzhong) signifies differentiation;

thus, in the True Suchness Gate (*tathatā-mukha*) as included in the following text, it says only "all" (*sarva*) and not "various. Furthermore, within the latter True Suchness Gate, there are also two [sections]. One.
The four phrases beginning with "All dharmas are utterly pure" constitute the *tathatā* as essence;

therein, the first three correspond to the three virtues of ultimate equality and so forth, while the last one corresponds to the three characteristics of being beyond verbal expression and so forth—hence it is said that "transcending and free from verbal expression" means being free from the two obstacles.
The two phrases beginning with "All dharmas are completely fulfilled" constitute the *tathatā* as characteristic; therein, the first phrase...
The phrase "non-empty suchness" refers to the subsequent term "empty suchness.
Regarding the "Great Universal King," this is the first of the ten alternative names for that which is entered, as listed below; it is also supported by the *Svabhāva-sūtra* as evidence.
The section titled "Fundamental" refers to the dharma that is entered, which is precisely the two characters "mind" (*citta*).
"Subsuming the particulars" refers to the gate of entry; that is to say, it is "subsuming the lower. Question: What constitutes the substance of this sentient being's mind?
Answer: It takes that which is entered as its own substance. If this is so, how can distinct phenomena constitute the substance of the universal mind? Answer:
It is the whole universal that constitutes the particulars, not parts that constitute the particulars. Since the whole constitutes the universal, there is no fault.
Therefore, the preceding text states that this Treasury of the Single Dharma-realm (ekadharma-dhātu-kośa) is omnipresent and perfect throughout those eight locations;

it cannot be divided and cannot be dispersed, being only a single essence and a single characteristic. Thus, one may know that the general and the particular are non-dual, and therefore it can serve as the essence.
One might ask: "Should one not rely on arising and ceasing to realize the single essence of Mahāyāna? It is precisely because...

Because the essence of that which is entered is non-dual, the answer is: based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), one cultivates and realizes only one's own dharma, not the dharmas of others.
This is like relying on the five teachings to realize the same principle; although one relies on a preceding teaching for cultivation, one does not realize the principle of a subsequent teaching.

It is not that the essence of the rational nature (*dharmatā*) is distinct in five ways; rather, it is because there are five types of mind according to the teachings relied upon for cultivation that it is said the essence is the same while the realization differs.

Furthermore, it is like a *maṇi* jewel whose substance is the whole (the mind of sentient beings), which can produce gold as a particular [manifestation] called a "gold jewel" (the One-essence Mahāyāna), and can produce silver as a particular [manifestation] called a "silver jewel" (the Three-natures Mahāyāna). This is just as described above: the whole produces the particulars.

If one is deluded regarding the production of gold and only understands the production of silver, one merely attains the name of a "silver jewel," but does not attain the name of a "gold jewel. This is due to the mind.
The name "delusion" refers to not obtaining [the pearl], yet it is not that the substance of the pearl itself is twofold.

It is like a deluded person who says, "I have already obtained the pearl that rains silver, yet I wish further to obtain that pearl which rains gold," failing to realize that a single pearl emits both.

One should reflect on this according to the Dharma: these distinctions are made by treating the specific and the general as distinct; they are spoken of in terms of "obtaining" and "not obtaining" based on the objective realm and the substance of the Dharma.
One may speak of "other" names based on the delusion or enlightenment of the mind, while "general" and "specific" are explained accordingly; thus, the subsequent passage states:

"The true mind apart from extremes—if viewed from the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), it is like a pearl that is identical to its reflection; if viewed from the gate of birth-and-death (utpāda-nirodha), it is like a pearl that is distinct from its reflection.
This is precisely what is meant.
Regarding the phrase "or from the 'entrance' (mukha) and so forth": the essence of the Dharma is one, yet there are two meanings for its gates.

That is to say, this single Dharma may be designated as the "One-Entity Mahāyāna" when taken from the perspective of its single entity as the gate, or it may be designated as the "Three-Natures Mahāyāna" when taken from the perspective of the three natures themselves as the gate;
therefore, it says "or" and so forth.

The answer is: Regarding the phrase "forming the single dharma-realm" and so forth, it may also be said that "the mind of the single dharma-realm forming the gate of True Suchness" and so on are likewise incomplete due to the elliptical nature of the phrasing (*huíwén*).
This is because the "mind of the single dharma-realm" is respectively the seventh and twelfth names among the ten different names for the lower dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the two verses above, etc.": "The original" refers to the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), specifically the two sections of text beginning with "That which is called the Dharma" up to "supramundane dharmas.
"The verses" refer to the commentary (*vyākhyā-śāstra*), namely the two verses beginning with "The assembly refers to the assembly of the four vehicles, etc.

and "It is this single dharma-realm mind, etc. It is clear that these [verses] flow from the words of the root text; since they are not explicitly stated here, one should apply them by analogy. Do not further assume that these examples differ.
The meaning of the textual exposition is that the one mind is the essence (*tattva*) and the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*) are its significance (*artha*).

Since there is no significance apart from the essence, the former two [the essence and significance] must exist together, just as waves depend upon water and cannot exist apart from it. If we follow this principle, the fundamental dharma entered [into the stage of Bodhisattvahood] is solely the one essence;
otherwise, why would it be necessary for the significance to flow down to this point?

Regarding the statement "the substance is great," etc.: although the three greatnesses directly constitute the Dharma itself, being beyond names and characteristics, they are forcefully described as such [i.e., as the three greatnesses].

This is because the various gateways—such as the truth of all phenomena (*tathatā*), equality, and neither increasing nor decreasing—are established primarily to manifest the Dharma through these gates.
Thus, although the three are distinguished separately, they are of one flavor with the aforementioned mind and do not differ; otherwise, how could this flow down to [the level of] ordinary beings?

This is because the three great dharmas each possess their own distinct substance; since the subsequent mind (*uttara-citta*) is superior, it reveals that the three greats themselves have no separate substance, as the subsequent mind flows from them.
If this is so, how are the two layers distinguished? The answer is: they are provisionally designated according to the faculties of beings and explained through successive unfolding.
That is to say, one directly unfolds the first eight kinds of dharmas entered within the fundamental [stage], and upon these dharmas, one further unfolds...
The initial eight kinds of doors for entry further open up the subsequent eight kinds of dharmas to be entered and the subsequent eight kinds of doors for entry;
these are established through provisional designation as two distinct layers. However, if one examines their actual substance, they are of a single flavor without differentiation.
The Buddha originally intended for sentient beings to awaken to and enter this single-flavored reality, but it is simply because they are unable to leave [delusion] behind.

To speak directly, one proceeds by forcefully explaining the two layers of the transformative teaching—the initial and the final—by means of provisional characteristics. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"I merely use provisional names to guide sentient beings. Furthermore, Qingliang says:

"In order to cause beings to awaken [to the truth], it is like a mani jewel whose inherent nature is luminous and pure, identical to space and of a single color; this color can only be perceived by those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)."

Those who see with the physical eye do not perceive [the pearl] (just as the Mahāyāna of non-duality is the aspect of the fruit, understood only by those who have realized the fruit, while those on the path of cause do not understand it).

Desiring only to enable those with physical eyes to see the substance of the pearl (just as one desires to lead people to awaken to and enter the single-flavored fundamental Dharma), one then uses objects of eight colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—to reflect upon it;
its substance follows these shadows and appears as if there were eight forms (just as one uses the eight provisional gateways, such as the "one substance" and "one mind," to open up that One).
(Taking "taste" as the first, there are eight layers of the dharmas entered. If one with clear vision sees the blue reflection of a pearl, they say it is a blue pearl;

if they see the yellow reflection of a pearl, they say it is a yellow pearl. (Just as those of sharp faculties can enter the eight gates based on the first layer alone and accordingly awaken to and enter the eight dharmas,) yet one with dim sight still cannot see;
therefore, in order to enable them to see, one again reflects upon it using the eight substances of deep blue, yellow, and so forth.

Just as a person of dull faculties cannot understand [the teaching] at the initial stage of the "heavy" [classification], it is subsequently explained again through eight sections—such as the "one essence and three natures"—in a more detailed and extensive manner. One should know that the method of explanation follows this pattern: what was brief at first is later expanded, as illustrated in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning.
Specifically, the deep blue is superimposed upon the shadow of the preceding light blue, and the deep yellow is superimposed upon the shadow of the preceding light yellow.

(As in the detailed explanation of the "one essence," which is opened up based on the preceding initial stage of the "one essence and one mind" section; and as in the detailed explanation of the "three natures," which is opened up based on the preceding initial stage of the "three natures and one mind" section.)

This is as stated in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning": "That which is called 'dharmas' refers to the mind of sentient beings," and so forth. This is because the eyes have varying degrees of clarity;
thus, they are reflected upon through two layers of depth (just as, because the faculties have varying sharpness or dullness, they are applied through two layers of priority).

Although reflected through these two layers, the substance of the *maṇi* jewel remains one (just as although two layers are opened, the essence of the Mahāyāna is fundamentally one). As for those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), within the midst of these variegated reflections, they immediately...

Those who realize that [the colors] are identical to emptiness and are pure color see only the manifestation of pure color with their physical eyes; they do not realize that it is identical to emptiness and pure color.

(If one is already in the state of the fruit, one realizes the aspect of the fruit within the causal stage; if one is at the stage of the cause, one realizes only the causal aspect and does not realize the aspect of the fruit.

Therefore, among the nine different names for what is entered below, the ninth, citing the *Madhyamaka-hṛdaya-śāstra*, says: "The true mind is free from extremes; if True Suchness depends on suchness, it is like a pearl being both different and the same."
If arising and ceasing depend on one another like the pearl and the grass in the "Halls of Many Similes," they are largely the same.

As for the question, "Is there no cause and condition? it means that while in the preceding section on causes and conditions there was no cause capable of giving rise [to anything], here, at the beginning of the text, in the section establishing the thesis, there is instead the non-duality that gives rise [to phenomena]. Since there is a dharma that arises, how can there be no [cause]?
Regarding the cause that brings about [existence], one may first challenge the subsequent existence by means of the prior absence of a cause;

next, one may challenge the subsequent existence by means of the prior absence of a cause. Since there is no cause capable of bringing it forth, how could there be a phenomenon brought forth? Therefore, it is asked:
why must it be established?
The phrase "not established" means that in the section on the establishment of the doctrine (*siddhānta-vibhāga*), it merely presents the meaning;

since the preceding reference to the passages concerning existence and non-existence already clarifies the establishment, it is said to be "not established. This is because, as stated next, it is taught apart from the formal scriptures.
The phrase "able to attain equality with all Buddhas" is spoken from the perspective of the fruit-aspect (*phala-bhāga*). Regarding this, there are two masters.

First, Master Xianshou’s *Fenqi* (Analysis of the Limits) states that the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) has two aspects: first, the fruit-aspect of the ocean of nature (*xinghai guofen*), which is precisely the meaning of the ineffable.
Why? Because it does not correspond to verbal teaching; it is the self-boundary of the ten Buddhas themselves. Thus, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says: "The causal aspect..."
The fruition aspect (*phala-bhāga*) can be described, whereas the causal aspect (*hetu-bhāga*) cannot be so described;

this causal aspect is the realm of Samantabhadra. These two are non-dual, their entire substance encompassing all. This may be understood by reflecting upon water and its waves. The commentary states:

"This is entirely identical to the two names in this treatise: the 'Ocean of the Perfection of Innate Virtues' and the 'Ocean of the Various Causes of Cultivation. (The above constitutes the dual discussion of the preceding and succeeding sections. Now...
Furthermore, first speaking from the perspective of the fruition, non-duality is like this: the great ocean is like the Buddhas, and the myriad rivers are like the [ordinary] beings.
One may only say that the ocean can contain the myriad rivers, but one cannot say that the myriad rivers contain the ocean;

one may only say that the provisional person sinks together with the ocean of fruition, for it is impossible for the real dharma to sink together with the provisional person within the ocean of fruition. Thus, the *Qingliang lüce* says:

Now, regarding the statement that the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*) may be expressed through words when considered in relation to realization and correspondence, all such [expressions] are termed the "causal portion" (*hetu-bhāga*).

This is because the cause can be cultivated and explained, whereas the fruition transcends cultivation and is beyond words. The commentary states: Since the fruits, such as the ten bodies (*daśa-kāya*), are accompanied by verbal expression, they belong entirely to the causal portion.

It is not meant that what is spoken of as fruition immediately belongs to the fruition portion; rather, it must be directly realized and verified to be designated as the fruition portion. Therefore, [it is said to be] "worthy."
The *Shuppin Daishō Han* (Exegesis on the First Chapter) states: "The four dharma-realms and the ten profound gates are all categorized according to the causal division (*inhun*).

These Buddhas belong to the causal division; because the causal division can be subsumed into the ocean of the fruit (*kahai*), it is said that [the practitioner] 'is able to attain' the ocean of the Buddha-fruit.
However, the ocean of the fruit cannot be subsumed into the causal division; therefore, it is said that 'the Buddhas do not attain' it. This is the meaning of cause and effect. If...

According to the intention of the Worthy Head (Bandhuprabha), the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhāga*) is that which is realized by those who rely on others, while the stage of the fruit (*phala-bhāga*) is that which is realized by those who have attained the fruit of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, regarding the limits of these divisions, it is said: "The realm of the ten Buddhas is the realm of Samantabhadra.

According to the intention of Qingliang [Yixing], practicing the cause based on words is called the causal division, while the realization of that which transcends words is called the fruitional division. Thus, the *Lüe-ce* states: "The cause can be cultivated..."

Regarding the statement that "if one speaks of the fruit, cultivation and detachment are lost," these two masters differ slightly in their interpretation. Xianshou says that the term "fruit" is restricted solely to the ultimate stage;
however, he also notes that while the term "fruit" generally applies to the causal stages as well, it is specifically the "benefit of the fruit" that can extend back to the cause.
In this treatise, the teaching that "both are abandoned" is entirely identical to Xianshou’s position. As for the delimitation [of the stages], it is said: "It does not correspond with the teaching."

Therefore, "separation from teaching" (*li-jiao*) refers to the self-boundary of the ten Buddhas; "separation from faculties" (*li-gen*) is likewise [the boundary of the ten Buddhas]. The *Qingliang lüce wen* states: "As for the fruit, cultivation is extinguished.
If it is "separation from words" (*li-yen*), "separation from teaching" (*li-jiao*), and so forth, then how could the profound principle of the original source not be a teaching?

If a teaching must correspond to faculties, how could it be "separated from faculties"? Answer: There are two senses. First, regarding the principle (*li*), it is said that it is not the same as the causal stage (*yin-fen*) which is designated as "faculties."

When there is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) based on a real faculty (*indriya*), it may be called a "real teaching" (*saddharma*). This is like a medicine being given in accordance with a disease, whereby the name "medicine" can be established;
if it were not applied to a disease, it could not receive the name "medicine. It is the same here: other dharmas are established as teachings by being applied to faculties.

Therefore, the treatise says: "Because it conforms to the exposition. That which is non-dual and lacks a faculty is the exclusive domain of the Buddha; since no faculty can be reached by it, it cannot be obtained as a teaching.
It is called "detachment" (*li*) because it refers to names; the meaning is that [the Buddha] is merely designated by means of unreal things. If this is so, why do the two treatises speak [of him]?
The answer is: in the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*), while explaining the "Ten Stages" chapter, the scope of what is permitted to be spoken is stated as follows:
"First, regarding the ocean of fruition, one may provide a general indication to let people know that there is a name which can be spoken of, yet one cannot point to and designate a person."
It may be said that, furthermore, based on a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), it cannot be pointed out or described; thus, it is both "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*) and "expressible.

If there are causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), then the fruit (*phala*) can be conveyed through words, and one enters the profound (*gambhīra*) by means of phenomena. Yet even the cause itself cannot be fully expressed;

one must not adhere rigidly to this interpretation. The commentary states: This is merely based on what is "possible" as a general indication to let people know that [the fruit] exists, and because there are causes and conditions, the fruit [can be indicated].
It may be said that there are two treatises based on discourse, yet ultimately neither possesses ultimate reality, because they are intended for specific faculties.

Second, regarding the teaching: these two are non-dual, and their entire substance encompasses all; this can be understood by reflecting upon them as being like water and its waves. The commentary states:

"This refers to the 'Delineation of Meaning' (Arthaviniścaya), which explains the non-identity and non-difference [of the two]. If one speaks in terms of their non-identity, this treatise is the teaching that is distinct from those faculties."
If one speaks of two theories based on their non-difference (that is, the aforementioned treatise), then within the "Ten Stages" chapter, Qingliang agrees with this;

the above two points are explained according to the underlying reasons for his silence, and thus there is no contradiction, as the perspectives differ in meaning. The general presentation of the main intent is now complete.

Below, we shall address the difficulties by re-explaining the textual meanings in detail. Regarding the second [point], "attainment" (*prāpti*) means the sense of fulfillment or accomplishment. Next, below...
If it were not so, although the text appears below, its meaning ought to reside above; thus, it would fail to be established.
This is precisely what the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dàběn jīng) cited below states: "Because that Perfectly Round Ocean attains the supremacy of all Buddhas, all other Buddhas cannot achieve it;
the Perfectly Round Ocean is superior. This possesses two meanings: first, that it refers solely to the mutual comparison of these two phrases themselves.

The explanation is based on the fact that while the former [the Buddhas] share the same non-extinction, the latter [the Bodhisattvas, etc. do not; therefore, it is said that they can attain and cannot attain [the fruit].

Next, the three [categories] beginning with the Bodhisattvas are also the same as the Buddhas in their non-extinction; however, since the ocean of fruition cannot be the same as the extinction of those three, the second and third [categories] are explained by comparing them against each other in relation to the two preceding phrases.
Furthermore, there are two meanings: first, within this context, the first phrase refers to the ability to attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the latter phrase, because one does not attain [Buddhahood] with respect to all Buddhas, it is said that this non-duality—since it belongs to the category of the fruit (*phala-bhāga*)—is able to attain Buddhahood;
whereas that which is taught as the root [of non-duality], being merely the category of the cause (*hetu-bhāga*), does not attain Buddhahood.

Thus, when comparing the Dharma to the person (*pudgala*), the distinction between attaining and not attaining is clarified; this refers to the non-attainment of the same fruit, not the non-attainment of the same [Dharma].
Question: These two preceding meanings both rely on the perspective of the resultant stage (*phala-bhāga*) to explain the sense of "disappearing" (*naṣṭa*) and "not disappearing" (*anaṣṭa*).
Since their logical force is entirely identical, why are they divided into two distinct categories? Answer:

Has it not already been stated that the first two phrases refer only to themselves, while the latter two phrases are explained in relation to one another? It is precisely because of this slight difference that they are divided into two. II.
Regarding this, because the Buddhas attain [the state] described by the latter phrase, it is contrasted with the Buddhas who have attained what is described by the former phrase.
Since that fundamental [nature] belongs to the causal portion (*hetubhāga*), one relies on words to cultivate the cause and can realize the Buddhas;

thus, as the Buddhas proceed from cause toward fruit through the cultivation of the cause and its realization, it is said to be "attained by the Buddhas. Now, this non-duality is merely the resultant portion (*phalabhāga*); it transcends cultivation and is beyond words.

Because one may cultivate the causes through gradual stages and thereby realize [the fruit], it is said that "all Buddhas attain it. If this were so, would it not follow that the Buddhas lack omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and how then could they teach it?
The answer is: because they have cultivated the causes until they reach the fruit and thus personally realize it for themselves, there is no contradiction.

This, then, is a case of speaking of the fruit by way of its causes; it is not a direct discussion of the fruit itself, nor is it subsumed under the fruit, as if the cause were submerged within the fruit.
If even the cause is difficult to describe, how much more so the ocean of the fruit? And how much more so could one directly discourse upon the fruit itself?
How, then, could one further speak of the Buddha’s universal wisdom and realization? This refers to people looking toward the Dharma and distinguishing between the two—attainment and non-attainment.

These are spoken of in relation to whether they are obtained through the cultivation of causes or not obtained through the cultivation of causes. The subsequent three types of persons should also be understood according to this principle.
"Entirely.
Regarding the phrase "that which all Buddhas have attained as equal," this is explained from the perspective of the causal stage (*hetu-bhāga*) and possesses two meanings.

First, it is said that [the equality] exists solely between the two phrases themselves; the intended meaning is that these are the accomplishments resulting from the causes cultivated by the Buddha. Next, [it refers to] the Bodhisattvas and so forth.

Third, because practicing the causal conduct can also lead to accomplishment, it is said that "it is likewise so. As for those eight fundamental dharmas, they are not causal practices that can be cultivated;
therefore, they cannot bring about the accomplishment of those persons, which is why it is said, "one does not obtain [them] from the Buddhas.
This interpretation is the same as for the three preceding persons. Second, the two phrases regarding "in relation to others" are spoken in mutual comparison; their meaning is entirely identical.
The preceding passage was easy to understand.

"Without its own" (*wu you qi si*)—here "own" (*si*) means "self" (*zi*). The above is the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*); from here below is the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
Why is it stated separately "up to the Mahāyāna"? This constitutes a general inquiry of two kinds:
first, a direct question that does not inquire into the underlying reasons; second, a difficult objection based on the examples of the principles explained below.

Regarding "penetrating the gate of the immovable rules" (*niyama*): "penetration" (*prativedha*) has the meaning of reaching and attaining, while "immovable" (*acala*) has the meaning of being without change.

Therefore, the preceding text states that the teachings and principles of all Buddhas of the three periods are naturally and eternally abiding, of a single flavor and equality, without shifting or turning, and without arising or ceasing;
hence it is called "immovable. As for "rules" (*niyama*), it refers to ritual protocol (*vidhi*).
"Also, 'also' (ye) refers to the Dharma; it means that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take this immovable and eternally abiding Dharma as their standard, thereby attaining that unsurpassed fruit.
As stated in the section on the gate of diligent cultivation through faith in the Dharma:
'That is to say, one delights in faith in the Buddhas of the three periods of time as one's own father of grace and as one's own mother of grace.'"
The Master cannot alter or destroy it, nor can he cause it to arise or perish;

it is the space-like vajra, the immovable principle, possessing inconceivable within the inconceivable, supreme benefits that perpetually and continuously revolve at all times and in all places because one cultivates all the factors conducive to enlightenment. This is what is meant by this.
Regarding the "peaceful carriage" (*ān-chē*), the *Qūlǐ* states it is a vehicle for sitting; it is like the small carriages of today.

As for "clarifying the spirit as one would the sea," this means that the intention and speech are like the sea—clear and limpid—and the spiritual sageliness is like possessing the ten virtues, just as the hundred rivers all share the same taste of salt water.
(From *Lùn*, Scroll Two)
Regarding the Gate of Suchness of the Original Mind: "mind" refers to each and every mental dharma, while "Suchness" is the gate.
Regarding the Gate of Arising and Ceasing of the Mind: "mind" refers to the single mind that encompasses all mental dharmas, while "arising and ceasing" is the gate.
Alternatively, regarding the name "Mahāyāna," since this name does not appear among the ten alternative names listed below, it is clear that this name is not a general category.
As for what is called the "characteristic of fabrication," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (86) states: When the Tathāgata is about to preach the Dharma, he manifests...
The four kinds of signs are: first, rising from a very low seat with composed dignity and ascending to a very high seat to sit solemnly;
second, abiding in the deportment conducive to preaching the Dharma; third, emitting the sound of a cough to indicate that he is about to preach;
and fourth, looking around in all directions like a king of nāgas or elephants. Therefore, these are called "making signs."
Regarding the phrase "because space contains form," the intended meaning is that because space contains form, it attains mastery;

thus, the subsequent text states, "because one attains mastery over all forms" and "because it contains the great elements. By analogy with this, the upper part [of space] containing space can be understood as follows:
the meaning is that just as the universal great void contains the distinct spaces of the east and west, why would it not be sovereign?

What difficulty is there in the gate of the distinct characteristics of the totality of phenomena as they enter into the same [state]? For both are provisional designations made in accordance with their meanings.
That which has no place of abiding refers to attaining mastery in the emptiness of non-abiding; thus, a "place of abiding" carries the meaning of an obstruction.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "single-mindedly reaching the place of abiding," these four lines consist of two lines that explain the Dharma and two lines that clarify them through analogy.

Each upper line pertains to the Dharma, and each lower line refers to the gate; their essence is the nature (*dharmatā*). Because the nature is itself empty, it accords with the fundamental meaning of the analogy: that [the mind] is originally so.
"Non-existence" refers to the fact that the great void has from the beginning no dwelling or attachment in directions such as east and west;

thus it is able to contain the distinct spaces of east and west. "One Mind" is like the nature of reality being inherently empty of existence; thus it is able to contain the distinct truths of essence and appearance.
Regarding "obstructions and so forth," this refers to the subsequent metaphor of "all forms and so forth.
Regarding "causing [beings] to abide in all dharmas," this refers to the subsequent metaphor of "accommodating the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

This is because, within the gate of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), there are both the two meanings of obstruction and non-obstruction; whereas, in contrast to the gate of suchness (*tathatā*), there is only non-obstruction and no arising or ceasing.
Since both [the internal and external] within the gateways are termed "obstructions," it is said that regarding all obstructions, mental discourse is like space;
it is without obstruction toward form, merely allowing form to abide.
"Because they are sharp and perfect" refers to the pure liberation described below, as the Second Patriarch said: "Fundamentally..."
The absence of afflictions is fundamentally bodhi; is this not the primordial perfection? When merit is fulfilled, is it not called the "perfect faculty"?
It is called "perfect" because it is a sudden faculty. Thus, it is termed "perfect."
The fifth is called "a square inch" (*fangcun*); this refers to the shape of the hair-tuft being one inch square. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"These two tufts are like a bright mirror," and thus it is called "a square inch."
First, regarding the phrase "the white tuft (*ūrṇā*) is a square inch": this character *máo* (tuft) was erroneously transcribed by later scribes; it should instead be the character *sè* (color).

Furthermore, among the citations provided as proof, there is only a difference between the two terms "white" (*bái*) and "disorderly" (*luàn*), whereas the two names *pīta* and *nīla* are entirely identical.
Therefore, we know that the character *máo* is an error. If so, how do we know that the character *sè* is not itself an error? The answer is: according to what precedes it.
Regarding the various names translated later and this treatise’s statement that "the five" are called *fangcun* (square-inch):
this translates *visākhā-nīla* as merely *fangcun*, without mentioning the color of the *ūrṇā-keśa* (white tuft). Based on the *Shuolun* (Explanatory Treatise), it says:
"In the first *fangcun*, only the celestial image of the previous life appears (this is white, not the white *ūrṇā-keśa*). In the second *fangcun*, [it] penetrates..."

Regarding "the five destinies manifest before one's eyes" (which refers to disordered forms), since both cases involve manifest form and the text does not speak of "manifest hairs," it is known that the character *se* (form) is correct and the character *hao* (hair) is an error.

As for the phrase "departing from the causes of transmigration" and so forth, the two things to be departed from are precisely the two—awakening and non-awakening—within the context of arising and ceasing. Therefore...

Regarding the statement that "the difference in activity is called the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), where a single mind or a single thought arising constitutes bondage," these two names are established in relation to one another.
Viewed from afar, they share the same meaning as "difference" (*anyatva*). "Activity" (*saṃskāra*) and "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*) both carry the sense of flux.
"Bondage" and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to being bound by characteristics. Only those who possess awakening are free from this transmigration.

Because "only suchness" (*tathatā*) and "liberation from the bonds of discursive thought" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna-bandha-vimukti*) are mutually explained, they are respectively alternative names for the "transcendence of the real" (*dūra-vṛtti-tattva*) and distinct designations for the "suchness that is far removed from bondage" (*dūra-bandha-tathatā*).
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Real" (*tattva*) signifies reality, indicating the absence of falsehood;

"Suchness" (*tathatā*) signifies being as-it-is, indicating the absence of change. Furthermore, this is what is meant by the Gate of Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), which is "neither negated nor established."
Regarding the phrase "each and every one is pure" (*ekaikaṃ śuddham*), there are two possible interpretations. First, it may be understood as a concluding term for the preceding section.

In this sense, "the former" refers exclusively to *bodhi* (awakening), while "the latter" refers exclusively to *tathatā* (suchness). This is because, within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), there exist both non-awakening (*abodhi*) and non-suchness (*atathatā);

thus, there are two. However, in the present context, since there is only awakening and only suchness, there is but one. The preceding "pure" (*śuddha*) concludes the section on being free from saṃsāra (*pravṛtti*).
Because the lower section clarifies the severance of the bonds of discursive thought (*vikalpa*), both "black" aspects are eliminated; thus, they are called the "two whites.

One interpretation states that each of the two gates—arising and ceasing—is presented with an upper heading followed by a lower explanation. The meaning is as follows: each is itself a "white," and being white in its own right, it is not merely white in contrast to arising and ceasing.
Because it is designated "white" in relation to the "black," it is said to be "each and every one is white and white."

Regarding the causes of the wholesome and the unwholesome, they are explained here in their general characteristics: "wholesome" has the meaning of *bodhi* (awakening), and "unwholesome" has the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*).

"To act" (*wei*) means to perform; it carries the sense of "to give. Regarding "experiencing suffering and pleasure": if one takes birth and death as such, then pleasure is *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"It bestows power upon delusion and bestows power upon awakening, thereby manifesting the phenomena of birth and death and *nirvāṇa*."
The phrase "identical with the cause" means that within the single Dharma-realm, the two kinds of mastery— conditioned and unconditioned—
are not distinct from those perfuming factors as unconditioned phenomena.
"One who is like an actor" refers to a master of illusion; therefore, the subsequent text states:
"For example, it is as if a non-illusory person were to manifest as an illusory person, bestowing power and function upon various illusory phenomena according to their requirements.

Thus, one's own body manifests as the bodies of various classes of beings while the [original] self-body does not appear; reflect on this principle accordingly. Therefore, the subsequent commentary explains: "The term 'garbha' (womb/store) has the meaning of concealment."
The "pure white single dharma-realm" refers to the single dharma-realm of pure white; it is named after its gateway rather than being pure white by its own essence.

As for the other explanation that the "true suchness gateway" is the "principle dharma-realm," this applies only to the gateways of the Exegetical School, for they do not differentiate between gateways.
Furthermore, the remaining nine dharmas are also established as names based on their gateways; they are not names in their own right.

"Unimpeded seeds of emptiness" (*ākāśa-bīja-avyāghāta*): "seeds" here refers to the nature (*prakṛti*). This means that the mind-nature is the principle of emptiness, which is True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Pervasive unimpeded seeds": "seeds" also refers to the nature. This means that the true nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is all-pervasive.
Within these four characters, the first is the gate, while the latter two are both dharmas. "Seeds of emptiness," "unimpeded," and so forth, are *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds.
This is an explanation. Therefore, the aforementioned *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) is also "nature" (*prakṛti*), yet it differs from the conventional meaning. To explain:

while the *vastu-dharmadhātu* (phenomenal dharma-realm) is designated as a "realm" (*dhātu*) because its aspects are not differentiated, when it is treated as a differentiated gate, this dharma is the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu*.
However, since the *dharmadhātu* is not identical to the phenomena (*vastu*) themselves, it may also be categorized by type.

It is also said that because the essence of True Suchness is the aspect of emptiness, True Suchness is empty, and furthermore, it is as-it-is empty and as-it-is not-empty, its categories are not uniform.
Therefore, among these four characters, the first two are the "gate" (dvāra) and the latter two are the "dharma";

it is named by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation) compound as being the unimpeded nature of the category of emptiness. The subsequent single name should be understood accordingly. As for those two long characters, they are both... [text ends].
The meaning of the "ultimate eon" (*parama-kalpa*).

That which is called the "true mind free from extremes" is precisely the "mind of sentient beings" mentioned in the preceding text. By being free from extremes, the central true mind is revealed as reality;
this is a synonym for the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), because it is simultaneously free from both those truths of the real (*tathya*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The *Sūtra on the Nature of Reality as Free from Extremes* states: "The Great Universal Spiritual King is neither a mundane phenomenon nor a supramundane phenomenon.

Regarding the phrase "differentiation and identity like a pearl," the intended meaning is that differentiation belongs to the diverse reflections manifested, while identity belongs to the single luminosity that manifests them.

Because differentiated reflections return to the light of equality, it is said that "difference and sameness" [are unified]. As the subsequent passage states: "By raising up True Suchness, one encompasses arising-and-ceasing;

all are identical to True Suchness. Next, regarding "sameness and difference," the reversal of the preceding [analogy] is easy to see; the "sole bright pearl" and so forth should be explained by analogy with this.
"This one" refers to the gate; its meaning belongs to the Dharma.

"All these" also refers to the gate; its meaning belongs to the Dharma. This means that while the mental dharmas (*citta-dharma*) are fundamentally one, they are spoken of as two according to their gates.
Therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "The mental dharmas are not one, for they are produced by causes; being one [in essence], they are conventionally named 'one mind'."
The Dharma is not something produced by all causes; because it is "all" [in its pervasiveness], it is conventionally designated as "all.

This establishes the heading above and the conclusion below. Alternatively, it may be read as "is one" and "is one": the former refers to the reality of essence (*tattva*), while the latter refers to the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, it may be read as "is all" and "is all": the former refers to the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), while the latter refers to non-awakening (*abodhi*). Of these two interpretations, the first is superior in principle.
The meaning of the text is complex.

Regarding the first point, "one mind" (*ekacitta*) and so forth: because the dharma entered through the True Suchness Gate (*tathatā-mukha*) is designated simply as "mind" and is neither one nor many, it is termed "one" solely from the perspective of that gate.
This is not the same as the dharma entered through the Arising and Ceasing Gate (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). Why?
This means that the first "one" mind is designated as "one" in relation to the various doors of its activity;

it is so called because it depends upon the second "one" mind and all the doors of activity performed by that second mind. Thus, while each single mind performs a "one," this "one" has something upon which it depends—the "many" performed by the many minds.
Therefore, one cannot say that it is called "one" based on its own capacity for action, since it lacks independence from others.
Because it can produce many, the first "one mind" cannot be established by name based on its own capacity to produce; rather, its designation is established solely based on that which is produced.
As for the second [type of] capacity, when viewed in relation to all that it produces, it receives the name "one.
Therefore, the subsequent sutra says: "The one mind of arising and ceasing is 'one' because its causes are many. This refers to the "one" of the self-capacity to produce in contrast to itself.

The first reason for designating [the second] as "one" is that it is the many things produced. Alternatively, since the first "single mind" is not one [in its own right], the second "single mind" is called "one";
this is the second sense of being "able to produce" as one, which receives the name "one" by depending on the fact that the first "ability to produce" was not one.
Since the first "ability to produce" is already designated as "not one," the first "thing produced" is named accordingly in contrast to it.

First, a sutra states that "mental phenomena are not of one kind"; this refers to the first [type of] agent, which is established as a single category because it depends on its own capacity to act and is contrasted with what is done by another.
Second, the capable agent is established as a single category because it is contrasted with what is done by itself and depends on the capacity of others to act.
These two gates are the two truths, while the single mind is the ultimate truth; thus, the subsequent sutra says:

It is said that it is neither great nor small, and so forth; furthermore, the preceding text states that the Great and Wondrous Devarāja is neither a mundane dharma (the conventional truth) nor a supramundane dharma (the ultimate truth), because the true mind, being free from extremes, constitutes the central reality.
First, that which is called the "Tathāgatagarbha-gate" because it is free from confusion refers to the fourth among the ten garbhas mentioned below—the *tathatāgarbha* (the *tathatā*-garbha).
It is not the same as the principle of arising and ceasing being confused by other cognitions, nor is it the same as the second [gate], where "garbha" is explained as being "unmixed.
Here, "mixture" (*miśra*) means defilement (*saṃkleśa*); since that which is to be distantly turned away from is the defiled dharma, this is precisely [that].
The Dharma is revealed by means of its gates; what is now called "intermingled" (za) refers precisely to "confusion.

It is simply because True Suchness (tathatā) has no other wisdom to intermingle with it that the Treatise states: "In the gate of True Suchness, the principle is solely self-principle and does not face wisdom."

Regarding the statement that "the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind has ten names," etc.: the first pair corresponds to the second [of the previous set], the second pair corresponds to the first;

the third, fourth, and fifth correspond respectively to the first four [of the previous set], and the sixth corresponds to the first three and the last four. The sequence of these two gates is identical.
As for the second being called the *tathāgatagarbha*, this refers to the latter six of the ten *garbhas* mentioned below; thus, the term "garbha" applies universally.
Since the meanings of "subject" (*neng*) and "object" (*suo*) are explained below, it is said that "concealment" (*fúcáng*) applies to both subject and object. Question:

Now, regarding these two gates named *Tathāgatagarbha*, how are they distinguished from the previous two dharmas also named *Tathāgatagarbha-gate*, given that the names overlap? Answer: This [term] possesses two meanings.

First, it is like how the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are both generally termed "mental consciousness" (*yìshí*); although they are both "consciousness of the mind," the "mind" (*yì*) itself is...
Because these two meanings of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are distinct, their two names do not overlap; here it is the same.

It is simply that because the two pairs—“concealment” (*chādana*) and “hiding” (*gopana*), and “non-confusion” (*asaṃkīrṇa*) and “non-disorder” (*avyākula*)—have distinct meanings, their two names do not overlap.

Second, those dharmas are opened up into the two distinct names of “distant turning away” (*dūravartana*) and “distant binding” (*dūrabaṃdhana*); this present gate opens them up into the seven treasuries (*kośa*), beginning with True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Question: Since they are distinct categories, each is clearly delineated and generally does not overlap; given that this is the case, why was a common name established for them from the very beginning?
Answer: It is to indicate that these two dharmas share a single essence, and to ensure that the number ten is complete by encompassing the six *piṭakas*.

Therefore, although the individual gate-dharmas each have their own specific names, a general name is established for them. If this were so, would not the name "Treasury" (*piṭaka*) assigned to the preceding gate fail to encompass the multiple treasuries, thereby lacking completeness?

Question: Why are the ten numbers not also established with distinct names? Answer: In the case of the two categories [of the four elements], the remaining names are all established by mutual correlation, like water and fire.
However, because this single name [for the numbers] has no other form to rely upon, it is simply established as one general name.

Fifth, regarding the gate of "having going and having coming" because there are upward and downward movements: this refers to the subsequent passage which states that arising and ceasing have two positions—first, moving upward, and second, moving downward.
Furthermore, as stated in the third [section]: "Initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodhi) turns its back on the ordinary and moves toward the holy;

it moves upward and goes upward, proceeding through successive stages. Accordingly, fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) following defilement turns its back on the holy and moves toward the ordinary; it moves downward and comes downward.
This is for the sake of sequential progression.
Regarding the "flowing on" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth, the interpretation according to other teachings applies to both the expanded and the condensed explanations;

however, for the time being, the condensed explanation refers to the flowing on of saṃsāra and the cessation (*nivṛtti*) toward nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the expanded explanation holds that "flowing on" is precisely the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), which is the cause of saṃsāra.

Turning [the perspective], suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is the fruit of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); returning [to the original], the path (*mārga-satya*) is the cause of *nirvāṇa*; cessation (*nirodha*) is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
This is explained by reversing the eighth section of the preceding gate.
Each has its respective basis. That which is called the Mahāyāna of the "later single essence" refers to its reliance upon the Mahāyāna of the "earlier single essence and single mind," and so forth.
If this were the case, then all of these should be opened from within the fundamental Mahāyāna;

why then do you say they are opened from within the "one dharma and three meanings"? This is because previously it was only stated that the gate of the earlier stage is opened for the sake of the later stage.
The Dharma is not such that a "heavy" (repeated) dharma of the first stage is subsequently made into a "heavy" dharma of a later stage. Therefore, the answer is:

because the initial heavy gate was originally opened out from within the initial heavy dharma; now, since the entire initial gate is taken as the subsequent heavy dharma, there is no separate initial gate apart from this.
Thus, it is said that the subsequent heavy dharma relies upon the initial heavy dharma, for this is spoken of solely in terms of the gates.
It is said that there is no contradiction because the meanings derived from the single dharma within the three aspects differ in their implications.

Regarding the statement "each takes its own support as its object," this refers to the supported [consciousness]. The *Benyou jing* (Sūtra on Original Existence) is cited below, stating: "The profound true principle is not the domain of others;
it is taken as an object solely by that which is its own support. Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā-śāstra* states: "Its own essence is self-manifesting and illuminating."

"All phenomena are thus" means that these are both the substance of the dharma (*dharmatā*) and the realization of the conventional meaning (*prajñapti-artha*) upon it, just as the luminous substance of a mirror reflects images upon its surface.

Regarding the phrase "because they share the same name but have different meanings," this sentence generally provides the reason for the subsequent section concerning how the differences are few while the similarities are many.
"Regarding 'Yao, when a single thought arises as bondage,' etc.: this refers to what is stated later in the text, namely, 'All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thoughts;
if one is free from mental thoughts, then there are no signs of any objective realms. This refers to the present section."
Because one can naturally enter and practice without deliberating upon any good or evil, the Inscription for Bodhidharma states:
"If the mind exists, one remains a common person for kalpas; if the mind does not exist, one attains perfect enlightenment in a single instant.

Furthermore, Qingliang said: "To realize the nature of True Suchness, one must forget deluded attachments; where there is mind, there is the path of birth and death; where there is no [mind], there is liberation."
Contemplating the city of Nirvana, who is the master of afflictions? Since even "Bodhi" is but a provisional name, do not harbor views of discrimination;
the Buddha-way is accomplished spontaneously.
Regarding the phrase "arising through birth and cessation," this refers to the four marks of merit below which diminish the four marks of faults.

Regarding the passage, "That which is quiescent is called the one mind," there are two masters who provide commentaries on this scriptural text. First, the *Haedong Ssu* (Commentary from the Eastern Sea) states:
"The 'Gate of the Suchness of Mind' explains the scriptural phrase, 'That which is quiescent is called the one mind.
The 'Gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind' explains the scriptural phrase, 'The one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha. This is because..."
Thus, because all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, fundamentally quiescent, and are solely this one mind, it is called the "Gate of the True Suchness of Mind.
Furthermore, within the substance of this mind, there is primordial awakening (*ādikṣaṇika-bodhi*) which, following along with ignorance (*avidyā*), functions as arising and ceasing;
therefore, in this gate, the nature of the Tathāgata is hidden and does not manifest, and is thus called the "Tathāgatagarbha," and so forth.
Regarding the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing," Master Nāgārjuna’s intent is as follows: "Quiescent Extinction" is the eighth of the ten names for a gate;

"One Mind" is the eleventh of the ten names for the Dharma. Furthermore, he states that "One Mind" is the tenth of the ten names for the Dharma, while "Tathāgatagarbha" is the second of the ten names for a gate. This is all.
He was well-versed in distinguishing the categories of the gates and principles, and his exegesis of the scriptural text accorded perfectly with the commentaries.

Regarding the two interpretations of "each relying on its own basis," one explanation states that because the gate of the dependent relies upon its respective supported dharma, the characteristics of the gate of arising and ceasing are easily known;
however, regarding the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is explained merely in terms of the gate-dharma.
Because they are conventionally designated as "conditions" from the perspective of the meaning of equality, it is not so;

for why is it that within the ten minds [of the *Awakening of Faith*], there is no mind named after the True Suchness Gate? One explanation states: within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing, the principle (li) within the gate serves as the supported essence (*āśraya*), while wisdom is the supporting function.
Since the function takes the essence as its object, one may also say that each takes its own support as its object, just as a pearl emits light.
The light returns to illuminate the substance of the pearl; this is precisely the meaning of distinguishing, in sequence, the differences between the two objects realized.
The former interpretation is correct, as it is explained as being the opposite of the preceding dharma.
"Distinct names and distinct meanings": this phrase generally explains the reasons for the preceding dharmas being distinct in form, numerous in difference, and minor in similarity.
"Dedication is itself faith, etc.": these four phrases show that from beginning to end they are mutually identical; first, it refers to the initial stage of the ordinary person.

The mutual identity of the end and the beginning; next, the mutual identity of cause and effect throughout the beginning and the end; next, the mutual identity of the stages of the sages throughout the beginning and the end;
and finally, the mutual identity of the causal stages throughout the beginning and the end.
Regarding the phrase "the ten stages being identical to the first stage," Qingliang’s commentary states: "The first seven phrases correlate the meanings to show their identity."
The final phrase, according to principle, dissolves all distinctions: that the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is the first means they equally realize Suchness;

that the first is the eighth means the first stage is not moved by afflictions, being identical to the "Immovable" (*acala*); that the ninth is the seventh means the ninth is identical to the seventh, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and that the seventh is likewise the eighth means it consists purely of the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*).
The second is the same as the eighth; the third is the same as the second, *śraddhā-kṣānti*; the fourth is the same as the fifth, *anulomikī-kṣānti*;

and the third is the same as the sixth: that which is attained in the third stage (*bhūmi*) as the light of the three types of wisdom is identical in meaning to the superior *prajñā* obtained in the sixth stage.
Regarding the phrase "born at fifty-one years," it should be understood that a mother of one year gives birth to a son of fifty years;

when these maternal characteristics are calculated together, they total fifty-one. Alternatively, reading from the beginning of the sentence, it may mean that because a mother of one year gives birth to fifty sons, this represents the fifty-one disordered positions.
Therefore, the subsequent text states that there are fifty-one stages of *ādikṣānti* (initial enlightenment).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because of wisdom, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind is true wisdom," etc., this section consists of two parts and possesses three meanings:

first, it distinguishes the difference between the preceding dharmas in response to an objection; second, "suchness" (tathatā) is that which constitutes the dharmas being explained; third, it distinguishes the difference between the preceding objects in response to an objection;

and fourth, "suchness" is that which constitutes the object of cognition (*ālambana*). If this were so, while there would be no contradiction regarding the arising and ceasing, there would be an obstacle to [the identity of] True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Question: Why is it that among the gates of *tathatā* (suchness), there are no texts stating that there is a cognizing mind? Answer:

Since it is said that *tathatā* is equal to its original state (*ben*), and the original state is already endowed with the capacity for cognition, the derivative state (*mo*) must also possess the capacity for cognition.

If this were not so, how could one speak of "equality"? The *Xianzong ji* states: "Suchness is unmoving, yet its dynamic function is inexhaustible. Furthermore, if *tathatā* were lacking the quality of cognitive capacity, how [could it be called suchness]?

Is it called the fulfillment of the Dharma of Non-empty Purity? If one relies on the "true essence" (*tattva*) without looking toward equality with others, there is no object of cognition (*ālambana*).

However, if one considers the "true characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*) and its equality with the source, then the sense of "mind" (*citta*) exists. Set aside intellectual speculation and do not be obstructed by mere words.
As for the third [point], it is difficult to distinguish from the preceding stage; however, the two differ because this stage is what is realized therein.
"There is not a single dharma that is not *tathatā*. The *Yan-ao-chao* states: "When one is empty, all are empty; there is nothing—neither the provisional nor the middle—that is not empty.
One should understand the subsequent inclusion of arising and ceasing by analogy with this. This refers to the two gates as being non-different;
however, the statement from "as for *tathatā*" down to "all dharmas" is based on the two gates as being non-identical.
That "all are entirely equal" means that the two gates are not different.

That "each is distinct" means that the two gates are not one; because each is distinct, there is no arising or ceasing within True Suchness (tathatā), and there is no True Suchness within arising and ceasing.
It is like still water and moving waves; thus they are neither one nor different. Therefore, above...

It is said that because True Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth are entirely equal, True Suchness subsumes arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), such that arising and ceasing are wholly True Suchness;

and arising and ceasing subsume True Suchness, such that True Suchness is wholly arising and ceasing. Therefore, it was stated above that [True Suchness] "comprehensively subsumes arising and ceasing" and so forth.
This does not mean that the characteristics of arising and ceasing do not exist within True Suchness; rather, it is not the case that True Suchness exclusively fails to subsume arising and ceasing.

Because the dharmas that are subsumed within True Suchness (tathatā) are distinct from the dharmas themselves, the characteristics of the true meaning subsumed within arising and ceasing are likewise so.
That is to say, "directly expressing the question and so forth" means that it is not like the preceding detailed questions and answers concerning being neither identical nor different.
"Yun" means "direct.
*Shimokkakenron Tsūgen Shō*, Scroll One;
*Shimokkakenron Tsūgen Shō*, Scroll Two.

Composed by the Dharma Master Zhìfú, a Purple-Robed Śramaṇa bestowed [with this title] by Imperial Decree, Grand Master of Compassionate Practice, Acting Director of the Bureau of Communications, and Minister of State for the Yímǔlǐ Mountain of the Great Liao.

As for the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*): True Suchness is without thought; it is not through conceptual thought that one can know the reality-mark (*dharmatā*). Since there is no arising, how could there be form?

When the mind is able to perceive that there is no thought within thought, this is the true suchness (tathatā) of thought; when there is no arising within arising, this is the true mark (lakṣaṇa) of arising.
Abiding without abiding, one eternally dwells in nirvāṇa; acting without acting, one transcends the waves and reaches the shore.
Thus, the movement of the functioning is inexhaustible, yet in every thought there is no seeking; for seeking is fundamentally without thought. (This is the record of Heze.)
Regarding the "Gate of Establishing Names," this refers to the fact that within the main text, two types of names are established for each of the gates of the Dharma.
Among these, "Mind" (*citta*) is the tenth name; "One Dharma Realm" (*eka-dharmadhātu*) is the seventh name.

Within the gates, "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) is the tenth name, and "The Gate of the Great General Characteristic" (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the ninth name. Logically, one should skip two positions and read as follows: "Mind" is... [etc.]
That this single dharma-realm is further called "True Suchness" (tathatā) means that it is the very essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate.
As for the fact that each has ten names, this refers to the ten distinct synonyms for each of the aforementioned gates and dharmas.
"Karma" (karman) refers to that which is performed; it belongs to the essential nature of the agent. "Action" (kriyā) refers to the function;
it belongs to the functional gate of that which is produced.

Regarding "one mind" (*ekacitta*) and so forth: it takes the substance of that which transcends the two [subject and object] as its essence. That is to say, "one" (*eka*) is not designated in opposition to "two" or "three";
rather, the true mind (*bhūtacitta*) is taken as the essence of "one. Furthermore, this "gate" (*mukha*) is not designated as "great" (*mahat*) in opposition to "small" (*parīttaka*);
since both the gate and the dharma are mutually absolute (*anapekṣa*), the single essence of the dharma performs the function of "greatness" for that gate. Moreover, by means of the dharma...
The entire body maintains the general function of that gate, and furthermore, by means of the boundary-nature (*dharmadhātu*) of phenomena, it constructs the conceptual characteristics of that gate.
Therefore, what was stated above regarding "the performance of activity" is now concluded; this section has merely explained the great general characteristic of the single fundamental *dharmadhātu*.
From here on, we belong to the essence of the fundamental dharma-gate. As for the name "dharma-gate," it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound); thus, it is the very essence itself.
Regarding the inclusion of functions and the convergence of activities within the gates: this is because the gates reveal the dharmas.

As for the various distinct characteristics and so forth, it means that in addition to these, one should further take up the nine alternative names for both the "entrants" and the "entered," and explain them by correlating their respective functions.
Furthermore, the name "one mind" serves as a designation for *tathatā* (suchness).
"Mind" (*citta*) has the meaning of being firm and solid; "Reality" (*tattva*) has the meaning of truly being free from falsehood. Since these two meanings correspond, the mind constitutes Reality.
"One" (*eka*) has the meaning of non-duality; "Suchness" (*tathatā*) has the meaning of non-difference. Since these meanings correspond, the One constitutes Suchness.

This is not the same as the previous [explanation] where they were named according to their respective order; therefore, the preceding selection states that it is certainly not "like this. It may also be understood by following what precedes.

The specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) denoted by these names are explained in full; however, we take only these two characteristics denoted by the names, as the other nine have already been excluded.

Regarding the statement that the *dharmatā* of true suchness (*tathatā*) is neither arising nor ceasing, this explains the nature of the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*) by means of the *dharmatā* of true suchness. As for "the fundamental... [the text continues].

The commentary on the nature of mind explains the character "essence" (ti). (This belongs to the main text. By means of both "neither arising nor ceasing" and "no arising and no ceasing," it explains the main text's "neither arising nor ceasing.

"Not" (bu) means "not so" (fei), "non-existent" (wu), or "without" (yi). This is because existence and non-existence are discussed here in terms of the essence itself, rather than being explained as existing outside of that essence.

Furthermore, regarding those who say "neither this nor that," the ancient masters have said: the mind (the true mind) is not existent (this refers to arising), nor is it non-existent (this refers to ceasing).

If the mind were neither existent nor non-existent, then to be existent would be to fall into the extreme of existence (the first two things to be discarded), and to be non-existent would be to fall into the extreme of non-existence (the latter two things to be discarded).
