Thus, when it is said that the seven [consciousnesses] arise by taking external objects as conditions, this is precisely because they share the same substance and the same seeds as the sixth consciousness, and are thus able to take them as conditions.

Furthermore, regarding the verse cited by the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*, what was previously explained states that the subtle state of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has no separate substantial entity.
This means that from the conclusion of the *Saṃvṛti-satya* chapter up to this present text, the lineage of the core meaning is transmitted as a single intent.

If one considers different types [of arguments] that share the same purpose of protecting the Dharma, it follows that [the mind] does not take external objects as its condition. Now, the author of this treatise maintains both the identity and the difference [between these views].
The Dharma-protector masters rely solely on divergent interpretations precisely because the teachings have provisional and ultimate aspects, and the principles have shallow and deep levels.

Regarding the "essence" (*tī*) of the manifest mirror-consciousness: "essence" refers to its nature (*prakṛti*), as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says, "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, "essence" refers to its functional substance (*vastu-tī*), as the verse states, "Like the sun and moon with their radiance," and so forth.
If that is so, regarding the "manifest consciousness" (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*) and so forth, this refers to the meaning previously stated in refuting the views of other masters.

That previous passage merely established [the position] through scattered statements; it was not a formal syllogism. Therefore, I shall now once again establish this formal proof (*pramāṇa*). The subject (*pakṣa*) is the manifest consciousness:

it must be the manas (*manas*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is subsequently stated to be the direct support (*sākṣād-āśraya*) for that mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), just like the [preceding] mind (*manas*).

Regarding the analogy of the faculties (*indriya*), there are two intended meanings: first, that the thesis has two sides; second, that within each side, there are two types—those that accord with reason when of the same kind, and those that contradict scripture when of a different kind.
As for the instruction to "reflect carefully," my careful reflection now is as follows: the latter five successive [analyses] are divided into two, while the former four concern...
In terms of phenomena (*vastu*), there are coarse and subtle levels; the latter [of the four characteristics] is the principle (*dharma-tā*), which is neither coarse nor subtle.
Within the first four [characteristics], they are further divided into three categories: the first is distinguished solely by way of persons and phenomena;

the next two are distinguished solely by way of mutual relativity—meaning the first is exclusively subtle and the last is exclusively coarse, while the intermediate four characteristics are both coarse and subtle. They are coarse relative to what precedes them, yet subtle when contrasted with what follows.
Thus, because the latter one is subtle while the other three are coarse, these six are exclusively coarse.
"Fundamentally untainted" refers to the two types of awakening—original and initial; "ignorance" refers to the two types of non-awakening—original and derivative.
Both of these possess karmic functions that manifest, yet they do not exist as substantial realities; therefore, they are called "karmic illusions."
The phrase "not a characteristic that can be cultivated" means that, in relation to that nirvana, it is not something manifested through the cultivation of a revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*).
The phrase "not a characteristic that can be produced" means that, in relation to that bodhi, it is not something created by a producing cause (*janakahetu*).
"Ultimately there is no one who attains": these two fruits are inherently pure and primordially present, and therefore there is no attainment.
Below this, the text addresses a latent doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If sentient beings have already entered nirvāṇa and there is no further new cessation, they are then identical to all Buddhas;
why then can they not manifest the rūpakāyas of reward and transformation? The explanation states: "The self-substance of the dharma-nature is originally non-existent."
Since visible forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) can be perceived, how could they cause the manifestation of form and so forth? Therefore, it is said that "there are also no visible forms.

Furthermore, a doubt arises: "If the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is not a phenomenon with visible forms and thus does not manifest form, for what reason do the Buddhas manifest various forms such as the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body)?
The explanation states: "As for those who see the various forms and so forth of the Buddhas..."

All of these are manifestations of transformation within the delusory mind of sentient beings, belonging to the category of subsequent "different characteristics" (*visama-lakṣaṇa*), and not to this category of "identical characteristics" (*sama-lakṣaṇa*).
Within the primordial enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of wisdom, there is no such nature of non-emptiness as these forms and so forth.

Furthermore, even within the non-empty, countless virtues of primordial enlightenment, there are no such marks of form. (The former sense [of the statement] means that form itself is the nature of non-emptiness; the latter sense means that wisdom itself is the nature of non-emptiness.)
The particle "而" (ér) serves to prevent the separation of the preceding and following phrases; thus it says, "one sees the appearance of form," and so forth, up to "the nature of non-emptiness.

How is it known that within the essence of those dharmas there is no appearance of form? The commentary explains: because the characteristic of the wisdom of original enlightenment (benjue zhi) is not a dharma that can be seen.

Regarding the phrase "following along with the distinctions of the illusory transformations of defilement" and so forth, the *Aṣṭādāśa-śāstra-vyākhyāna* (Record of the Separate Explanation of the Awakening of Faith) states that there are two gates:

first, that which relies on metaphors; second, that which pertains to the phenomena themselves. As for the metaphor, it is like an illusory rabbit produced from a cloth; this has two gates: first, the rabbit; second, the cloth. The rabbit also has two meanings:

first, the meaning of the distinction between its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the meaning of its emptiness of substance (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). The cloth also has two meanings: first, the meaning of abiding in its own state; second, the meaning of its substance... [text fragment].
Regarding the meaning of the "rabbit" established herein: the cloth and the rabbit are neither identical nor different. Furthermore, there are four propositions concerning their non-difference:

first, because the meaning of the rabbit being established upon the cloth and the meaning of the distinct characteristics of the rabbit are merged into a single limit (*ekānta*), they are not different;

this is the explanation of non-difference by way of the primary following the secondary. Second, the meaning of the cloth abiding in its own position and the meaning of the rabbit’s essence being empty [are likewise merged].

First, because they are unified as a single limit through their shared meaning, they are non-different; this is the first point of non-difference, wherein the branches return to the root, and based on the root, it is clarified that they are not different.
Second, because the root to which the branches return and the branches from which the root is subsumed are both fused without obstruction and coexist, they are non-different;
this is the second point of non-difference, clarifying that the root and branches both exist together without obstruction. Third, by... [the text continues with the fourth point].
The end that is subsumed within the root and the root that follows the end—since both of these are extinguished, they are not different.

This is the second point, the meaning of non-difference through the simultaneous extinction of both root and end, which clarifies their equality. Regarding this second meaning of non-identity, there are also four propositions;
first, the meaning of the cloth remaining in its own position and the meaning of the rabbit’s horns being distinct—these two...

They are "not one" because they are mutually opposed; this mutual opposition constitutes the sense of "not one. On the cloth, there is the established meaning of the rabbit, while on the rabbit, there is the meaning of its body being empty;
since these two meanings are mutually destructive, they are "not one. Third, they are "not one" because these two states—mutual opposition and mutual destruction—are distinct positions.
That is to say, as for opposition, each is opposed to the other and they remain far apart from one another; as for destruction, [they cancel each other out].
Thus, they oppose one another and even devour and harm one another; for this reason, the near and the far are not one.

Fourth, through extreme mutual harm, they are both extinguished and not extinguished (this is not mere harm); through extreme mutual remoteness, they both exist and do not exist (this is not mere opposition).

This meaning of neither being extinguished nor existing constitutes "not one. Furthermore, these instances of formation and destruction are not one; moreover, these four "non-onenesses" are not different from the four aforementioned [non-onenesses].

Nor are they of a single meaning, because they are not intermingled. Furthermore, since the principle that the four aforementioned [aspects] are not different from these four [aspects], which are not one, yet are also not different, pervades all cases, it follows that if one takes up the various aspects through the gate of non-difference, they are utterly harmonious;

whereas if one takes up the various meanings through the gate of non-unity, they are utterly contradictory and contentious. That which is both utterly contradictory and utterly harmonious is "unobstructed."

Regarding the second point, explaining it in terms of the Dharma: the headband is a metaphor for *tathatā* (suchness) and the *tathāgatagarbha* (which corresponds to the differentiation of illusory phenomena following defilement);

the rabbit is a metaphor for the birth-and-death of sentient beings and so forth (which corresponds to the differentiation of illusory phenomena through inherent defilement). That they are neither identical nor different also has ten gates, which may be understood by analogy with these metaphors.
Furthermore, the rabbit is simultaneously born and dead without obstruction, and the headband is simultaneously hidden and manifest without obstruction. This...

The various gates of birth and death, concealment and manifestation, and the interlacing of the adverse and the favorable are all fused together; reflect upon them as before, and they will be understood.

(Since this treatise frequently employs metaphors of illusion throughout its preceding and succeeding sections, I have cited the "Chapter on the Rabbit" to bring about immediate understanding. Those who contemplate deeply may find it obscure, but do not reproach me for the prolixity of the text.)

One who can awaken to the single characteristic praises the preceding hundredfold assemblies for their diversity yet ultimate convergence into the same. Indeed, because there is a lingering attachment to difference, it must be dispelled;
that is the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), which is far removed from the three characteristics and perfects the three virtues. Because this is precisely the One Mind, it is called True Suchness.
The statement that "one who can awaken to the single characteristic as being the dharma of no-characteristic" praises the subsequent stage of sweeping away traces to enter the profound mystery.

Fearing that one might stagnate in [the notion of] sameness, it is further negated; this is what is meant by the True Suchness Gate (Tathatā-mukha), which says: "That which is called 'True Suchness' is likewise without characteristics."

Regarding the phrase "the exposition seeking the meaning" (*yìzhī shù*) and so forth: this means that the preceding section on the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) follows the scriptural text entirely;

therefore, it is said that "based on this scriptural text, the gate of common characteristics is established. Now, as for the gate of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), one merely takes the intended meaning of the scripture rather than relying on its literal wording;
therefore, it is said that "the exposition seeking the meaning establishes the gate of distinct characteristics."

Regarding the direct explanation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are two meanings: if one refers to the preceding text, there is no further explanation of them because that was the arising and ceasing of the mind;

if one refers to the subsequent section, it has not yet explained the extraordinary and inconceivable nature of causes and conditions. Therefore, it is said that the former is the primary explanation while the latter is supplementary.
The Commentary says: "Within this very passage there are two gates. This refers back to the initial statement regarding arising and ceasing where it was said, "In this, there are two gates.
Question: In both instances, the word "in this" (*atra*) is a term referring to what is proximate;

why then is that [previous] section restricted solely to the preceding statement, while in this current section it is said to extend through the subsequent text as well? Answer: It is the same as before; it does not encompass the subsequent text. Why? Because... [text continues].

This refers to the conclusion of the explanation of this proclamation, where it is immediately concluded by stating: "The 'Gate of Resolving Doubts through Explanations Scattered According to the Text' has already been taught.

Thus, one knows that [the previous claim] is incorrect. Furthermore, it is asked: The *Śāstra* states, "Next is the Gate of Extensive Explanation," and herein two chapters and so forth clearly encompass what follows;

why then is the preceding text not the same as this? The answer is: That was the major section (mahā-vibhāga), which has already been completed here; this is the subordinate section (avāntara-vibhāga).

Regarding the section on the "Gate of Extensive Explanation by Way of Analogy through Irreversible Examples," its text is diffuse and does not explicitly state that it pertains to this specific section;
therefore, it applies to the subsequent text. However, the phrase "in this section" (此中) is definitively restricted to the current section alone and does not extend to what follows.

Consequently, since the preceding and succeeding parts differ, they cannot be treated as a single standard. Furthermore, since that single utterance has no connection whatsoever with the text of the subsequent section, how could it [be applied there]?
Suddenly, anticipating this, [the author] has now raised both points together in this single statement to encompass the subsequent section;
therefore, one must point out that the underlying principle ought to be thus: since the two passages differ, how can they be treated as identical?

"First, 'collecting the meaning to reveal the tenet' (*śāstrārtha-saṃgraha*) means to gather the meanings of the various causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and to manifest the tenet of this treatise regarding those causes and conditions;
alternatively, it refers to what is the tenet common to all the teachings. Thus, the ancients said:

'The Confucian tenet is the five constants, the Daoist tenet is spontaneity (*svabhāva*), and the Buddhist tenet is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is precisely what is meant. It is truly because this chapter correctly discriminates the causes."

Regarding the sense of "condition" (*pratyaya*) within the essence of the manifest consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*): its essence possesses two meanings, namely, principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*).

If one relies on the essence according to principle, because the former [the object] is viewed in relation to that consciousness, it has the meaning of being a "cause" (*hetu*), as it accords with the divine cognition. Now, when viewed in relation to those [objective] images (*nimitta*), it can possess the meaning of a "condition."

Because the object (artha) and the consciousness (vijñāna) are distinct, if one considers them from the perspective of their actual substance, the preceding consciousness, when viewed in relation to the [subsequent] consciousness, possesses the sense of being a cause (*hetu*), as their mode of comprehension is identical.

However, because the subsequent consciousness, when viewed in relation to its object-image (*nimitta*), may possess the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—since its comprehension is distinct from that [of the preceding consciousness]—one may apply the same logic to the object-image: it also possesses both the sense of a cause and an object-condition.

That is to say, while the manifest image is provisionally attributed to the subjective perceiver, when viewed in relation to that very image, it possesses the sense of being a cause; thus, it returns to its original identity with the consciousness.

Therefore, if one considers it in relation to that consciousness, it possesses the meaning of being an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), yet it is distinct from "cognition" (*vijñapti*) because their meanings are contrary.

If it pertains to the object itself, it merely acts as a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*), for it lacks the essential nature of a mental dharma and is deficient in the sense of being contrary to the cognition of that mind-consciousness. Thus, the treatise does not explicitly designate it as possessing the further meaning of being a "cause-condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*);

this may be due to an omission in the text or because the phrasing is elliptical. Even when considered in terms of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa*), it also possesses the meaning of being a cause; furthermore, even insentient things are a form of non-enlightenment (*abodhi*).
Therefore, regarding the characteristics of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the *Qiānshān* edition reads "six coarse [phenomena]" (*ṣaḍaudārika*), whereas the current version is erroneous.
As for the statement that "retribution is the beginning," etc., the question is: how does retribution serve as the cause for karma? The answer is: because of the retribution... [text fragment].

Furthermore, because the superior [level] again creates karma identical to that of other teachings, it subsequently gives rise to delusion due to the gravity of that karma. Thus, the preceding text states that the characteristic of cessation is universally applicable;

when viewed from the perspective of the self [the lower level], it all exerts power upon the superior [level]. Alternatively, one may simply say that they are designated as "karma" and so forth only in relation to their respective fruits.
In this way, within our own school (*svayūthya*), they are established through mutual dependence, standing in opposition to one another and serving as both cause and effect.
Furthermore, this is precisely the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): since beginningless time, these ten factors exist simultaneously and possess no temporal sequence.

As the aforementioned treatise states, all four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) coexist; just as a house cannot be completed if even one component is missing, they are mutually dependent, and only through their mutual reliance can the house be established.
Likewise, if even a single factor among the [twelve] links of existence is missing, the arising of a sentient being cannot be established.
Because they can only be established through the mutual dependence of ten factors, these ten arise with one another as conditions;
now, according to the sequence of their meanings, we shall explain the downward-to-upward and upward-to-downward causal conditions, just as a son nurtures his father.

Furthermore, regarding "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth, there are three successive stages of refutation: first, refutation by way of impermanence (*anityatā*); second, refutation by way of selflessness (*anātman*);

and third, refutation by way of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*). This is based on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, which frequently establishes these gates. The preceding [section] refutes the attachment to emptiness and the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) by means of conventional analysis (*prajñapti-vyavahāra*);

this section refutes the attachment to existence and the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) by means of analyzing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*). Together, they constitute the dual [refutation].
This is the Middle Way, which equally distances itself from the two extremes; it is the contemplation of the three aspects of the one mind simultaneously.
As for the phrase "Why is this so? (何者), this refers to the question: "Why is it that sentient beings possess mind and consciousness? This explains the initial inquiry.

The first round of question and answer established that because there is mind and consciousness, there is Buddha-nature. This subsequent inquiry and explanation establishes that because there is Buddha-nature, [there is mind and consciousness].

The mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) is established precisely through the two aspects of nature (*prakṛti*) and cognition (*vijñapti*). Furthermore, for the purpose of reaching ultimate quiescence, there are two main divisions:
first, the refutation of provisional and limited names; second, the establishment of the real and universal designation. Within this, there are three parts, which correspond to the Three Truths:
first, up to the phrase "all are illusory transformations," which constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); the following two phrases constitute... [the remaining portion of the text].
The final four phrases of Paramārtha’s translation correspond to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). The preceding statement that "it is quiescent" means it is not existent;

the subsequent statement that "it is also quiescent" means it is not empty. Because it is like "empty emptiness," it belongs to the true essence (*tattva*). This is identical to what the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"I say that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are empty (ultimate truth), yet they are also provisional designations (conventional truth), and they are also... [the middle way].

Regarding the meaning of the Middle Way (the First Noble Truth): because this treatise explains the causes and conditions of prior arising and ceasing, it is identical to those things produced by causes and conditions.

If one discusses phenomena (*dharma*) from the perspective of their objective realm, the three truths are fused and integrated without restriction. If one speaks from the perspective of the mind, the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) in every thought-moment are likewise without obstruction.
If one gradually cultivates and practices them while further incorporating the three types of cessation (*śamatha*), then even the contemplation of emptiness carries the essence itself.

True cessation with provisional contemplation (*zhen-zhi jià-guān*) involves the cessation that accords with conditions while carrying skillful means (*fāngbiàn*); cessation with provisional contemplation that accords with conditions (*suíyuán zhì zhōng guān*) involves the cessation that is detached from the discrimination of the two extremes.
These three modes of cessation and contemplation are instantaneously and simultaneously present within a single mind, for such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Thus, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi said: "In destroying all delusions, nothing surpasses emptiness (*śūnyatā*); in establishing all phenomena, nothing surpasses the provisional; in reaching the ultimate of all natures..."
Because the Great is within the Middle, therefore in the One-Middle all are the Middle; there is nothing that is not empty of the Middle, nor anything that is not the Middle of the provisional.

The same applies to the provisional. This is precisely the phenomenal aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): it is like the three eyes of Maheśvara, which are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they separate from one another.

(Master Daomeng transmitted mind through mind, without employing names or numbers, directly for those of the highest capacity and wisdom, so that they might forget the trap and forget the intent; thus it is the same as yet different from this teaching. Master Zhiyi exhausted principle and reached its ultimate...)

Because it is the gateway in which the nature is fully perfected, it differs from the Chan school yet is not different from it. When the three contemplations are perfectly accomplished, the Dharmakāya is attained without seeking; one is thus liberated and does not remain like a pauper.
Regarding the mundane truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is said that all are the *ālayavijñāna*, because they all possess the sense of "storing" and the capacity to "encompass.

Furthermore, because they act as the cause and can maintain the fruit, they are all the *manas*, because they all possess the sense of "producing" and "relying upon. They are all... [the text continues].

Since all consciousnesses possess the meaning of arising based on the mind (*manas*), they are likewise all "not [the ālayavijñāna]. The former was based on their being not different [from it], while this is based on their being not one [with it].
Therefore, each of the nine aspects has its own distinct name; they are not all designated by the general names such as *ālaya* and so forth. Question:

How do we know that this is not explained in terms of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)? Answer: Because within this conventional realm, the emptiness of intrinsic nature has not yet been taught; next, [it is taught] in relation to...
Only then does Paramārtha begin to explain it.
Regarding "inconceivable" and so forth: this means that although it is one, the three aspects are not identical and thus cannot be conceived as one;
yet, although it is three, the single essence is without distinction and thus cannot be conceived as three. Furthermore, it can be both three and one, and is neither...

The three are not one, yet they cannot be definitively conceptualized as the three dharmas of emptiness, conventionality, and the middle. This is because while the principle is perfect, words are partial;

when words express it, the principle is lost, and thus it cannot be conceptualized. Furthermore, since phenomena are without marks (*animitta*), if one attempts to think of them through mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*), confusion arises, and thus they cannot be thought of.

Moreover, they cannot be definitively designated by terms such as *ālayavijñāna* and so forth. Because they are spoken of by way of provisional names (*prajñapti*), the three names are also applicable.
It is because they are unimpeded. This is the general proof; in the prose explaining the principle, the names of the truths each possess the meaning of being unimpeded.
Regarding the "non-arising of the seven, five, etc.": within these five phrases, the first three refer to the True Truths (*satya*), and the latter two refer to the Middle Truth.
The seventh, fifth, eighth, and sixth [phrases] correspond to the three subtle and six coarse [aspects]. Thus, the eight consciousnesses and nine characteristics are all empty; this is then...
True reality (*satyārtha*) is also emptiness; "non-existence" means it is not existence, and "emptiness" means it is not non-emptiness.
This is the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "all phenomena," there are three parts below this: first is the designation as empty, and next, from "all" onwards, is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Within this, there are again two [aspects]: the first is the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and the latter, "all sentient beings," is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The subsequent passage, "even the body does not exist," refers to the emptiness of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-śūnyatā*). Thus, among the five—namely, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*)—the former three constitute non-enlightenment (*a-vibodha*);
the present passage refers to the emptiness of those same three aspects of non-enlightenment. This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "and can cause [them] to act," the Venerable Xianshou says: "This refers to first inducing [the seeds] to arise and then maturing them;

subsequently, it induces those that have matured to obtain their fruit. Because these two stages differ, other teachings state that 'the karma that initiates action is initiated once, while the karma that moistens is moistened many times.
Here, it is the same. This *saṃtati-vijñāna* (continuum-consciousness) possesses two meanings: first, it is named 'continuum' (*saṃtati*) based on its own nature, which is consciousness itself."
The preceding proponent argues that because the consciousness associated with the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is not severed, this "successive consciousness" derives its name from another;
such a thesis can cause afflictions, karma, and suffering to continue without interruption.
Regarding the phrase "the revolving of mind-only" (*cittamātra-parāvṛtti*) and so forth, the *Nāga-śāstra* clarifies that the root text possesses two meanings.

First, it states: "If that is so," and so on. The commentary below this serves to resolve potential objections. Within the former, there are again two parts: first, based on the treatise, it reveals that the text explicitly negates all phenomena;
for the eleven types of manas mentioned above all arise based upon the fundamental awakening of true mind (*tathatā-citta*). Therefore, the present passage is stated to provide a concluding summary.
"Returning to Mind-Only" is divided here into two parts: first, the interrogation and explanation that correctly elucidate the preceding section;

second, the interrogation and explanation of the reasons why "all phenomena arise from the mind," which follows the phrase "all phenomena are mind-only. This latter part addresses the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the treatise while simultaneously clearing away the notion of "mind," because when false phenomena are exhausted, the true mind also ceases to exist.
If this is so, since the mind does not perceive the mind, and this is an explicit statement, why is it called "hidden" (*guhya*)?
The answer is: That [passage] dispels the deluded mind, while this one brushes away the true mind; therefore, they do not contradict each other in principle.
Second, regarding the "above and below," both explain the meaning of the original treatise. First, the interrogation and explanation clarify the main point:

it is because the aforementioned single mind follows ignorance to produce the eleven consciousnesses that it is said that the three realms are merely the transformation of mind. This mind, following its habitual perfuming, manifests as if it were real, yet it is called "empty" because it is hidden.

The nature of emptiness manifests deceptive appearances as real states, which are termed "false. Although these manifestations of falsehood are manifold, when their causes and conditions are investigated, they are seen to be produced solely by the mind. Therefore, the root text says: "For this reason, the three realms are false," and so forth.

Next, the following section explains this meaning. First, the intent of the question is: since sensory objects currently exist, how can it be said that they are "mind-only"? Subsequently, the intent of the answer is as follows: [The answer: Because all phenomena arise from the mind, they are called "mind-only. Just as a painter creates various forms through the power of his own mind, so too does the mind manifest the various appearances of the triple world. Furthermore, because these appearances are devoid of intrinsic substance, they are called "false. Moreover, because they are not established apart from the mind, they are called "mind-only. This is why it is said that the three realms are false and mind-only. As for the phrase "the three realms," it refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. "False" means lacking true reality; "mind-only" means that there is nothing external to the mind.

This is because all phenomena are produced by the mind and have no other basis. This is the meaning of the passage. Furthermore, the subsequent text explains the reasons for this. First, the question asks: if external objects are presently perceived, how can one say they are merely the mind? The answer subsequently clarifies that although objects appear, they are in fact transformations of the mind and have no external existence. Thus, it is established that the three realms are false and mind-only. This concludes the explanation of the first part of the text.

It is said that one perceives through the false conceptualization of persons; since "false conceptualization" (妄念) has the meaning of "discrimination" (分別), it is said that [perception] arises from false conceptualization.
Furthermore, it is like all discriminations within a dream, which are simply the discrimination of one's own mind.

Thus, there is only mind and no external objects. As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states: "Because one relies upon consciousness-only, the meaning that objects have no substantial reality is established."
Thus, one eliminates that object by means of the mind. Next, regarding the passage "all phenomena are mind-only" and below, which explains that "the mind does not see the mind" and so forth:
since objects do not exist, consciousness does not perceive itself; therefore, because there are no objects, consciousness does not arise. The second half of the verse in the treatise states:
"Because objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise. This, then, is the elimination of that mind by means of the object.
Regarding "that which is signless cannot be apprehended," this refers either exclusively to the mind or universally to both mind and its objects; all are empty and signless.
Next, from "If that were so" onwards, the text explains that one should know that from the mundane world up to the cessation of various phenomena. Within this section, there are four parts:
first, the summary of their mutual connection; second, ignorance is the root; third, the deluded mind is the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*), because all objective realms...

The realms (*dhātu*) are constituted by this, namely the manifesting consciousnesses (*nirmita-vijñāna*) and so forth. If ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been exhausted, these consciousnesses continue to dwell upon and sustain their objects without ceasing;
for this reason, the following provides an analogy to explain that all these objects abide in dependence upon the mind.
Thus, apart from the mind they have no substance, and just as a reflection has no form outside of a mirror, the mind likewise has no substance [apart from its objects].
Furthermore, internally there is no essence; this third point, "only mind and false delusion," explains the external by subduing doubt.
The doubt arises as follows: "Since it has no essence, why does it appear so vividly? Therefore, the treatise explains: "Only mind and false delusion.

These are all false manifestations upon the True Mind; where could an essence be found that can be apprehended? Fourth, from "with the mind" onwards, one uses internal reflection to verify that it is only mind.
Question: How is it known that objects manifested on the mind are illusory? Treatise: It is answered by saying, "Because the mind arises," and so forth.
This is known because when the mind arises, phenomena arise, and so on. This meaning follows from the previous statement:
"By the power of ignorance, the mind moves unconsciously, even to the point of manifesting all objective realms. Thus it is said, "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise."

Thus, because the mind and its objects mutually perfume and stir one another, it is said that they "arise. If ignorance ceases, all consciousnesses cease; therefore, it is said that the mind ceases and various phenomena cease.
This means that the source of the mind returns to purity, which is why it is called "ceasing. The intended meaning is this:

since the mind follows non-awakening and falsely manifests various objects, it is verified that these objects are merely the mind and have no independent substance. This is the essential purport of the entire teaching.
By means of the principle of the conjunction of causes and conditions, the meaning that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is established, and the meaning of non-abiding is revealed;
thus, the conjunction is concluded as belonging to the mind. This is why Xianshou is entirely in agreement with Nāgārjuna:

for various teachings state that because things arise dependently they lack intrinsic nature, and because they lack intrinsic nature they arise dependently. Furthermore, "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are [empty]."
Because they are equal in terms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, they attain equality; furthermore, this is the intended meaning of the treatise.

Subsequently, because the mind is directed downward to once again point back to the root treatise and correlate it with the assigned dharma-gates, the conclusion below exhorts: "One should examine them carefully according to their respective order.

This means that while the previous explanation merely provided a general interpretation of the textual meaning, the present [passage] again directs [the reader] to assign [the terms] specifically to the original text. Whether one relies on the first meaning or...
It may be said that the meaning of the first three successive stages belongs exclusively to the *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Commentary), yet it can also be understood as applicable more broadly.

Regarding the phrase "the various fundamental false attachments" (*vividha-mūla-viparyāsa*), one might ask: according to the interpretation in the *Vyākhyā*, these should pertain only to the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Why, then, does the subsequent section on the "category of the attachment to a person" (*pudgala-grāha*) belong to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? The answer is: the preceding [intention] and the subsequent consciousness are neither identical nor different. Now, based on their non-identity...
Because they are distinct, there is no contradiction; thus, the preceding root text refers to them as the "continuously evolving consciousness.

Regarding the three types of ordinary beings: the first person performs various karmas, the second person gives rise to the grasping of a self (*ātman*), and the third person gives rise to the grasping of phenomena (*dharma*);
these are the three distinctions.
Regarding the phrase "difficult for the hair-tuft to contend with" (*máo tóu nán jiǎo*), the *Qieyun* states that "contend" (*jiǎo*) means to compete;

the general meaning is that at this stage, contending with those afflictions and karmic actions (*kleśa-karman*) in terms of their power and capacity is extremely difficult. According to the citation in the *Chao*, this is the character "awaken" (*jué*); thus, it refers to the fact that the afflictions and karmic actions are difficult to perceive and awaken to.
"Definitely 'not attached' (*azhu*): according to the Qianshan edition, this character 'attached' (*zhu*) does not exist.
'Excellently superior and inconceivable' refers to the description of the third person in contrast to the preceding two.
Therefore, the inscription above designates this as the 'Section on Comparative Evaluation' (*jiaoliang fen*), because it evaluates the relative superiority and inferiority among the three persons."

Regarding the phrase "originally based on the perfuming of ignorance" and so forth, the intended meaning is that the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) is perfumed by ignorance, thereby acting as the causal condition for the arising of those consciousnesses.
Because these causal conditions are profound and subtle, they are difficult to clarify;

thus, the two preceding individuals cannot fathom them through thought or speech, and even their investigation into the causal conditions from which those consciousnesses arise remains ultimately unfathomable.

From the initial stage of right faith—that is, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)—one can realize the severance of fundamental ignorance at its root; this also extends through the ten stages of faith.

Because the subsequent text is abbreviated, it speaks only of those above the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*). Furthermore, regarding the "Worthy Dragon" (*kṣānti-nāga*), the text is again abbreviated and speaks only of those who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*).

Thus, we know that these are explained merely according to their superior excellence. As for the next phrase, the three levels of worthiness involve comparative contemplation and observation; therefore, [it follows] next.

Because the ten lower noble truths are directly realized through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those who cling to "associated defilement" (*saṃprayoga-kleśa*) should be understood according to the intent of the following explanation: that which stains pure conduct by being associated with the [defiled] mind is called "associated defilement.

This term applies generally to the entire aggregate; however, clinging specifically to a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) is restricted to the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). "Associated" refers to the defilement itself, interpreted as a *karmadhāraya* compound (the association is the defilement).

Furthermore, "clinging" (執) in the term "affliction of clinging-correspondence" (相應染) is a name derived from a specific factor representing the whole; it is also analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the specific term distinguishes the general.
Alternatively, "clinging" (執) may refer specifically to the affliction of correspondence (相應染), distinguishing it from the subsequent affliction of non-correspondence (不相應).

Thus, while the two characters "clinging-affliction" (執染) apply to both essence and function, the two characters "correspondence" (相應) are restricted solely to function. Accordingly, the analysis may be made as a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The following two cases follow this principle; the three types of non-associated [factors] should also be understood by analogy with this. Regarding the commentary’s further point concerning the correspondence between mind and mental objects (*citta-viṣaya-saṃprayoga*):
the phrase "the gates of permanence and impermanence" refers to the determination of eternal abiding, which corresponds to the passage on time;
"the essence-nature remaining unchanging" corresponds to the passage on place. As the treatise states: "From the very beginning (this is time), its self-nature is pure (this is place)."
Regarding the phrase "the gate of the impermanence of the permanent" and so forth: "permanent and eternal" (常恒) is contrasted with "impermanence" in the subsequent passage;

"permanence and change" (恒常變異) is contrasted with "place" in the subsequent passage. As the treatise states: "Permanent and eternal" refers to time, while "unchanging" refers to place. Furthermore, the term "permanent and eternal" also applies to place.

Regarding those aspects of the text that are visible: the phrase "the so-called lower clause" explains the upper phrase "the gate of the impermanence of the permanent," while the phrase "furthermore, failing to understand the lower clause" explains the upper phrase "the gate of the permanence of the impermanent.
That within the fundamental [nature] there is ignorance—these are both semantic phrases, not literal textual phrases.

Regarding the passage beginning with "As in the original, reaching the one," etc., Xianshou says: "If persons of the Two Vehicles reach the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), they have ultimately abandoned the afflictions of both seeing and cultivation.
Regarding "corresponding to faith" (śraddhā-samprayukta):
from the stage of the Ten Understandings (daśa-vyākhyāna) onward, the faculty of faith is perfected and there is no longer any falling back; this is called "corresponding to faith."

Therefore, in the *Dichilun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya), the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi are collectively termed the "Stage of Practice through Faith" (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*); the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-vṛtti* likewise states this.
Because these bodhisattvas have attained the vision of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), afflictions (*kleśa*) do not manifest; thus it is said they are "distant" from them.

This does not refer to their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), for they intentionally retain these afflictions. As the *Saṃgraha* states: "If one does not sever the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), one is no different from an ordinary person."
If one does not retain the seeds [of affliction], one is no different from those of the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, there are two intentions for retaining delusions: for oneself and for others.

This is explained according to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao). If one refers to the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), it is only from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward that one speaks of retaining delusions, as stated in other treatises.

The commentary states: "The difference between the Initial and Final Teachings regarding the retention of delusions spans one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; the provisional and the real are thus clearly illuminated."

Regarding the phrase "subsequently attained [wisdom] and so forth": although the wisdom of fundamental realization (*mūla-jñāna*) eliminates the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it does not yet realize that the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is itself purity.

Because this [obstruction to knowledge] is not designated by the term "elimination," and because it is only through the wisdom of subsequent attainment (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*)—which perceives it as pure—that the designation "elimination" is established, it is said:
"This is what is eliminated. Thus, these two types of wisdom take the objects of the two truths as their respective domains and eliminate the delusions of the two truths individually.

In other writings as well, there are discussions on mutual identity (*samasamāpatti*): for instance, when the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) are refuted and the characteristics of the continuous mind (*prabandhacitta*) are extinguished, the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) simultaneously severs both.
Furthermore, in being able to reveal various dharmas and meanings according to how each sentient being should attain understanding, the fundamental wisdom also takes the conventional as its object.
Since this is the case for both principle-wisdom (*li-zhi*) and insight-wisdom (*li-zhi*), it is likewise so for the wisdom of cognition (*liang-zhi*).

This is indeed so; therefore, Qingliang [Zongmi] states that within the eighth of the ten levels of distinction between the two schools of Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang)—the distinction between the subject and object of abandonment and realization—the two types of wisdom each possess two capacities: first, the capacity to abandon delusions, and second, the capacity to realize the principle.

Regarding what is called "original enlightenment following defilement" (*mūlajñāna-anuśayita-saṃkleśa-citta*): original enlightenment, in its universal functioning, is neither identical to nor different from the phenomena produced by it.
Now, based on their non-difference, it is precisely the mind-king that is produced; this is because we do not grasp at the true mind as the producer.
Thus, it may also be called the deluded mind produced by original enlightenment following defilement. As the subsequent text states: "In dependence upon defilement and purity..."

The distinction between the mind that relies on original enlightenment (fundamental awakening) is termed "pure mindfulness," while that which relies on non-awakening is termed "defiled"; this signifies that each follows its own respective and proximate cause.
Therefore, because the bases upon which they rely differ, they are said to be "associated" [in the former case] and "non-associated" [in the latter].

Since there is no basis for the distinction between defilement and purity in the absence of [a separate] non-awakening, the two attain association; for original non-awakening has no further basis for defilement.
Because of this principle, the treatise states: "The mind itself, in its lack of awakening, is eternally without distinction; the mind is thus the three subtle [states], which are the deluded mind.
This is because it either arises based upon that true mind or evolves based upon that deluded mind.

Consequently, there is no other defiled dharma upon which it depends that could manifest as distinct from those three subtle states; therefore, it cannot be said that both [the true and deluded minds] are attained separately.

If this is so, how does it accord with the previous statement that ignorance (*avidyā*) as the cause gives rise to the three subtle states? Is this not a case where cause and effect are distinct? Answer:

That [previous] passage speaks of cause and effect based on the conventional distinction between the prior and subsequent stages of the subtle and the coarse. Now, however, we are speaking in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), which exists simultaneously and cannot be divided into two distinct entities.

This is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned treatise’s statement: "The three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) do not measure [the higher stages], for the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are not their objective domain. This refers to the very same principle.
Regarding the phrase "the three types of characteristics are identical": this means that although their bases differ, they are known to have the same object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If so, why [is it said] "identical"? The intention is: if they are thus identical in being known as having the same object-condition, why does that sūtra state that they function in opposition?
The statement that "the contrary follows above and the compliant follows below" must refer to those two aforementioned movements of up and down;
since the corresponding defilement opposes its upward movement and complies with its downward movement, it is described in this way.

Regarding "contradiction" (*viruddha*): contradiction means the sense of being different. That is to say, these three phrases correspond respectively to the preceding three phrases as their opposites:
"the mind itself is non-awakening" (*cittam evāpratibodhaḥ*) is the opposite of the previous "mind recollects phenomena" (*cittaṃ dharmān manasikaroti*);

"there is no distinction between the extraordinary and the ordinary" (*na viśeṣo 'sti*) is the opposite of the previous "based on the distinction between defilement and purity" (*saṃkleśavyavadānaviśeṣāt*). The subsequent phrase should be understood accordingly; therefore, it is called "contradiction."
Regarding that which should be carefully examined and discerned, the root treatise sets forth the reasons for the obstruction of wisdom in three sections.

First, because all phenomena are eternally abiding, quiescent, and immovable; as the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states, "All phenomena are eternally abiding" (just as a rabbit's horn is fundamentally a hemp cloth).
Second, it is because through ignorance one fails to realize that the myriad phenomena are entirely [the nature of reality].
When it is said that there is a "separate dharma" distinct from true suchness (tathatā) and false seeing, this refers to all dharmas mentioned above. Therefore, the aforementioned treatise states:
"Because one does not know true suchness as being a single dharma, the mind arises through non-awakening and possesses conceptualization. It further states:

"Because one does not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm, thoughts suddenly arise in a manner dissociated from the mind; this is called ignorance (avidyā). (It is like a person who is deluded by an illusion...)
This means that because one subsequently clings to a real rabbit through false perception, one cannot comprehend the conventional nature of a single atom.

Due to the inverted mind that clings to a real rabbit, one will never truly understand even a single hair of an illusory rabbit. As a verse says: "If one does not realize *tathatā*, there is no way to understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusory things—though they exist, they are not real.
The commentary states: the first two sections of the treatise correspond to the first line of the verse.
Because it does not descend subsequently, the verse below provides a separate record, also stating that ignorance (*avidyā*) is non-comprehension;
since movement is itself stillness, one is thus unable to discern distinctions within movement.

Regarding the "two obstacles" (*āvaraṇa*) and "two hindrances" (*vibandha*), one interpretation states: the two obstacles are exclusively severed during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and do not persist into the fruit;
therefore, these two hindrances—being afflictions (*kleśa*)—pertain to both cause and fruit, and are thus said to be "severed.

As for the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it pertains only to the fruit and is thus said to be "not severed," because its substance is not severed during the causal stage. This is because, within the causal stage, one is severable while the other is not.

Furthermore, this is explained with respect to the intrinsic nature of ignorance (*avidyā*); it also applies to its function, as it is severed through cultivation. Therefore, the preceding text states:

"From the stage of association with faith, one observes and realizes its severance," and the aforementioned commentary also says: "To diminish the power of ignorance" refers precisely to the function of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
One interpretation holds that while the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is said to be exclusively severed, the obstacle to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)...
Regarding the fact that [ignorance] is never interrupted, the verse of the *Śāstra* states: "Thus, these six types of ignorance are non-distinct in their essential nature.

Furthermore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says: "Fundamental ignorance can act as the material cause for illusions within illusory persons, and it can act as the material cause for virtues within those possessing virtue;
it cannot be apprehended as either one or many. Moreover, Qingliang says: "I [take] ignorance as..."
Because one realizes the path of perfect awakening through its essential nature, the repayment of the debt of ignorance is inexhaustible.

Since it has been stated that they are identical in essence and function together, and that "it is not possible to sever half [of them]," the fact that the repayment of the debt is inexhaustible implies that they are not severed. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"In this context, 'severing' means not abandoning ignorance; it is not a severing by means of eradication. If this is so, how is it then?

Is the meaning of "severance" established? It refers to the severing of afflictions such that the mind no longer gives rise to them. However, citing the primordial severance (*mūla-prahāṇa*) to prove the initial [severance] is because the treatise states:

"The virtues now first arising have existed from the beginning. Furthermore, since both [the initial and primordial severances] are equally ignorance (*avidyā*), it is said that they are like the color of a single night;
this metaphor for fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is that people perceive this darkness just as they perceive other delusions. Thus, one perceives ignorance through delusion.

When one with reddened eyes sees light, it is like the Buddha’s wisdom awakening to see that ignorance is pure; it merely requires changing the person's eyesight, there being no need to eliminate the darkness.
This accords with the tenet of this treatise. Question: As stated above, the characteristic of cessation is in fact a dharma of pure merit;

should it not likewise be "non-interruption" (anupaccheda)? Answer: It was stated above that there are two gates of "interruption": first, the meaning of identity of substance and identity of characteristic.
Therefore, it is said that the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is pure because it cannot be severed;

thus, the *Caryā-apratiprasrabdhi-sūtra* states, "Desire itself is the path," and so forth, based on the principle that two things may have different entities and different characteristics. Furthermore, it is said that awakening to the characteristic of cessation as being truly a fault is something that can be severed;
thus, the *Mūla-jñāna-sūtra* speaks of "fundamental ignorance, darkness," and so forth. Now, according to this alternative perspective (*paryāya*), their essence (*tattva*) is likewise [different].

It is not something to be severed, for how could it be the same as the common meaning of "constantly proceeding"? Furthermore, it may be that the characteristic of cessation also involves the integration of the true and the false;
however, because one perceives the falsity as a defect, it must be severed in every respect. Because one has not yet perceived the truth as a virtue, it is never severed.
Now, this fundamental falsity is also not severed, as it differs from the characteristic of cessation; since it is not severed, it is characterized by cessation.
The "non-interruption" (a-prahāṇa) in relation to this [state] and the "non-interruption" [of the two paths] are not the same; therefore, the aforementioned treatise states:

"The ten stages are not the domain [of others], the three levels of worthies do not measure them, and only a Buddha can fully comprehend them; one must not speak of them recklessly. However, according to the scriptures, such terms as "provisionally named" or "figuratively designated" are used;
thus, these words are verified.

(Treatise, Fascicle 5). Regarding the characteristics of origination and cessation (*utpāda-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), according to the fundamental intent of the treatise, one enters this section specifically to explain the characteristics of the causes and conditions for origination and cessation within the "Establishment of the Meaning" (*siddhārtha-vibhāga*) division.
The two characters "origination and cessation" (*shengmie*) are precisely the name of this section;

the "characteristics of causes and conditions" merely clarify the specific distinctions among those dharmas of origination and cessation. Therefore, it can simply be said that these are the "causes and conditions of origination and cessation."

Because it is the characteristic of cessation, the long section is divided into three parts to explain those three types; the first two have already been completed, and now the third shall be addressed.

Regarding the phrase "the wind is severed," the commentary cites the treatise, noting that there is the character *xiàng* (characteristic) following the character *fēng* (wind); this refers to the wind.
The preceding sections directly address the *prajñā* of signlessness; the term "sign" (*lakṣaṇa*) here refers merely to the wind and does not pertain to the meaning of the mental faculty (*manas*).

As for the phrase "the mind attains continuity": because the fundamental essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is indestructible, the characteristics of the mind continue in succession to form a collection of delusions;
this may be equated with the previous metaphor of the continuity of the characteristics of the wind.

Regarding the phrase "coarse, heavy, arising, and ceasing," the intended meaning is that the characteristics of coarseness and subtlety, as well as arising and ceasing, correspond or do not correspond with the substantial essence of those coarse and subtle minds.
Thus, the original text states that "characteristics" (*xiàng*) refers to "characteristic-phenomena" (*yìxiàng*).

This is largely consistent with the four characteristics (*cixiāng*) among the hundred dharmas (*bǎifǎ*), which are subsumed under the category of non-corresponding formations (*bùxiāngying xíng*) as provisional phenomena; whereas the eight consciousnesses (*bāshí*) are subsumed under the category of the real phenomena of mind (*xīn shífǎ*).

However, coarse, provisional characteristics are associated with the mind because they are manifested through their marks, just as great waves are associated with water because their movement is coarse.

Subtle, provisional characteristics cannot be said to be associated with the essence of the mind because their marks are hidden, just as a flowing stream that is not flowing cannot be said to be associated with the moisture of water because its movement is subtle. Therefore, the scripture is cited:
"Flowing and pouring forth" refers to the arising and ceasing; "arising and ceasing" refers to these two [aspects].
"Partial conformity and non-conformity" means that the intent belongs to the two categories of correspondence and non-correspondence.
Regarding the "entirety of the aspect of independent activity," since it is said to be the most subtle and exclusively within the domain of the Buddhas, one should say it is "independent."
One portion of the coarse aspect of karmic characteristics has already merged with the coarse aspect of the resultant state;
since this is severed across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is like the movement of wind that must gradually subside, and the waves likewise gradually cease.

One cannot, however, say that the waves ceased first. Therefore, the preceding text states: "From the stage of faith-correspondence (*śraddhā-pratipanna-bhūmi*), one observes, trains in, and severs [defilements] until reaching purity."
The statement that "the mind-ground attains detachment according to its capacity" refers to this.

Now, based on the explanation of the fourth [level] within the fourfold classification—the subtlest of the subtle—it is said that it cannot be entirely subsumed under the coarse within the subtle, because it functions as the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).

However, when viewed horizontally in contrast to others, it is merely subtle; thus, it belongs only to the fourth [category]. When viewed vertically from the perspective of the preceding levels, each preceding one...

Regarding the statement that "the subsequent [factors] are coarse because they are subtle," this means they pervade all stages and are abandoned gradually. If so, how can they be abandoned simultaneously with the coarse factors?

The answer is: because the meanings of "contrary to the faculties" (*indriya-vipakṣa*) and "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*) differ; furthermore, this may simply be stated according to the point of their final exhaustion.
"The mirror-consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*) manifested by false conceptualization" refers precisely to the aforementioned perfuming (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false conceptualization;
furthermore, it is as explained above that the essence of the mirror-consciousness functions as the cause.

Regarding the phrase "because they are gradually countered in their respective order," this refers to the sequence of the principles involved rather than a sequence of temporal duration. If that is so, what [is the meaning]?

Is it not the case that one abandons [afflictions] by proceeding from the coarse toward the subtle? The answer is: Yes. As the preceding treatise states, this is for the purpose of distinguishing the sequence of awakening through initial realization (*ādikṣaṇika-abhisamaya*);
therefore, for now, we speak of abandoning the coarse based on the subtle. In reality, however, they have been abandoned simultaneously from the very beginning.
Regarding "not abandoning" and so forth, there are two aspects here: first, not abandoning is called "severance"; second, severing obstacles is called "severance. These also have two meanings:

first, the principle of the emptiness of essence is non-dual, while the essence of phenomena is non-existent; this refers to the fact that afflictions are fundamentally empty by nature, as taught in many scriptures.
Second, the essence of wisdom-obstacles is fundamentally existent; this is what is taught in this treatise. The verse says: "In accordance with the meaning..."
Establishing different names does not entail any difference in their essential nature. Furthermore, it is said that there are these six kinds of fundamental ignorance and so forth;

however, when speaking from the perspective of their identical substance (*tongti*), there is no such thing as "darkness" in principle. Because this substance possesses the meaning of "existence" while being non-existent in principle, it is called "non-abandonment" despite being termed "severance.
Because that substance is empty in essence and non-existent in principle, it is called "severance" through its removal. Therefore, they are established as one.
The meaning of "cessation" (prahāṇa) is distinct.

That is to say, regarding the statement that "the mind which has severed the afflictions is correctly explained as 'severing' because [the afflictions] do not arise," this is intended to dispel doubt.

Specifically, one might doubt that this is not the same as [merely] not abandoning ignorance while calling it "cessation"; therefore, it is now clarified by stating "because they are severed and do not arise. This is largely consistent with the general characteristic [of cessation].
The meaning of the severance of the self-nature of the school’s tenet—that ignorance is also like the severance of the bonds of conditions—is seen extensively in the preceding text.

However, as for the phrase "if [they are] equal," since the topical outline (*pīṭhikā*) has already determined this, the current commentary further explains: "The above generally clarifies the intent of the objection;

from here below, the text is properly analyzed. Next, it says: "Fundamental awakening perishes together [with the delusions], leaving nothing behind. This encompasses two meanings; if one relies upon...

Since the topical outline (*ko-wen*) already addressed the difficulty regarding that which precedes the seal, if one were to follow this interpretation, it would only constitute a subsequent objection.

Now, as we are correctly introducing [the topic], these two points are contained within the phrase "if the mind ceases. That being so, the intention is that what arises later depends on what arose before;
thus, having first explained what has already arisen, there follows the discussion of "if" and so forth.
Regarding those of false certainty (*mithyā-niyata*), the mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that one proceeds from the stage of fruition to the stage of the noble ones constitutes right certainty;
furthermore, reaching the initial stage of faith constitutes indeterminate certainty, while reaching the long-flowing stream constitutes false certainty.

If it is argued that entering into falsity gives rise to the manifestation of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and thus does not constitute creating falsity oneself, this is incorrect. Why then do you not manifest and transform within that assembly of the correct and non-dual?

Regarding the phrase "the mutual perfuming of the defiled and the pure," the intent of this section encompasses both general and specific meanings. Generally, it comprehensively clarifies the three preceding chapters;

that is to say, these are the characteristics of the causes and conditions of the mind’s arising and ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha*), and since each of them contains the principle of perfuming and arising, they are all displayed collectively by this text.
Otherwise, why would it follow after those three chapters? Specifically, however, it clarifies only the arising of one [characteristic].
"All dharmas" refers to the gate of arising and ceasing. The initial discourse states: "The mind’s arising and ceasing is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*," and so forth, up to:
"This consciousness has two meanings that can encompass all dharmas and give rise to all dharmas.

What are these two? First is the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); second is the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*). This is a general clarification. As for what is called the "meaning of awakening," it continues as follows:

Because the nature of defilement and the distinctions within illusion are different, they are explained separately as encompassing all phenomena; that is to say, since both awakening and non-awakening are cited, there is no phenomenon not included.
From this point onward, the arising of all phenomena is explained separately; that is to say, because there is no phenomenon that does not arise from the four kinds of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Question: How does one transcend those characteristics of causes and conditions? Answer: The three chapters in continuous succession correctly clarify what was established above.
As for the remaining portions not yet exhausted, they will be explained separately later; once the latter two are exhausted, they will no longer be discussed. Thus, the second treatise states:

"Such various characteristics of the differentiation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that encompass sentient beings will be clearly revealed in the section on the 'Determination of Particular Characteristics' (*viśeṣa-viniścaya-bhāga*). This is what that refers to.

Regarding the phrase "there are six meanings," etc.: first is the wondrous existence (*miao-you*); next, two are the true emptiness (*zhen-kong*); the second is named emptiness; the third is the emptiness of characteristics (*xiang-kong*);
the fourth is the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence; the fifth excludes the heterodox paths (*waidao*); and the sixth excludes the provisional and the small vehicles (*quan-xiao*).

As Dharmapāla states, because both the subject (*neng*) and the object (*suo*) each possess four kinds of meanings, only then can they establish perfuming (*xunxi*); all other dharmas are not so. This is the case here.

It is likewise because both the agent and the object each possess six kinds of meanings that they are established as having "perfuming" (*vāsanā*); all other cases are not so, following this same principle.
Furthermore, within the summary [of these categories], there are immeasurable meanings, not merely six.

Regarding the subsequent inclusion of the *antarābhava* (intermediate state): this refers to the four lower dharmas each being opened into two types, with the sole exception of the *ālambana* (objective field), which remains as before and is not included.
However, based on the meaning of their single substance, they are divided into two types of perfuming. Among the remaining three types, each includes one of the others:

within the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness) is included the *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness); within *avidyā* (ignorance) is included the branch-ignorance; and within *tathatā* (suchness) is included the deluded mind. This is the correct [interpretation].

The substance consists of four and the meanings consist of eight; this is because within each of the [first] one, two meanings are distinguished. Thus, within those that are included, the substance and meaning each have four:

namely, the other two [aspects] each have one, while the deluded mind is divided into two—due to the perfuming by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the perfuming by the *manas*—thereby forming four.
Regarding "all defiled phenomena" (*sarvakliṣṭadharma*): because the deluded mind (*vikalpacitta*) that is concomitant within True Suchness (*tathatā*) is also termed "defiled.
*Bhanda* and so forth refers here to the "Forest of Assembled Ghosts" (*bhūtagaṇavana*). *Kṣemamantrī* is translated here as "Fragrance of Fear."
"Brahmavana" and so forth are here translated as "Forest of the Abode of Immortals. "Dhama" and so forth are here translated as "Immortal Fragrance.
That there is truly no defiler refers to immutability; that there is the appearance of defilement refers to following conditions.
To claim that there is truly no pure karma would contradict others while conforming to oneself;
whereas to maintain that there is the function of purity contradicts oneself while conforming to others. This is all the more so given that it possesses the six aforementioned meanings.

Furthermore, because it is said that "all are illusory transformations," this differs from the fixed-characteristics teachings of the provisional vehicles (*upāya-śāsana*), which cannot be further altered such that defilement and purity might interchangeably become one another.
Now, there is no fixed nature; the provisional designations of defilement and purity merely undergo transformation according to conditions, and thus there is no further obstruction.
Third, regarding the "Gate of Initiating Questions and Answers to Resolve Doubts" and so forth:

[Question] Since these latter two gates both belong to the second category, the aspect of purity (*śuddha-lakṣaṇa*), how can they constitute the main body of the text? [Answer] The former two gates are the actual [subject matter].

The explanation of the latter two sections serves to resolve the difficulties regarding the defiled category without obstruction, while specifically addressing the difficulties concerning the pure category.

If this is so, one might ask why they should not be divided into two major parts—the first for the formal explanation and the second for resolving objections. The answer is: to avoid excessive textual prolixity, we have merely extended the divisions.

Question: Since the *Xia lun* (Treatise on the Lower Part) speaks only of the two conditions of difference (*chā*) and levelness (*píng*), and does not mention "cause" (*yīn*), its topical outline refers to this as the "Gate of Manifesting Understanding through the Dispersed Presentation of Conditions. Why, then, is "cause" mentioned here? Answer:

Regarding causes and conditions, there are both general and specific senses. Specifically, the cause is proximate while the condition is remote; generally, however, they are not distinguished as proximate or remote. Now, in this context...

This [term] applies generally below, yet it is specific above; thus there is no contradiction. "Each" (*ge*) means "separate" (*bie*). It is precisely because it separately explains the two distinctions of "difference" (*cha*) and "levelness" (*ping*) that it is so stated.

As for "reaching the actual subject" (*zhi bu shi zhu*): this applies both to the dharma (the principle) and the metaphor (*yu*). "Reaching" (*zhi*) means "ultimate" (*ji*). "Section" (*bu*) means "category" (*lei*). "Actual" (*shi*) means "true" (*zhen*).
Furthermore, "Lord" (*yǔzhǔ*) means reliance, just as space is the ultimate reality that acts as the sovereign of all things within its various categories;
this principle is easily understood. Moreover, the primary essence of the thousand mountains is the character *dū* (都); *dū* signifies totality. This text is even more direct:
True Suchness and space are the totality of totalities. Therefore, [it is so].

That which makes the ocean of birth and death deeper is precisely the *pariṇāma* (transformation); Xianxiu states that the three subtle [consciousnesses] of the *ālayavijñāna* constitute the essence of this transformation.

That which fully undergoes all retributive suffering is precisely the *bheda* (segmentation); Xianxiu states that the *vijñaptimātra-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminating consciousness of objects) constitutes segmentation.
Regarding the "substantial entity" (dān-ti):
as for the "four poisons" and so forth, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the four poisonous snakes are in the same basket, just as the four great elements are in the same body.
This explains the term "original body" (*ben-shen*); thus, the preceding phrase explains the character "original mind" (*ben-xin*). Furthermore, it says: "lust, anger, and delusion."
Arrogance is also called one of the "four poisons," which explains the fundamental mind; the preceding phrase, however, explains the primary body itself.

Furthermore, these two final lines regarding the aforementioned transformational death (parināmikī cyuti) collectively manifest its great peril; they do not belong specifically to the text of this treatise.

Regarding the phrase "the power of perfuming as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-vāsanā-bala*): "as it is" (*yathā*) means "resembling," and "truly" (*bhūta*) means "real. The meaning is that the eighth consciousness, which is a void object, resembles something real;

yet the sixth consciousness, failing to understand this, falsely conceptualizes it as dharmas, like mistaking the vapor of a mirage for water, or taking what is actually dry and void to resemble something truly moist.

As for those who hold this view, they claim that the eight objects lack a governing subject (*adhipati*), yet appear as if they had one; and that the sixth consciousness, being non-comprehending, falsely discriminates them as a person.

Just as water in a mirage lacks the function of a boat for crossing, yet appears to have that function—according to these two types of perfuming, there are two levels of distinction in meaning regarding the objects manifested within the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*): the objects of the sixth and eighth consciousnesses are coarse.
The subtle is likewise; the eight [aspects] are like seeing a clear sky with open eyes, while the six are like seeing a darkened sky with closed eyes.
Although clarity and darkness differ, the substance of the sky is not two; though the coarse and the subtle vary, the substance of the object is one.

This is not the same as the Initial Teaching (Śākyaputrīya), which maintains that both the substance and the shadow exist. What is presented here is precisely the statement that there is only the shadow and no substance; this principle applies to all preceding and succeeding cases.
