Regarding the phrase "because it increases the熏習 (vāsanā) of grasping," a question is raised: why do the latter two [aspects] not arise? The *Bieji* (Separate Record) answers: "The latter two are the fruit of karma;
they are not the subject under discussion. If that is so, why does the preceding text state that the six aspects arise because of objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*)?
The commentary explains: "The former was based on a general discussion, while this refers to specific determination. This is because these latter two are the deluded mind."
The function of this [ignorance] does not arise directly from the object.
The middle section further asks: "What is it? It is answered that fundamental non-awakening is termed the "root," while seeing and craving are termed the "branches.

Although the capacity to permeate is designated as the "subordinate," they share the same substance of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), yet possess two distinct types of functional power. Therefore, as indicated in the preceding text, they are treated as a general whole.
The commentary states that because both the upper and lower [realms] provide assistance, this section corresponds to the deluded mind perfuming ignorance;
furthermore, the former refers to the causal conditions of the upper and lower [realms], while the latter refers to the universal causal conditions.

Regarding the subtle suffering of transformation (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*), a separate record quotes a sutra stating: "With the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) as the condition and uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as the cause, one obtains the retribution of transformation.
This is what that refers to. Question: The *Treatise* speaks of "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*), while the sutras speak of "uncontaminated [consciousness].

Since their meanings are like those of water and fire—how can they be the same? Answer: They are a single entity that possesses two aspects. First, with respect to the defiled portion (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*) of the basis, it is called... [text continues]

The karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is like a pure substrate that is perfumed; when the pure wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-prativedha*) relies upon that "subsequent name" (*manas*), it is called the "perfuming of the mind.

This is what the Sūtra means when it says: "The cause of birth is delusion, also known as false conduct. Second, regarding the aspect of being able to carry purity, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

This refers to the wisdom following the root of "arousing the mind toward realization" (*cittotpāda*), which carries that karmic consciousness and is termed the "enlightened mind. This is truly because from the beginningless past until the moment of [realization]...

In the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), the true and the false are blended, and the defiled and the pure interpenetrate, like gold mixed with ore; names are established accordingly. Furthermore, Master Xianshou said:

"Because this karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) can nourish and permeate the ignorance residing in the ground (*bhūmi-sthita-avidyā*), it becomes deluded regarding the signless (*animitta*) and is able to give rise to the evolving aspect (*vivarta-lakṣaṇa*) and the manifesting aspect (*nirbhāsa-lakṣaṇa*).
This continuity causes those of the Three Vehicles, although they have emerged from the triple world and departed from the realm of objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*)," [to remain bound].
The coarse suffering of the *vipāka* (ripening) is still experienced by the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet this subtle suffering has existed from time immemorial;

however, in order to distinguish this subtle [suffering] from the coarse, it is explained in terms of the state when one has already abandoned coarse suffering. (The first part explains the preceding section; the second part explains the subsequent section.

Because the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (active consciousnesses) can serve as the nourishing熏 (*vāsanā*) for its arising, at that time ignorance gives rise to the coarse afflictions of views and craving, which mobilize body and speech to create seeds.

Regarding the statement, "Because the various karmas cause ordinary beings to undergo the suffering of segmented birth," the commentary explains: "It is simply that the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) directly perfumes ignorance.
This differs slightly from the previous explanation, while the rest is entirely the same.

As for the phrase "because it is the fundamental nature of its own essence": the "own essence" belongs to the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness), and its "fundamental nature" belongs to ignorance; thus, it is the foundation of its own essence. From... [text ends].
Because it is named according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, the preceding text states that the deluded mind of karmic consciousness arises from its own substance due to ignorance;
thus it is called "its own substance.

Regarding the phrase "because it penetrates and pervades," the name and meaning are the same as that [previous case]: because it penetrates the pervasive causes and conditions, it is "pervasive"; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

It is as stated in the preceding text: "Each has two bases, namely the basis of penetration (*prativedha-āśraya*) and the basis of constituent parts (*aṅga-āśraya*); therefore, it is called 'penetration'.

Regarding "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*) and so forth, according to this scriptural passage, since it mentions only "the fundamental," one should understand that what was previously referred to as "its own substance" (*svabhāva*) is implied here.

Because it is fundamental, it penetrates thoroughly; because it is pervasive, it is also exclusively the root. Within this penetration and pervasiveness, the secondary branches are mentioned incidentally.

By analogy with that, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is divided into two parts, which is the same as this case; within the power of downward perfuming, the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) is included incidentally.

Regarding the phrase "the views, attachments, and so forth that arise from the fundamental," Xianshou says: they are called "arisen" simply because they originate from the fundamental. As for the two types of perfuming mentioned—what are these two?
According to this principle, both cause and effect encompass both the fundamental and the newly arisen;

likewise, the three greatnesses and the three bodies also encompass both the new (initial awakening) and the fundamental (original awakening). This is like gold existing within ore, which is called "fundamentally present"; later, when it is extracted from the ore, [it is realized as such].

Not manifesting a formal realization is the power of *upāya*; skillfully transforming sentient beings is what is called *upāya*. Being unstained by worldly entanglements is the power of *prajñā*.
Thus, the gateway of *prajñā* contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while the gateway of *upāya* engages with existence (*bhava*). In engaging with existence, one never loses sight of the void;

therefore, one constantly dwells within existence without being stained by it. Not wearying of existence, one contemplates the void; thus, while contemplating the void, [one remains engaged with existence].

Not realizing [this] is what is called the power of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇabala*), wherein provisional wisdom (*upāyaprajñā*) is fully present; because likes and dislikes are clearly discernible, it is said that provisional and ultimate [wisdom] have distinct functions.
Regarding the *ariḷarada* tree, in the translation of the Holy Dharma it is called the "petal-tongue" tree (*caṅkeli*).

Regarding "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*) and so forth: this corresponds to the first [of the five types of ignorance], as it arises in conjunction with the True [Suchness]; thus it is called "profound.
Because it is coextensive with the True [Suchness] and without limit, it is called "vast.
Regarding "all" and so forth: this should correspond, in order, to the latter four [types of ignorance], as they afflict and harm the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), like sharp thorns.
Because it perfumes and taints the Buddha-nature, it is called "extremely defiled. Because greed and hatred rely upon it, it is called "delighting in attachment.

It refers to the various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*), the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-saṃsāra*), the two attachments, the two obstacles, tainted wholesome states, and the inferior uncontaminated states attained through effortful application (as stated in the *Xiangshan*). Therefore, it is called "inexhaustible."
The meaning of "because it can obstruct the cold air so that [growth] may arise" is as follows:

by means of the internal nature of fire, one is able to block and obstruct the cold air of the *śīta* (cold) season, thereby allowing the wood to become harmonized with the warmth of the *yāna* (spring) and attain growth. Therefore, it is stated below that "it undergoes perfuming and flows on.
Regarding the first, "Bharadvāja and others": these two are Sanskrit names; in the records, the first is translated as "Possessing Existence" (*Sattva*).
The second [category] of skillful means is called "lack of skillful means.

Regarding the character *cuán* (攢), the rhyme dictionary states it is pronounced *zhuǎn* (在丸反) and means a thicket; it refers to trees growing in a cluster. It may be a scribal error; it should instead follow the radical for metal (*jīn*).

Regarding those who practice the path, it should be stated in conjunction [with the following]: it is because their karma is subtle (the wood); because they advance according to the rules of training (the drill);
because of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (the time); because the Buddha resides within body and mind (the place); and because of the fifty-one stages (the sequence).
As for those who do not depend on the merit of practice, the *Mūla-śāstra* asks: "If one does not encounter the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or virtuous..."
Knowledge and so forth take this as their condition; this is precisely "other-conditioning" (parapratyaya) and not "self-cultivation" (svabhāvanā).
How can it be said that there is the merit of self-cultivation? The answer is given by means of the previous analogy: "If no one knows, it does not rely on expedient means.

This text contains two meanings, as it serves as a general analogy for both self- and other-conditioning. For this reason, within the synthesis [of the verse], both conditions are present; Aśvaghoṣa clarifies this point.

Nāgārjuna relies on the hidden [meaning] to clarify only self-conditioning (*svapratyaya*), whereas [the present text] combines other conditions. Thus, Qingliang said: "To separate them results in injury to both;

to combine them results in the beauty of both. This is precisely what is meant. Furthermore, because this root treatise merely employs the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), the current commentators specifically clarify that which is "equalized"—namely, self-conditioning.
For one must rely upon teachers and friends to cultivate oneself; thus, this is the root commentary.
Because these two texts each describe a different condition, they are not contradictory. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "It is like drilling wood to seek fire;

if one stops counting the breaths before the fire emerges, the momentum of the fire will cease. So it is with those who are indolent. This refers to the internal condition (*svapratyaya*). Furthermore, the *Cittabhūmi Śāstra* states:
"The wondrous fruit of Bodhi is not difficult to achieve, but a true spiritual friend is difficult to encounter. This refers to the external condition (*parapratyaya*).
This refers precisely to other-dependent origination (*paratantra*).
If there were no nature of fire, it would fundamentally lack power; thus, the explanations of "non-existence" and "lack of essence" also mutually clarify one another.
Furthermore, the statement that the nature of fire lacks power and function is likewise identical to the former case.

Regarding the phrase "by cultivating roots of goodness" and so forth, Xianshou (賢首) judges that the former refers to one's own level (*svabhāga*) while this refers to superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
Qingliang (清涼) explains: "Showing" means to manifest; "teaching" means to instruct and exhort toward cultivation; "benefiting" means to bring about awakening and profit;
and "rejoicing" means to cause delight by conforming to [the practitioner's] faculties.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the realm (*viṣaya*) of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*)," according to the explanation of Qingliang [Zhiyuan], there are two meanings for "realm": first, the meaning of limit or demarcation (*pramāṇa*);

second, the meaning of the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Here, too, there are two meanings. One interpretation states that internal original enlightenment is the cause and the manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the external condition;
because the condition assists the cause, it is said to be "the realm of original enlightenment. The term "this" (*shi*) in the phrase "this meaning of limit" is a particle used as an auxiliary.
One interpretation states that the Response and Transformation bodies (nirmāṇa-kāya and sambhoga-kāya) are the objects of arising;

because they intend to accomplish the principle of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi), it is said that they "complete the realm of original enlightenment. The term "this object" (*so-en-gi*) is a particle used to separate the clauses.

Furthermore, the realm of original enlightenment belongs to that which is transformed (*sho-ke*). Next, it is stated that the second [category], the realm of the object, also belongs to that which transforms (*no-ke*), namely the Original and Arising [enlightenments].

Because there is no duality, the preceding passage states that the nature which acts as the objective sphere takes this as a condition (*pratyaya*) to bring about and accomplish the wholesome mind of all sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "that which functions as perfuming" (*yong xūn xí zhě*), it refers to the person; it is not a term for restating a previous point. "Functioning" (*yòng*) means performing an activity, which is the sense of being a condition.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), the phrase "the first [is] the use of perfuming" was omitted; therefore, the word "this" serves as a reference to the two types previously indicated—the second being the use of perfuming.
Since the current treatise provides this phrase, it is not merely a reference to what preceded, but is a direct explanation of the person who acts as the condition.

Furthermore, it is also a reference to the two types previously mentioned—the second being the use of perfuming. If that is so, how does this differ from that previous treatise? The answer is as follows:
That which was cited belongs to *ādikṣānti* (initial awakening), while this which is cited belongs to *mūlajñāna* (original awakening); thus, the two are not identical.

Nevertheless, although their names differ according to whether one is in bondage (*saṃvṛta*) or has emerged from bondage (*niḥsaṃvṛta*), the essence of the conditions for original awakening and initial awakening is always one.
Therefore, citing the aforementioned original awakening as the present initial awakening is logically consistent and free of contradiction.

First, regarding "having discerning conditions" (*savikalpa-pratyaya*) and so forth: if one manifests those various classes of bodies as differentiated conditions, "differentiation" refers to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound where the condition and the act of maintaining are identical.
As the treatise says: "Or [manifesting] as kinsmen, parents, and so forth.

If one manifests only those bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as equal conditions, "equality" likewise refers to the *karmadhāraya* analysis where the condition and the act of maintaining are identical.
This refers to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it applies universally to the group of those fixed in the right [path] (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*"): because those at the stage of the Worthy (*ārya*) retain their afflictions (*kleśa-avasthāna*) and undergo the body of segmented birth (*prādeśika-kāya*), they are for the most part born in worlds where no Buddha resides and exist in states of distracted mind;
therefore, they only manage to see various types of retinues and the like. If, however, [they are in a state of concentration...]

The Buddha’s era and the stage of abiding in meditative concentration belong to the latter category of roots that serve as equal conditions; therefore, the former explanation does not mention the three stages of the ordinary person (trīṇi kula-putrāṇi).
Regarding "receiving the conditions for the Path," "receiving" means to realize and witness, and "Path" refers to the path of fruition (*phalamārga*).
Regarding the phrase "that is reality" (*jissai*) and so forth: according to the Qianshan edition, there is the character "one" (*gyō*) beneath the character "reality" (*jissai*).

This means that previously, because one merely gave rise to a mental aspiration within the inner mind, it was called "the power of the vow of compassion. Consequently, in this case, the external body actually performs the deed; thus, it is called "actual practice" (*jissai gyō*).
The former refers to the equality of mind, while this refers to the equality of body. Next is the equality of nature (*shōhei*).
The first two lines above discuss this directly in relation to the Buddhas; the following pair explains it by way of the faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding "hair on the horns": sentient beings are like cow hair, being extremely numerous and vast, whereas the Buddhas are like the horns of a rhinoceros, being exceedingly rare.
Furthermore, as for the hair growing upon those horns, because it is so extremely rare and difficult to encounter, [it serves as a metaphor]. Moreover, [the text continues:]
While all Buddhas do not appear in the world as frequently as the hair on a rhinoceros’s body, their appearance is as rare as the horn-hair of a rhinoceros.
According to each individual world, this is truly like the hair on a horn; yet, across the accumulation of many kalpas, they are likewise infinite.

Thus it is said that although all Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless, if one does not cultivate meditative concentration (samādhi), there is no way to encounter them; even if one were to encounter them, [it would be of no avail].

Because they do not encounter the unconditioned equality, the Prajñāpāramitā states: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. This is precisely what that means.

As for "those who see only themselves as distinct," this is because, due to the aforementioned identity within true suchness (*tathatā*), all bodies of diverse classes are understood to be nothing but their own self-nature.

As for "my own self having no distinction," this is because, due to the aforementioned identity within the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there is no differentiation between the dharma-body and one's own true self.
Regarding the passage in the original text concerning "the perfuming of this essence and its function," the intent is as follows:

the aforementioned power of the identical essence (*samatā-jñāna*) is taken as the essence, while the manifestation of activity is taken as the function. Furthermore, because the latter [of the two] constitutes the essence, the treatise states:

"Beholding the Dharma-nature body of all Buddhas" and so forth; this refers to the essence. Because the former two constitute the function, the treatise states: "The power of compassion and vows should... and so forth.

The "transformed Buddhas" and so forth mentioned above refer precisely to their functional activity (*yong*); therefore, the passage below simply states that they are "equal to the Tathāgata," without mentioning that they are "equal to one's own internal permeation.
Alternatively, because the general meaning of the middle section embodies both essence and function, this term "essence and function" may also point back to it.

Furthermore, the word "this" (*ci*) is a term used to indicate something proximate; it belongs to the preceding general explanation, while "essence and function" subsequently belongs to the following specific explanation.
This is because, within the general [category], there is no distinct clarity regarding essence and function; therefore, it is said that "the above is a general object-condition.
If one were to speak of essence and function individually, each would have two types. Their essence and function as perfuming belong to the object-condition of equality (*samatā-pratyaya*);

their non-yet-correspondence belongs to the object-condition of what is to be responded to (*pratipadya-mūla*), for they look toward the capacity to transform others—whether responding or not yet responding—and thus manifest equality as the object-condition.
Furthermore, according to this section, the meaning of "equality" does not reside within the faculties themselves, because it is taught that the faculties of the three vehicles are intermingled;

rather, it refers only to the equality of the objects of focus— namely, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who appear as the primary objects— because they consist exclusively of a single class of pure beings.

Regarding the statement that "it is perfumed by the *manas* and the *mano-vijñāna*," a question is raised: it was previously stated that for the three stages of the *śaikṣa*, perfuming occurs only through the *mano-vijñāna*;

once one has entered the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), it is then the *manas* that is perfumed. Why, then, is it said here that perfuming belongs to the stages prior to those? The answer is: because it possesses two meanings.

First, it is said that the previous statement was based on the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions] within the stages themselves, referring specifically to the afflictions to be severed at each respective level. The present statement, however, refers to the preceding levels.

Because the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions] must rely on the mental faculty (*manas*) to be severed in the subsequent stage, it is said that the perfuming of the mind occurs prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

One interpretation states: previously, one spoke only of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) because the teaching concerned the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the severance of attachment to a person; now, because the teaching concerns the suppression of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it applies to the mental faculty as well.

Regarding the phrase "only by the power of original perfuming" (*vāsanā*), the meaning is as follows: since the mind-words (*manojalpa*) are identical to those of the Buddha, the beginning is identical to the fundamental;

thus, it is said to be "only by the power of original perfuming. Furthermore, this may depend on the power of faith in the higher [stages], but here it depends on the power of the *mūla-bodhi* (fundamental awakening) that has been realized; therefore, it is stated as "only by the power of original perfuming."

Regarding the phrase "there is no superiority or inferiority": because defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) have no beginning and pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) have no end, their essence and function are entirely equal;

thus they are said to be "identical. This follows the literal meaning of the text. Alternatively, according to the intent of the treatise, the two are mutually integrated and the defiled and pure penetrate one another;

therefore, they are said to be identical. One might fear that, based on what has been explained above regarding the mutual permeation of the true and the false, the defiled and the pure would become separated and remain fundamentally distinct, leading one to abandon the false.

Because one seeks the truth, the two are now harmonized and interfused without obstruction. This is the general explanation; as for the specific explanation, it means that both True Suchness (*tathatā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) each possess two meanings:
first, the meaning of opposing oneself while conforming to others; second, the meaning of opposing others while conforming to oneself.

Because of these—namely, on the level of True Suchness, opposing oneself while conforming to others, and on the level of ignorance, opposing others while conforming to oneself—the defiled phenomena arise.

Because the熏習 (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time has continued without interruption, and because through ignorance one opposes oneself and complies with others, as well as opposing the *tathatā* (Suchness) and complying with oneself, even after attaining the pure dharmas, these [defilements] do not cease;
thus it is said that there is no distinction between broad and narrow, for their functioning is identical.
This is precisely the meaning of the non-duality between the emptiness of the essence of that ignorance and the unchanging *tathatā*; therefore, it is so called.

There is no distinction of superior or inferior, as their essential nature and characteristics are identical; this is precisely what the aforementioned treatise refers to when it says that they do not maintain their own nature and have no fixed abode.

and Imperially Conferred Purple Robe Śramaṇa Zhifu. (Treatise, Fascicle Six) From this point onward,
the above explains the preceding "Section on Establishing the Proposition," stating that "this is the mind’s arising and ceasing through causes and conditions."

Having concluded the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this passage follows because it proceeds to explain their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics, and functions. Why, one might ask, does it not explain the Mahāyāna itself?

The answer is: it is precisely because sentient beings are unable to enter directly that our World-Honored One, relying on the Dharma, provisionally teaches the gates of the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, as well as the gates of intrinsic nature, characteristics, and functions, so that they may realize and enter [the truth] with every word and phrase.
This is the Dharma; therefore, a single gate universally reveals that Dharma, as all profound sūtras are likewise so and cannot be explained individually.
Whether there is an explanation or no explanation lies herein. This is as explained at length in the first section:

regarding the essential nature and characteristics of original *tathatā*, this refers back to the "Section on Establishing the Meaning," which states "essential nature, characteristics, and function. However, the term *tathatā* is used here to designate it according to its specific meaning.
It may also be approached by referring to the passage immediately following the preceding section, which states: "The meaning of the permeation (*vāsanā*) of *tathatā* has two aspects:

first, the permeation of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vāsanā*), etc. This is entirely identical [to the present text]. Although that passage is cited here, it serves to explain the essential nature, characteristics, and functions established in the previous "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*li-yi-fen*).
While the text in the aforementioned treatise was dispersed and its meaning obscure, I have now gathered it in one place so that it may be clearly illuminated.
Regarding the title of this section, it is called "Clearly Revealing.
From the phrase "from the very beginning" up to "the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body," there are two parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "That is to say.
Within this, there are two further divisions: first, the meritorious qualities that have names; second, the innumerable meritorious qualities. Looking ahead to the next section...
Third, regarding the detailed explanation of the specific sections, this general heading is omitted; the same applies to the other chapters.

However, while the commentary’s structural outline (*ko-wen*) judges only the general meaning, the present text provides a meticulous and detailed differentiation of the distinctions; thus, there is no contradiction between these two versions of the text.
Regarding the phrase "up to fulfillment" and so forth, the commentary below explains accordingly:

from the stage of being bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana-bhūmi*) up to the stage of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-bhūmi*), throughout these two states of bondage and liberation, there is nothing that is not fully possessed; for this reason, the two names for the *garbha* (womb/storehouse) must be established.
Regarding the statement that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has no increase or decrease and so forth:

these five pairs of meanings do not imply that within the five types of persons, there is an increase in magnitude for those who come from the future, nor a decrease in size for those who have departed from the past.
Alternatively, it may mean that what precedes does not depart and what follows does not newly arrive; therefore, it is said that there is neither coming nor going.
Regarding the statement "one is established as one": this receives the designation "one" in contrast to the number five.
Regarding "the same is established as the same by its own nature": this establishes the same name in contrast to different persons, or because it depends on all five persons together;
thus, because it depends on the preceding five persons, the single name "same" is established, and there is no confusion between the two. The *Yan’ao chao* states: "To loathe difference."
Those who cling to delusion and loathe the truth thus give rise to the distinct differences of the six realms, yet their nature does not differ.

Those who abandon the particular abandon the source to follow the branches; thus, while the three vehicles have distinctions, their nature has no distinction, and it is therefore said that there is only the single truth.
Regarding the phrase "because it is spontaneously eternal, abiding, and ultimately real," these six phrases should be read by skipping back and forth twice. One way is:
first, "spontaneously eternal," "unmoving throughout the three periods of time," and "quiescent, yet further quiescent"—this is based on time.
Second, regarding location, as explained in the section on the excellence of causes and conditions above; alternatively, each of the six phrases may stand alone as a distinct point.
Regarding the meaning: first, time; second, place; third, the three periods; fourth, the four characteristics; fifth, the exclusion of arising and ceasing; sixth, the exclusion of falsity.
If this is so, why is the title of the section "Time Does Not Shift" (*kāla-apravṛtti*) and not "Place"? The answer is: it is because this follows the explicit text of the root treatise itself.
Alternatively, one may understand that time is revealed by means of place. This refers to the functional significance of the six kinds of natures (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*).

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'nature' (*prakṛti*) is cited alongside the virtues," the intent is that because the nature inherently possesses the provisional meaning of differentiation, the name "virtue" is established.
Among the fourth virtue, the Sūtra says "originally existing" (*mūlataḥ sat*), which refers to the aforementioned "spontaneous original existence" (*svabhāva-akṛtaka-pūrvam-bhava*);

it is not obtained through the power of another, thereby explaining the "original self-nature. Furthermore, the Sūtra says "clear and bright" (*vimala-prasanna*), which explains the "original purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) by being free from the accumulation of defilements.
It further states that "departing from extremes" refers to the Middle, which is precisely the supreme accord with the Middle Reality;

thus it explains the character *ben* (original) in the term "Original Mind. Regarding the phrase "the two awakenings, original and initial," this applies generally to all four types of awakening, as they all possess inherent virtue (*xingde*).

This is discussed collectively because the terms "original" and "initial" awakenings are not being distinguished separately. However, within the initial awakening of defilement and purity, there are two meanings: first, departing from [delusion] through the perfection of nature.
Defilement further has two meanings: first, if it were not identical with the pure *ādi-bodhi* (original awakening), it would constitute the existence of emotion (*qing*) [as opposed to principle];

second, even if it were not different from it, it would entail the severance of principle. Since these two are non-dual, defilement is severed in terms of its nature; however, this refers solely to the existence of emotion and does not pertain to the non-existence of principle, for it is only now that [the mind] arises due to being deceived by defilement.
Now, based on this quality and the subsequent "immutable" (*bùbiàn*) quality, the remaining qualities each possess their own characteristics.
Regarding the four types of awakening, the *Sūkṣma-viniścaya-śāstra* states that each of these four awakenings possesses the three great aspects (*tri-mahātmya*).

The subsequent discussion explains that the cultivation of the impure and pure *samyak-bodhi* (correct awakening) accords with the three great meanings of the *mūla-bodhi* (original awakening). It says: "For what reason are all [the stages] collectively termed 'conforming to the nature of phenomena' (*dharmatā-anuloma*) within the summary of the four gates?
(The question above is answered below: It is because one wishes to demonstrate that the essence of the space of the nature of phenomena is vast.
The Great Perfection (Dzogchen) is without limit; its characteristics and functions are unimpeded and sovereign, devoid of beginning or end.

All practitioners who train in its four gateways are likewise so, for they accord with suchness (*tathatā*), being vast, perfect, and without boundaries according to their respective intentions (*āśaya*).
Commentary: If even a single drop from a celestial pond possesses the flavors of the hundred rivers, how much more so the source itself?

Since it is known from this that the original text itself possesses the merit of the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*), one should understand that the remaining three types of awakening (*bodhi*) each likewise possess the three greatnesses;
this is explained in many passages, such as those concerning the two characteristics and the four mirrors.
Regarding the four obstacles, as explained in the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* and other texts, they are: (1) the birth-and-death of expedient means (*upāya-jāti-maraṇa*, ignorance);

(2) the birth-and-death of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-jāti-maraṇa*, untainted karma—the first two being the causes of transformation and the latter two being the results of transformation); (3) the birth-and-death of existence (*bhava-jāti-maraṇa*); and (4) the birth-and-death of non-existence (*abhava-jāti-maraṇa*).

These four types of transformation, as cause and effect, are able to obstruct the Dharma-body and its four virtues. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* explains that these correspond to the stage of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*).

Because it serves as the condition that gives rise to the defilements of transformation (*pariṇāma-kleśa*), when these are severed, the pure qualities of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha-guṇa*) are revealed.
Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conceptual karma is able to act as the cause for transformation; since there is transformation, it is not autonomous (*asvatantra*).

Therefore, when the inferior uncontaminated [karma] within the causes is severed, the quality of the true self (*ātman*) characterized by autonomy is revealed. Transformation is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), which possesses four subtle [aspects].
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); since there is the suffering of conditioned existence, it is not peace or bliss.

Therefore, when this body is removed, the quality of bliss is revealed. Because the body subject to transformation and change ultimately ends in destruction, when this characteristic of destruction is removed, true permanence is revealed, as explained at length in the sūtras.

Thus, the meaning of "purity" (*viśuddhi*) here is stated in relation to specific obstacles, whereas the previously mentioned meaning of "purification" (*vyavadāna*) is stated in relation to general obstacles.
Second, regarding the differences:
"the flames and illusions" refers to the four aforementioned hindrances; "non-practitioners" refers to the aforementioned spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

As for the phrase "cool and unchanging," the first three characters refer to the pure original enlightenment (*viśuddha-mūla-avabodha*), while the single character "changing" refers to the state of defilement and purity.

The term "sovereignty of original enlightenment" (benjue zizai) applies to both types of original enlightenment; since "coolness" (*śītalatā*) is not [separately] treated as one [of the two], it is translated below in contrast [to its opposite] simply as "torment" (*saṃtāpa*).
Regarding the phrase "like a bright mirror," etc., this should be assigned to the two kinds of original enlightenment—defiled and pure—and named accordingly as "conformity" and "opposition."
Therefore, the intrinsically aware mind (prakṛti-prabhāsvara) that accords with defilement follows the perfuming influences to conformingly establish defiled dependent origination;

it is like the south side of a mirror, which is the face itself—this metaphor illustrates how it can manifest images according to the substance. The pure intrinsically aware mind does not follow the perfuming influences to establish pure dependent origination;
it is like the north side of a mirror, which is the back itself—this metaphor illustrates how it does not manifest images because it opposes the substance.

Regarding the question, "What are the distinct characteristics of these three enumerations?"—this inquiry concerns the reasons why the three original texts differ. The answer provided below has two bases;

according to the literal text, it only presents the first basis, while according to the underlying intent, it implicitly reveals the latter two. Regarding the final point, the purpose of the Buddha’s sūtras is that those with sharp faculties do not become confused.
First, as for the phrase "the upward-flowing transformation," this should refer to the *prajñā* (awakening) that accords with defilement.
The "upward-flowing transformation" (ūrdhvasrotas-parāvṛtti) refers to gradually ascending to higher stages according to the perfuming of defilements, as described above; it is as stated:

"the originally existing cause and effect perfume [the mind] to give rise to faith," and so forth. The "downward-flowing transformation" (adhahsrotas-parāvṛtti) refers to gradually descending to lower stages according to the defilements being countered, as stated in the preceding text;
it is the same as the original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya) severing delusions from the top down.
If this is so, and [Buddha-nature] is eternally capable of severing delusions, why does the subsequent text say that it "causes one not to act"? The answer is:
because it is not explicitly stated. Furthermore, the preceding text says that when karma is initiated, the Buddha-nature and its roots of goodness gradually diminish;
this is excellent evidence. Alternatively, those who flow upward are Bodhisattvas and the like, while those who flow downward are Śrāvakas and the like, according to their respective order.
The commentary explains *pariṇāma* (transformation/decline) as "breaking, destroying, and transforming qualities so that they do not arise.

Therefore, regarding *pariṇāma* here [in the context of downward flow], it cannot be the same as the meaning of "downward turning" (*adhaḥ-pravṛtti*) in the sense of being constant. If one insists on equating them, this [downward flow] is precisely the transformation into defilement through following conditions;
how then could it be said to "break, destroy, and transform qualities so that they do not arise"? Thus, they are not the same.
Regarding the meaning of that downward-turning process, the term "eight negations" refers to what is stated in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*:
"Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going. This is it.
By what means is the former [the essence] eliminated and the latter [the characteristics] explained? This may also serve as a general question encompassing both.
"Does it possess an essence and characteristics?"—"essence" refers to the nature (*svabhāva*), which is answered by the first subsequent phrase;
"characteristics" refers to the meaning (*artha*), which is answered by the second subsequent phrase. Next, the phrase "because of" (*yasmāt*) serves to inquire into and explain the latter meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the self-nature of self-nature" and so forth: "self" (*sva*) refers to purity, while "other" (*para*) refers to defilement.
As the *Prathama-śāstra* states: "Self refers to all dharmas of the pure category; other refers to all dharmas of the unwholesome category.

This means that because their qualities are not uniform, it is called the "self-nature of self-nature. If [this nature] were associated with afflictions, it would be something to be eliminated; however, here there is no defilement by affliction.
Therefore, this is the virtue of non-interruption.

Regarding the phrase "ultimately different from itself," the *Zhǔnchāo* (Excerpts on the Standards) cites a treatise which includes the character "not" (*bù*) beneath the word "ultimately" (*zhōng*), meaning that the characteristic is not different from the substance.

"Unable to act as one" means that the substance (*tattva*) is not distinct from its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Question: What is the difference between this meaning of "non-distinction" and the previous meaning of "not being separate from the two"?

Answer: They differ in terms of intimacy and remoteness. If one relies on the present text, "one" refers to the magnitude of substance (*tattva-mahat*); "itself" refers to the magnitude of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*).
Since the magnitude of characteristics itself constitutes the magnitude of substance, it is said that "it acts as one. This is viewed in contrast to the entirety of "not being separate."

Because there is no confusion [with other categories], it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. "In the state of being enveloped" (*saṃvṛta*) is a designation for that which is concealed; "garbha" means "to conceal.
This refers to what was explained above as spanning from the stage of those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana-bhūmi*) up to this point.

That which is also called the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is a designation for that which has emerged from the entanglements (*nirmāṇa*). It is called the "body of reliance" (*āśraya-kāya*), as explained above:
it is the ground of the supreme, great awakening wisdom (*anuttara-buddhajñāna-bhūmi*).

Regarding the "correct principle of our own school" (*svayūthya-siddhānta*): because this mind free of conceptualization (*amanasikāra-citta*) is the realm of the Buddha, it constitutes our own school's position.
Those who practice non-Dharma and deviant paths yet possess a mindful mind are within the realm of Māra; therefore, it is called "non-Dharma.
The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states: "With the exception of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.

A verse says: "If one discriminates and recollects through conceptualization, this is the net of Māra; to be unmoving and without discrimination is the seal of Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), as described above regarding non-arising."
This explains the point where non-extinction and birth-and-death extinction are conjoined.
"Because it is the ground of all the stages of fundamental ignorance" refers to both the fundamental and derivative aspects of ignorance;
since the derivative exists upon the fundamental, it is so described.
"Clarifying this as its opposite" means that the fundamental awakened wisdom (*mūla-awakening*) is clarified by being contrasted with that [delusion]; all subsequent instances follow this principle.
"Transcending the revolving view" means that "revolving" refers to arising; this is precisely what was referred to above as "arising" and so forth.
The phrase "because the two kinds of mastery are absent" means that the two kinds of real selves—those of persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—do not exist.

Regarding the passage in the original text, "affliction, decay, transformation, and so forth," this follows the commentary on the preceding section: decay, destruction, and the alteration of qualities are termed "decay and transformation" (*pariṇāma*) because the subject and object are distinct.
Regarding the phrase "the virtues of the original nature" (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and so forth, this explains the text of the root treatise.

If one follows the interpretation of Master Xianshou, the former [passage] refers to how the deluded mind seeks externally, yet such seeking is insufficient; whereas this [passage] refers to the fact that the pure dharmas of the nature are inherently full, so what need is there for external seeking?
This accords with the preceding text which states: "Such virtues have existed spontaneously and originally from time immemorial; they do not depend on the power of conditions."

Because they are established [as such], they may also be understood as "substantial greatness" (*tattva-mahat*), just as in the analogy of a single room where the dust and sands represent "characteristic greatness" (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*).
This is like a thousand rays of light, each individual ray filling the entire room;

because each individual characteristic fills the entirety of the substance, it is said that all these virtues are entirely undifferentiated in their essence. Within the single *dharmadhātu*, their magnitude is equal, for they correspond to one another.
Delusory phenomena are like water and fire; they cannot each individually fill an entire room, nor can they each individually fulfill the entirety of a single entity.
Therefore, it is said that because the mind that perceives and the objects perceived are distinct, the merits of original enlightenment (benjue) are not yet fulfilled.
"Yuan" (圓) means circumscribed and pervasive; "man" (滿) means overflowing and sufficient.
*Asitacchannaśvatī* (阿尸多遮那尸帝) means "the tree of boundless oneness. Regarding the analogies and their corresponding meanings:
first, the analogy illustrates named, quantifiable merit; second, the analogy illustrates unnamed, immeasurable merit;
third, the analogy illustrates that if delusion is great, virtue is likewise great, and if delusion is small, virtue is likewise small; fourth, they are identical in being white in color.

Therefore, the first analogy corresponds to the "Mind Aroused through Accomplishment of Faith" (*śraddhā-sampanna-cittotpāda*): the mani-jewel is yellow within and its outer ore is also yellow, symbolizing that there is the *tathāgatagarbha* (original enlightenment) within and the discerning consciousness without;
the fifth analogy for wisdom is that both smelling and tasting constitute the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body;
the sixth analogy for prajñā is that both tasting and seeing together form the single flavor of liberation; and the seventh is as Sengzhao said: "How distant is the Way? (Is it not near?)

It is said thus because: first, phenomena are true as they encounter them; second, the eight [aspects] are identical in that they both arise from the one mind; third, the true and the deluded exist as such by the very nature of dharmas;
and fourth, they ultimately converge in the Mahāyāna. Thus it is stated.
Regarding "merit and darkness" and so forth, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The woman of merit is the elder sister; wherever she goes, she brings auspiciousness.
The woman of darkness is the younger sister; wherever she follows her sister, she brings calamity. These two are never separated.
This passage explains at length that true and counterfeit merit are like the sisters Kṛṣṇakarṇī and her companion, who are inseparable; hence this metaphor is employed.
What is here called the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is the ocean of the supreme fruition (*phala-sāgara*).
Furthermore, "not limited by the number of kalpas, extending to the end of the future" refers to the supreme *rajas-kalpa* (aeons as numerous as motes of dust).

Regarding the two principles of "reality-reality" and "provisionality-provisionality," the four characters "real-real" and "provisional-provisional" are respectively assigned to the four bodies (*catur-kāya*).

This refers to the Dharma-body (substantially real), the Body of Self-Enjoyment (substantially real), the Body of Enjoyment for Others (provisionally established), and the Transformation-body (provisionally established).

In this treatise, the four bodies are clearly elucidated; in the commentary, the four bodies are explained as containing two pairs: that is, by citing the Dharma-body, it includes the Body of Self-Enjoyment;

by citing the Transformation-body, it includes the Body of Enjoyment for Others. Thus, there are: the gate of manifesting the signless, the gate of appearing according to [the capacity of] beings, the gate of perceiving the coarse, and the gate of perceiving the subtle.

This is explained clearly: the "two principles" (*dvi-naya*) refer to the two dharmas manifested by the two individuals, the Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and the Person-knowledge (*pudgala-jñāna*);

alternatively, they refer to the two dharmas attained by the two individuals, the other-dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, they are called the "two principles. Alternatively, these may be combined into the general designation of "the two principles" as the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*).
Since the dharma is named after the person, this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive determinative) referring to the two principles of the real and so forth. This is what is stated in the treatise.

The terms "separating the phenomena" (ge-fa) further involve: above, they actually refer to persons; below, they actually designate phenomena. Above, they metaphorically refer to persons; below, they metaphorically belong to phenomena.
These are the "real" of the real and the "metaphorical" of the metaphorical. When speaking of the two principles, these are the two—metaphorical and real.

"Subsuming function into essence" (she-yong gui-ti), such as "real," etc., refers to the *karmadhāraya* (holding the object as its own activity). Furthermore, the words within the treatise are auxiliary expressions, and furthermore, they are phenomena (*dharma*).

The *Xiāngyún* (Commentary on Characteristics) states: "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is real, while empty space is a provisional (*prajñapti*) phenomenon; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise so.

This is because True Suchness consists of two types—the pure and the defiled-pure—and thus it is called 'real-real. Empty space also has two [aspects], and thus it is called 'provisional-provisional. The principle of the two types of true emptiness is the same as before.
In the original text, the mention of "True Suchness" alone is intended to implicitly include empty space, thereby subsuming the provisional back into the real. This...
The "also" [in the term] *dharmakāya* (持業) may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Regarding the phrase "by this meaning," it refers precisely to the aforementioned sense of "effacing traces":

that is to say, when the practitioner’s mind attains nothing, being free from the traces of oneness or duality, existence or non-existence, and when both self and other are simultaneously severed and all effortful practice is equally forgotten—this is it.
The profound resonance is naturally and inherently endowed with all merit, requiring no external power, because it is not a dependent, false, or illusory phenomenon.
Thus, Qingliang said: "The True Source cannot be accomplished through effort; it is essential that one abandons deluded effort for the source to be realized.
The Deep Source cannot be attained through practice; it is only when practice is exhausted that the source is perfected. Based on this, the application of the Great [Vehicle] is also universal.
"Original enlightenment" (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*):

"the same, the same, the same" refers to the threefold equality of person, dharma, and [enlightenment]. The three preceding instances of "different" (*visama*) should be understood as the opposite of this.

"Non-dissolving and non-fusing" means that "dissolving" refers to exhaustion and "fusing" refers to blending; it does not mean that defilement and purity are exhausted and blended to return to a single essence.
The above section as a whole concerns conventional designations based on relative observation. Next, "like two" clarifies the reality of absolute transcendence.
"Like" (ru) means "as if"; "observation" (guan) means "reliance. It is as if the two—truth and falsehood, emptiness and emptiness—are utterly transcendent.
The traces are not dependent upon the dharma of falsehood;
"provisionally establishing equality" and so forth refers to the preceding proof of the three meanings of equality.

From here on, it proves the previous point that they are of one essence, concluding with the ultimate, wondrous, and auspicious severance of all [distinctions]. Having thus answered the first of the three questions, the extensive text indicated therein follows.
One should respond that the other two [categories] are also included.

As in the original text, regarding the phrase "by means of existence" and so forth, these nine phrases of the treatise fully employ the three types of equality mentioned previously: namely, the first three phrases refer to wisdom (*jñāna*), the fourth phrase refers to principle (*tattva*), and thus wisdom and principle are equal.

Regarding the substance of these four preceding phrases and the function of the subsequent three phrases: * The first three phrases [refer to] wisdom; * The fourth phrase [refers to] principle; * That is, wisdom and principle are equal; * The substance of the above four phrases is as such; * Next, the three phrases [refer to] function. Thus, it is established.
The first seven phrases concern persons, while the latter two phrases concern dharmas; that is, they correspond to the equality of persons and dharmas.
These latter two phrases should also be read as continuing through the preceding "equality" terms, in order to manifest the meaning of the equality between those two.

Regarding "only *a* and *a*" (*wei a zuo wei a zhe*), according to the Qianshan edition, the character *wei* (only) does not appear below it; the *Shengji* commentary is likewise. It states: "*A* means spontaneity.
Furthermore, there is no other textual explanation for the intended meaning: the upper *a* belongs to the True Body (*dharmakāya*), which is precisely the signless (*animitta*);
the lower *a* belongs to the Responsive Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is precisely the manifested response. This is like jewels emerging from a pearl: both are spontaneous.
Because it is mindless, it may also be construed above with the *dharmakāya* of this treatise and below with the *jñānakāya*;
since both its essence and its function are spontaneous (*svarasa*), this interpretation accords with the text. It may also be understood as referring to the underlying meaning:

because it acts spontaneously and is merely spontaneous, the preceding section explains the "above," while the subsequent section explains "why" and so forth; thus, the following explanations merely follow accordingly.
"Only one's own self" means that "the former 'self'" refers to the Dharmakāya, while "the latter 'self'" refers to the Svābhāvikakāya (Essence Body); thus, it is called "one's own self."
"Because there is no other body" means that there is no other Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) or Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya). The text states:
"There is no realm of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), for it is free from purposeful activity.

Regarding the phrase "because there is no obstruction," the intended meaning is as follows: while a reflection actually pervades both the water and the moon, in the present context, it specifically refers to [the former].

Because it is water, one may also say that it is merely not related to the substance of the original moon; just as there is no Buddha apart from birth, it is said that [the reflection] merely follows the sequence of sentient beings.

In the section below on "Resolving Doubts through Question and Answer," it is stated that because this is based exclusively on the original moon, one may also say that the original and the reflection are non-dual, for there is no separate reflection apart from the original moon, just as there is no response apart from the Truth (the Real). Therefore, it is called "form" (rūpa).

Regarding the phrase "the mind is non-dual": according to the intent of the subsequent passages, this actually applies to both [aspects]. The metaphor of manifesting images can be understood through this.
This is because the Buddha’s birth takes as its own substantial reality the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) previously described—namely, non-arising and non-ceasing.
If one examines these two closely, they do not differ by so much as a hair’s breadth. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction."
It is further said that the Dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately without distinction. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"To contemplate the true mark of the body is likewise to contemplate the Buddha. This means that when the awakened mind turns upward, it is provisionally designated as "the Buddhas," while when the deluded mind turns downward, it is conventionally termed "sentient beings.
Now, this is also a provisional discourse that manifests both aspects. This is explained extensively in the Commentary.
"Because one cannot thoroughly comprehend the most profound tenet" explains the root treatise’s inquiry:

since it is not understood that the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) manifests [the world], the Buddha asks how the objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) can be said to be manifestations of the evolving consciousness.

The answer is that the manifesting consciousness necessarily arises in dependence upon the evolving consciousness; thus, the single mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is in conjunction with that which arises and ceases.

Within the *ālaya*, there are four kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) minds. If there is no weariness with or seeking after [liberation], and the afflictions, karma, and birth-and-death are thick and flourishing while the unconditioned is weak and inferior, remaining hidden and unmanifest, this is called "not seeing the Buddha.

If weariness and seeking arise, and greed and hatred become thin and subtle, such that birth-and-death becomes weak and non-arising/non-ceasing gradually manifests, this is called "the appearance of a Buddha in the world. Now, regarding this...
Generally, those of lesser capacity do not understand that it is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) itself—manifesting as neither-arising-nor-ceasing—that is called the Buddha;

they mistakenly believe that a Buddha comes from elsewhere outside of this. However, the object-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) exists right within the evolving consciousness; it is a single entity, though distinguished in meaning by its coarse and subtle aspects.

This is not like the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-zong*), which posits that apart from the eight consciousnesses there are six or two additional consciousnesses through which one sees the Buddha, asserting that these are definitely distinct entities.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "what ordinary beings see" and so forth: since the two bodies of retribution and response do not pertain to the provisional teachings, those from the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa) upward possess the fortyfold body of other-retribution.

Therefore, prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), as well as among the various vehicles of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), there is no differentiation based on the specific categories of minor transformation;
they are simply termed the "response body" (*nirmāṇakāya*). For this reason, it speaks only of "ordinary beings" and does not mention the two vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "progressively more excellent in their respective order," a question is raised: why do other teachings speak of only ten stages, whereas here forty are mentioned?
The answer is: this present account is based on the ultimate meaning (*bhūtārtha*), while others rely on what is predominant; therefore, there is no contradiction.
*Chakāriśanadīya* (遮伽梨娑那提衣) means "Jade-Luminous Silk Robe" (*yùguāngyàoluóyī*);
this is the name of the robe used for the adornment of Śakra.
*Kaṃśidatama-palace* (鍵尸多陀摩宮) means "Palace of Blissful Transformation" (*ānluòbiànzhuǎn*). These robes and palaces exist solely as manifestations.
Even if one were to apply a forced provisional designation to this, it would still express that compassion is the dwelling and patience is the garment; thus, Qingliang said:
"The Buddhas possess only the single body of non-obstruction; it is merely that they appear different according to the faculties [of beings] and their teachings."

Regarding the coarseness or subtlety of consciousness: "coarseness" and "subtlety" are like the tarnish on a mirror; the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) are like the clarity of the mirror.
If the defilements of the mind are coarse, the Buddha’s clarity must be subtle; as the defilements of the mind gradually become more subtle, the Buddha’s clarity necessarily becomes manifest.

Thus, these characteristics of subtlety and manifestation both depend upon the mind and its defilements, not upon the Buddha and his clarity. It is also like oil and water, where the appearance of reflections is either clear or dim accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the nature of wisdom" and so forth: just as waves are subsumed within water and can thus be called water—if they did not subsume the water, how could they receive the name "water"?

Since the water exists within the waves, one should know that it is the same when the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is subsumed within the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it is then called the Dharma-body.

However, because the previous Wisdom-body (jñānakāya) subsumes that form-body (rūpakāya), and the form-body is exhausted, it is like waves being identical to water; the characteristics of the waves are empty.
Therefore, because the waves do not exist, the preceding passage states, "The substance of form has no shape," and later there is no such phrase.

This clearly shows that although the preceding and succeeding sections are two, they mutually encompass one another; yet what is subsumed by the former is lost, while what is subsumed by the latter remains. This is precisely because the waves are illusory while the water is real—the intent of the commentary is the same.

As for the mind, it consists of the other four aggregates: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. What are their characteristics? That which experiences [objects] is feeling (*vedanā*).
To grasp at signs is perception (*saṃjñā*); to engage in conditioning is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*); and to discern is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If one can rely on this body and mind to clearly and minutely contemplate their characteristics, seeing only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in all places and never finding the marks of a self or a person, this is called the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
