Regarding the phrase "the pure dharmas of all conditioned phenomena" (*sarvasaṃskṛta-viśuddha-dharma*), it is because within the present treatise there are two types of objects of observation: first, the mundane (*laukika*), and second, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "all those above and below," the principle applies both upward and downward and should be read twice. Here, first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is explained as possessing two meanings:
first, it belongs exclusively to non-awakening (*abodhi*), because the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
thus, in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome, it is called pure or impure. Second, initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) is the pure dharma.

Therefore, the *Daichao* states: "The meaning of initial awakening newly arising is identical to that of the conditioned; non-awakening is precisely the impure dharma. These two dharmas mutually transform and corrupt one another.
Following this, the text subsequently explains the world (*loka*). This is because it encompasses both non-awakening and awakening as a single principle.
Thus, in the preceding section on the ten distinctions of the gate of having a world, the world is fully present; here, the world is complete because it is endowed with awakening.
Due to merit, one conceives of the world as real because one does not realize that the three realms are illusory. Thus, the false perfumes the true, giving rise to all defiled appearances;
the true perfumes the false, giving rise to all pure karmas. These two mutually subvert one another.

Furthermore, the Door of Birth and Death is called "transformation and decay," while the True Suchness Door is said to be that "all phenomena exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought."
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna said: "If awakening (*bodhi*) is defiled and deceived by that [ignorance], it only arises now; it cannot be called 'correct'.
Moreover, the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* and other texts state that the *parinirmita-vaśavartin* (transformation) death-and-rebirth is suffering because it is like gold mixed with ore.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Therefore, the foolish do not give rise to a sense of fear regarding the suffering of the Avīci Hell as they should."
The various sages regard the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as suffering because these aggregates are the nature of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

The commentary states: "If even their mere constant flux gives rise to great terror, how much more so when they are subject to disintegration? It is logically certain that this is great suffering. Yet ordinary beings perceive only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) and fail to realize the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Aside from the Buddha, there is nothing that is not suffering; how much less, then, can one feel attachment toward anything else? Thus judges Yuxi.
It is said that this suffering is explained solely in terms of the meaning of being destructible, rather than merely the destruction of pleasure.

Regarding the phrase "the first is produced by itself," the intended meaning is that one enters the Mahāyāna dharma of the three natures through the gate of meditative observation based on the gate of the arising-and-ceasing aspect;
therefore, among the ten distinctions mentioned above, the tenth is called the "One Mind" which has two aspects, and the Mahāyāna is termed the "Single Essence."
"Single-mindedly following what is produced" refers to the Mahāyāna as the "one-three self," while "single-mindedly following that which produces" refers to it as the "one";
thus it is said, "the one acts as one.
Regarding "all mental activities and so forth," the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Just as when a single eyelash is placed on the palm of the hand, a person does not perceive it."

If one places it upon the eye, it causes extreme harm and discomfort; yet the fool, like the palm of a hand, does not perceive the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), while the wise person, like the eye, gives rise to intense revulsion toward its conditions.
It is for this reason that [the text] connects the two aforementioned types of "corrupt practices" (*bhraṣṭa-caryā*).
As for the analogy of "that dream" and so forth, the ancient masters said: "Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly present; upon waking, the great trichiliocosm is empty and void.
The world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are like bubbles on the ocean; all noble sages are like lightning flashes or the floating dust of the *ālayavijñāna*."
The coming and going of clouds in the sky and the bubbles of the three poisons arising and submerging in emptiness are explained in sequence as being like dreams, lightning, and clouds.
Regarding the phrase "conditioned by various bodies and so forth," the *Āgama* Sūtra states: "In the past, there was a king whose sensual desires were insatiable.
A bhikṣu admonished him with a verse, saying: 'The eyes are a pit of rheum and tears; the nose is a bag of foul mucus; the mouth is a pool of saliva and spittle.'"

The belly of this vessel is a storehouse for excrement and urine; however, because the King lacks the eye of wisdom and is addicted to forms, the poor monk saw it as defiling the renunciation of the path of cultivation, and thus said, "up to and including, because of being far removed from greed."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and again, and again," the character *zhi* (之) signifies "to go.
As for the statement "establishing great vows that arise throughout the ten directions," if one follows this treatise, the character *yuan* (願, vow) possesses two meanings;
therefore, it is read twice here.
Regarding the phrase "for example, like a bird deprived of wings," etc.: this verse consists of four similes and eight lines, with two lines forming each pair.

Only the initial "for example" (*tadyathā*) and the middle "and" (*ca*)—along with the character "function" (*guǒ*) at the end—pervade downward and connect upward through the four [sections]. One should read it four times.

Within the "correspondence of the dharma" (*dharmasama*), the first stanza and the subsequent two characters "and function" (*gònggù*) should likewise pervade downward and connect upward through the four.

Next, read this: however, among these four, the first two lack *vipaśyanā* (insight) because they share with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas the deluded adherence to the Dharma of seeking quiescence;

thus, the first is exclusively the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding), which belongs to the synonym of "wisdom of suchness" (*tathatā-jñāna*), yet its fundamental nature is the same as that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as it falls into the "long void" of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
If one fully cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it belongs to the "wisdom of suchness-as-it-is" (*yathāvad-jñāna*) and is also called "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

One does not fall [into the extreme] because of the emptiness of the nature of nirvāṇa. Now, the meaning here is this: with two wings and two dots, one may soar through the great void; with the two wisdoms operating in tandem, one may roam within the emptiness of nature.

Because of the absence of subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one fails to reach the conventional and engage with existence; by practicing only the wheel of cessation (*śamatha*), one realizes the true and falls into emptiness.
The latter [type of practitioner] is likewise the same as the two vehicles who, being deluded regarding the Dharma, do not understand it. Thus, these two aforementioned types are the first.
That is to say, one will inevitably fall into the realm of quiescence and subsequently fail to achieve the knowledge of all modes;
for the latter two [perfections] lack *śamatha*, and thus, like ordinary beings, one cannot traverse the true path nor escape the pit of delusion.

Regarding the phrase "not falling into the evil realms," the *Yùxī* (Jade Stream) commentary cites the *Lùn* (Treatise), where the character for "merit" (*gōng*) is actually the character for "pit" (*kēng*). This reading is also acceptable.
However, the character "merit" (*gōng*) is more suitable when connected to the preceding four [characters].
Regarding the phrase "because one does not fall into the pit," the *Chāo* (Excerpts) cites the *Lùn*, stating: "Because one does not fall into the pit," as found in the *Kāi-tài* edition.
This is also a case of a corrupted character.

Regarding the point that "it can never be abandoned," the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (Chapter on Questioning the Light) states: "For example, when a powerful king leads his realm, all people look up to him with devotion;
concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are likewise that upon which Bodhisattvas rely. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom..."
Regarding this saving of sentient beings, Qingliang (Zhiyi) further stated: "Without Chan there is no way to exhaust its stillness; without wisdom there is no way to deepen its illumination.
Furthermore, the *Tiantai Zhiguan Jinglun* (and other treatises) all convey this same meaning.

For this reason, because it is the essential gateway for perfect and correct sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation—free from those partial and deviant views—"stopping" (*śamatha*) corresponds to sudden awakening, and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) corresponds to...

Because gradual cultivation and moment-to-moment sudden awakening are not mutually exclusive—each moment being both gradually cultivated and suddenly awakened—the Seventh Patriarch stated that "sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation" constitutes the perfect and subtle path.
Since this concerns the fundamental principles of practice, both must be carried out together.

In my previous response to Emperor Tianyou, within the third section on the "Mysterious and Subtle Gate of Mental Contemplation," there were two parts: first, a direct exposition; second, a resolution of objections.

Now, one should suddenly believe that the true realm (dharmadhātu) is inherently present, that ignorance and birth-and-death are inherently non-existent, and that nirvana is inherently perfected—pervasive, pure, and without center or periphery."
Allowing it to reflect its own essence as independent, any attempt to conceive of it is immediately erroneous. If even a single thought does not arise, the past and future limits are severed;

this is called "true and real. "True" means distinguishing from delusion; thus, it differs from ordinary people who are mired in confusion. They rely solely on deluded thoughts within the eight consciousnesses to practice giving, precepts, and so forth, taking these to be spiritual cultivation.

Having no source from which to lose the truth, one suddenly gives rise to delusion and fails to return; it spreads vast and boundless like a thin cloud covering the sky, its arrival having no point of origin, momentarily filling the six directions and shrouding all in darkness.
Suddenly a long wind arises, and in an instant everything is cleared away; for a thousand miles there is not a speck, and the myriad phenomena appear with vivid clarity.
When the wind of skillful means arises, it illuminates delusion so that the lack of inherent nature is revealed, and the multitude of beings are made manifest.
When the roots of virtue are perfected, the eighty thousand afflictions are all *pāramitās*; when the sands-of-the-Ganges of delusive obstructions are exhausted, this is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

If the cataracts of the eyes are not removed, empty flowers will arise in confusion; yet once the Dharma-eye is purified, what affliction will not be dissolved? If one remains stuck in rigid attachments, many kalpas will pass in vain.

it does not mean that at the time of awakening one has not yet cultivated, nor that the awakened mind is already cultivated [without effort]. It does not mean that there is no awakening during the time of cultivation; rather, [cultivation] must exist within the awakened mind.

Because cultivation is continuous, one awakens to this fruit in every thought-moment and cultivates this cause in every thought-moment; since these two occur simultaneously, cause and effect penetrate each other.
However, as the text would become cumbersome if written out in full, they have been arranged here in their proper sequence.
The upper section concludes with a direct exposition; the lower section addresses and resolves objections. An objection is raised as follows:

"If one has already attained Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment, why is it necessary to further progress through the stages and practice cultivation? The answer is: For all practitioners, it is essential to suddenly realize that the eight consciousnesses and the six sense objects are fundamentally non-existent;

this does not mean they were merely made non-existent through some process of deduction. Furthermore, the true, pure merits are fundamentally possessed; these are not something produced through cultivation.

This "new" [state] is like a person who is lost and mistakes the east for the west; the nature of the west is fundamentally non-existent, yet it is only after awakening that one realizes there was no east to begin with.

Although the original east is not something newly created after awakening, even so, because the habitual tendencies of greed and anger accumulated over countless kalpas arise spontaneously and are difficult to exhaust instantaneously, one must forcibly rely upon the true nature that has been realized as a provisional support.

By gradually cultivating supreme practices, one gradually eliminates that which was originally non-existent—the delusion. This is the arising of function from the essence, a provisional cultivation of that which is not to be cultivated;
it merely polishes the golden countenance within the mold and unrolls the sutra within the dust. Therefore, the *Commentary on the Profundity of Teaching and Transformation* states:

"A phantom person transforms a phantom; this is transformation without a transformer. Furthermore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says: "Cultivate practices like illusions and dispel [delusions] like..."
Furthermore, ancient masters have said: "Cultivate the myriad practices as illusory flowers; sit peacefully in a water-moon *bodhimanda*; subdue the celestial Māras who are like reflected images;
and realize the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream. These are all instances of forcibly and artificially practicing that which cannot be practiced;
therefore, it is said they are "like illusions and dreams. One need only understand that one's own mind is fundamentally the true essence, a luminous and penetrating clarity.
When one possesses clear and thorough knowledge, it is naturally understood that all things are like illusions and dreams and are not real.

If one practices in this manner—whether performing a single prostration, a single recitation, offering a single incense stick or flower, or even saving a single mosquito, a single gadfly, a single ant, or a single insect—the merit is boundless.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To practice for even a single thought-moment in accordance with reality is true requital."
It is because of the Buddha’s grace that Master Qingliang said, "A single hair's worth of goodness is inexhaustible even if the realm of space were to end"—this is precisely the meaning.

Furthermore, it is like the case of Su Liang, who suddenly attained the Way and immediately established ritual and music, yet gradually completed their full preparation. (This is like the descendants of the noble Gao family who, during a time of minor disorder, fell into servitude;

from birth they had never known their own nobility, but when the times cleared, their parents recognized them as being entirely noble men. This is like sudden awakening to the fact that one's very body is the Buddha; however, because one's conduct and habits cannot be changed all at once, one must cultivate gradually to abandon the state of an ordinary, base person.
Regarding the phrase "cessation and contemplation are of one substance" (*zhiguan yiti*), Qingliang says:
"The quiescence of the dharma-realm is called cessation (*shi*); being quiescent yet constantly illuminating is called contemplation (*guan*).

He further states: "To realize the function through the substance is itself contemplation; to realize the substance through the function is itself cessation. This is like a lamp: [the light is the function and the vessel is the substance].
Furthermore, because illumination is itself the lamp, they do not have separate entities;

otherwise, there would be a great fault. This refers to what the original text says: "If cessation and contemplation are not complete, then one will be unable to enter the path to Bodhi, which constitutes a great failure."
"Forever free from ill repute" means that within the Pure Land there is not even the name of actual evil realms, let alone actually undergoing suffering therein;
this is an illustration by way of contrast used to explain the main text, which states: "forever free from the evil paths."
"Immovable from meditative concentration" means that one does not waver or regress from this determination.
Regarding "generating a resolute mind" and so forth, these four types of minds correspond respectively to the four kinds of faults, such as doubt and fear.

Regarding the phrase "upholding, reciting, and so forth," the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* explains that there are ten distinct types of Dharma-practice (*dharmaparyāya*): preaching, listening, reciting, chanting, copying, making offerings, giving them away, reflecting, upholding, and cultivating.
Although this current treatise mentions only four practices for brevity, its intent encompasses all ten without omission. Any one of these ten possesses this merit.
Because this is clearly explained in the subsequent verses.
Regarding the phrase "this non-dual dharma" and so forth, the meaning is that because these superior fruits manifest as the divisions of those inferior causes,
they are called "the Buddhas."

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other such texts, the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) commentary states: "Extensively cultivating the myriad practices, one accords with reality to perfect virtue;
pervading the entire Dharma-realm, one realizes Bodhi. Just as a flower possesses the function of producing fruit, so too do practices possess the capacity to evoke the result.

Now, these matters are symbolized by means of concrete phenomena; thus, the flower is cited as a metaphor. "Adorning" (*yan*) refers to the perfection of practice and the attainment of fruition, which accords with the Principle.
It is called "ornament" (*yan*) because it manifests with brilliant clarity, wherein both the true nature and its characteristics are absent, and both subject and object are utterly severed.
This is because there can be no practice flowing from the True without being in accord with the True; how could there be a practice that adorns the True without arising from the True?

Thus, the True encompasses the extremities of delusion such that there is no practice not cultivated, and delusion penetrates to the source of the True such that there is no characteristic that is not quiescent. Therefore, it is called "Flower" (*hua*).
It is "strict" (*yan*).
Regarding "the perfectly round ocean," as stated in the preceding text, it refers to the "perfectly round ocean of inherent virtue" (*xingde yuanyman hai*).

The upper "round" belongs to the causal stage (*yin-fen*), while the lower "round" belongs to the resultant stage (*guo-fen*); because these are the "roundness of the round," it is called "perfectly round. Therefore, it is referred to above as the "perfectly round ocean."
It is not said that "perfect" (yuan) belongs solely to the lower perfection, for it is precisely that which is taken as the primary; thus it may also be "perfect and yet perfect.
This is like saying "mysterious and yet mysterious," meaning it reveals the fruit-aspect (*phalabhāga*) as being ultimate and uniquely honored.

Furthermore, while the upper perfection encompasses both cause and fruit aspects, the lower perfection takes only the fruit aspect; such a mental expression refers to the "perfection within perfection."
Regarding the phrase "because of being encompassed or not encompassed," the intended meaning is as follows: Vairocana is the cause and the Perfect Ocean (Enmei) is the fruit.
Within these three worlds, there are two divisions—cause and fruit—corresponding to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The fruit division is encompassed within the Perfect Ocean, while the cause division is encompassed within Vairocana. Now, Vairocana Buddha encompasses only that cause division which is not encompassed by the Perfect Ocean.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the main body [of the teaching] and its branches; the *Yi-fen-qi* (The Delimitation of Meaning) states:

"If it concerns the One Vehicle of the Separate Teaching, this body of Śākyamuni is not merely three bodies, but is also ten bodies, manifesting inexhaustibility. Furthermore, the basis for the realm of those ten Buddhas is twofold:
first, the land, and second, the ocean. Their perfect fusion and sovereign mastery are ultimately ineffable. (The former portion proves the fruit; the latter portion proves the cause.)
Regarding the two oceans of worlds, there are three [categories]: first, the Lotus Treasury Ocean of Worlds, which should be the realm of ten Buddhas and their equals;

second, beyond the triple-thousandfold world system, there are ten successive layers of worlds—such as the nature of worlds and oceans of worlds—which should be the realm of wheel-turning kings of ten thousand sons or more;
third, immeasurable worlds of various kinds, all of which pervade the Dharma-realm.
The realms, such as the tree-shaped world and others, all pervade the void of the *dharmadhātu* without mutually obstructing one another.
These three aforementioned stages are all places where the ten bodies of Vairocana manifest and transform beings; furthermore, these three stages are perfectly interfused and unobstructed.
Since each individual world possesses both coarse and subtle aspects, one should know that this is entirely distinct from the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This is the ninth section, "The Scope of Gathering and Transforming," within the text. Regarding the phrase "For example" and so forth:
the three successive metaphors clarify those three dharmas because they are equal like the earth, vast like the ocean, and clear like space;
thus, while the three characteristics differ slightly, there is no confusion between them.

"Entering into non-existence (*amātra*)" means that upon entering, one realizes it; thus, Qingliang says, "entering" is a term for thorough understanding and realization, while "non-existence" refers to emptiness.

This intent pertains to the emptiness of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), as it is signless (*animitta*). It is said that upon ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*), one initially realizes signless consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-kārikā* states: "When, with respect to an object of cognition, the intellect finds nothing at all to be apprehended, at that time one abides in consciousness-only, free from [dualistic grasping]."
This refers to the grasping of two marks. Furthermore, as the phrasing has not yet been fully resolved, it should be read as "monks" (*saṃgha*);
this is the Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya*.

As for "the tip of a hair," this refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where one advances or retreats according to conditions, like the tip of a hair on the ground being blown east or west by the wind.

Therefore, the "three corners" refer to the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the three levels of the virtuous), which are firmly established and free from regression, as they can withstand the force of the winds of affliction.

The "four roots" refer to the stage of application (*prayoga*), so called because they give rise to the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding "the bright mirror" and so forth, Qingliang says: "The holy teachings serve as a bright mirror to illuminate one's own mind; one's own mind serves as a lamp of wisdom to illuminate the profound meaning of the scriptures.

Regarding "facing the seventh consciousness" and so forth, this refers to the fact that the original treatise does not explicitly state the seventh *manas* consciousness, even though its presence is implied by the wording above.
Regarding the statement "now it is said 'approaching' (lin) the seven consciousnesses and so forth," "approaching" (lin) means "to illumine.
As for the letter *i* and so forth, this refers to the Sanskrit letter *i*, where two dots are above and one dot is below, forming the character *i*;
it signifies the three bodies (*trikāya*) of bodhi, the perfect realization of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Just as one who enters the Lake of Attainment (*prāptasaras*) and possesses the capacity for birth should have the four great rivers flow forth, so too does this treatise produce the four nirvāṇas.
Regarding the phrase "I [depart] from the self-abiding place of the Four Kings," the *Cāo* (Excerpts) quotes the treatise as saying: "I depart from the self-abiding places of the Four Kings. (2)
Fundamentally, all [versions] agree that the text explicitly states that beneath the base of Mount Sumeru lies the palace where the Nanda Dragon resides;
since the teachings of the entire period of the Buddha’s life were gathered there by the dragon, when the masters of this treatise reached the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
they sought out the base of Mount Sumeru and descended to the dragon palace— thus the treatise says.
Regarding the passage from the *Śāstra-saṃgraha* cited in the commentary which states, "If one recites the original text of the treatise with one's own mouth," and so forth:

these two sentences are not redundant. The former sentence corresponds to the investigation of the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), while the latter corresponds to the contemplation of the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*); thus, the two are distinct.
The phrase "the past sins of this person" refers to the transgressions of one who slanders the Dharma; it means there is no place where such faults can be extinguished.
This clarifies that among all great sins, none is greater than slandering the Dharma.

Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that even if one were to travel throughout the ten directions and pass through the three miserable realms again and again, one should hear this and be as cautious as if treading on thin ice; do not slander it.

Regarding the phrase "Therefore, etc.," this single verse now concludes the preceding discussion: the first half concludes the exhortation to faith, and the second half concludes the cessation of the preceding slander; thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "May one wish, etc.," the upper line refers to the inexhaustible time, while the lower line refers to the inexhaustible realm.

This clearly demonstrates that the compassionate vow was originally boundless; thus, Qingliang said: "When the gate of vows for all sentient beings is exhausted (the time), then the practice is fulfilled in every atom (the place)."
The verse says:
The section on the causes has been briefly explained; the section on the fruits cannot be fully proclaimed.
May all beings, both noble and ordinary, sink together into that ocean of fruition.
Commentary on the Mahāyāna by Śramaṇa Vasubandhu: A Draft for Penetrating the Profundities, Scroll Four (End)
